{{History of printing}}

A '''printing press''' is a machine that applies pressure to transfer ink onto a surface made of paper, cloth, or a similar material. Its workers are known as '''printing press operators'''.<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://www.google.com/books/edition/Bulletin_of_the_United_States_Bureau_of/W3DPB-b0c1AC?hl=en |title=Bulletin of the United States Bureau of Labor Statistics |date=1990 |publisher=U.S. Government Printing Office |pages=416–47}}</ref> It marked a significant improvement on earlier methods, in which the paper was rubbed by hand to transfer applied ink to the printing surface. 

The printing press was invented by the German goldsmith [[Johannes Gutenberg]] around 1440, and [[global spread of the printing press|its subsequent global spread]] revolutionized literary production and communication during the early modern period. The spread of printing brought about an era of [[mass communication]] in European society, allowing information to quickly spread across Europe and contributing to the [[Reformation#Printing|Reformation]] and the [[Scientific Revolution#Printing|Scientific Revolution]]. The cost of printed texts declined and their availability increased, facilitating higher adult literacy rates across Europe. Books increasingly appeared in [[vernacular language]]s rather than [[Latin]], and national languages were standardized.

The basic design of the wooden handpress was largely consistent for over three centuries, until the [[Industrial Revolution]]. By 1800 [[Charles Stanhope, 3rd Earl Stanhope|Lord Stanhope]] had built a new [[cast iron|iron]] printing press printing a sheet at one pull. In 1814, ''[[The Times]]'' adopted [[Friedrich Koenig]]'s new presses, which incorporated [[steam power]] and rotary motion. [[Richard M. Hoe]]'s [[rotary printing press]], introduced in 1843, enabled much higher output; later rotary presses could produce millions of page impressions in a day. During the twentieth century, the letterpress was largely replaced by [[offset printing]], [[phototypesetting]], and [[digital printing]] in commercial work.

== History ==
{{Main|History of printing}}

[[Johannes Gutenberg]] invented the movable-type printing press around 1440, utilizing four existing technologies: the [[screw press]], [[movable type]], the [[codex]] book format, and mechanized paper production.{{sfn|Man|2002|pp=26, 115, 136}}{{sfn|Childress|2008|pp=51–55}} The economic and cultural changes of [[late medieval]] Europe brought about viable commercial conditions for his press. The urban [[middle class]] grew alongside [[history of capitalism|trade and commerce]], while the growing number of [[Medieval university|universities]] since the twelfth century had increased demand for books. Hand-copying was slow and expensive, and by the fifteenth century, the supply of manuscripts was much less than the demand.<ref>{{sfn|Eisenstein|1980|pp=45–47}}; {{harvnb|Febvre|Martin|1997|pp=15–20}}; {{harvnb|Man|2002|p=87}}</ref> Gutenberg integrated these four technologies into a single working system and added a number of innovations of his own, including a [[hand mold]] for casting type and an oil-based ink suited to metal type.{{sfn|Childress|2008|pp=51–55}}

=== Technological factors ===
[[File:Holzspindelkelter von 1702.jpg|thumb|left|upright|alt=Large wooden screw press with various wooden bars and central screw|Early modern [[wine press]]. Such screw presses, used in Europe for a wide range of uses, provided Gutenberg with the model for his printing press.]]
The first factor, the screw press, permitted direct pressure to be applied on a flat plane. Used for a variety of tasks{{sfn|Wolf|1974|pp=21–35}} and [[Roman agriculture|introduced by the Romans]] in the 1st century AD, it was often used by farmers for [[pressing grapes]] to make wine and [[olive oil|olives to make oil]].<ref>{{harvnb|Onken|2009}}; {{harvnb|White|1984|pp=31ff.}}; {{harvnb|Schneider|2007|pp=156–159}}</ref> Gutenberg may also have been inspired by the paper presses which operated similarly to the screw press and were used across the [[Holy Roman Empire|German lands]] from the late 14th century.{{sfn|Schulte|1939|p=56}} He adopted the basic design of the screw press, thereby mechanizing the printing process.{{sfn|Wolf|1974|pp=39ff.}} Printing brought the machine different demands, and Gutenberg adapted the construction so that the [[platen]] (a flat surface) exerted even pressure across the paper with minimal smearing. Gutenberg introduced a movable undertable with a level surface on which the sheets could be swiftly changed.{{sfn|Wolf|1974|pp=39–46}}

{{multiple image|align=left|image1=metal movable type.jpg|width1=200|alt1=Rows of small metal letter blocks arranged in a wooden compartmented case, with some resting atop a tray|caption1=Movable type sorted in a letter case and loaded in a [[composing stick]] on top|image2=Gutenberg Bible, Lenox Copy, New York Public Library, 2009. Pic 01.jpg|width2=215|alt2=Museum-setting photograph of the Gutenberg Bible, a book with two columns per page|caption2=A paper codex of the 42-line Bible, Gutenberg's major work}}
Movable type is the [[typographical principle]] of writing a text from individual reusable characters. The Chinese artisan [[Bi Sheng]] invented the first movable type in the 11th century during the [[Song dynasty]], using characters made of baked clay.{{sfn|Wilkinson|2012|p=911}} Around 1300, [[Wang Zhen (inventor)|Wang Zhen]] developed a set of movable wooden type, arranged on revolving tables, which he used to print a local gazetteer. Wang wrote about his invention in his agricultural treatise.{{sfn|Wilkinson|2012|p=911}} Woodblock printing remained the primary method in East Asia. The oldest surviving book incorporating [[Type case|metal movable type]] is the ''[[Jikji]]'' dating to 1377, produced under the Korean state of [[Goryeo]].{{sfn|Wilkinson|2012|p=911}} However, none of the various East Asian methods gained widespread usage, largely due to their relative inefficiency. The [[logographic script]] used in China included thousands of distinct characters, resulting in high production costs for a full set of type.{{sfn|Wilkinson|2012|p=911}} The Gutenberg press benefited from its use of the [[Latin alphabet]] with a relatively small set of characters.<ref>{{harvnb|Childress|2008|pp=51–55}}; {{harvnb|Hellinga|2007|p=208}}: "Gutenberg's invention took full advantage of the degree of abstraction in representing language forms that was offered by the alphabet and by the Western forms of script that were current in the fifteenth century."</ref>

The codex book format also dated to the [[Roman Empire]],{{sfn|Roberts|Skeat|1983|pp=24–30}} and was of utmost significance in the history of the book. By 500 AD, Christian and Muslim scribes had shifted from using [[scroll]]s to using codices.<ref>{{harvnb|Roberts|Skeat|1983|pp=1, 38–67, 75}}: "The most momentous development in the history of the book until the invention of printing was the replacement of the roll by the codex; this we may define as a collection of sheets of any material, folded double and fastened together at the back or spine, and usually protected by covers." (p. 1)</ref> The codex proved more convenient than the scroll format because of its greater legibility, compact arrangement, lower costs, and the availability of both [[left and right pages]].<ref>{{harvnb|Roberts|Skeat|1983|pp=45–53}}</ref>

Medieval papermakers had successfully mechanized the production of paper. Water-powered [[paper mill]]s were in usage by 1282,{{sfn|Burns|1996|p=418}} resulting in much greater production and replacing the tedious processes associated with Chinese<ref>{{harvnb|Thompson|1978|p=169}}; {{harvnb|Tsien|1985|pp=68–73}}; {{harvnb|Lucas|2005|loc=p. 28, fn. 70}}</ref> and Muslim papermaking.<ref>{{harvnb|Thompson|1978|p=169}}; {{harvnb|Burns|1996|pp=414–417}}</ref> The number of papermaking centers grew rapidly in late 13th-century Italy, causing paper to become much cheaper than [[parchment]]. These centers became more common in Germany a century later.{{sfn|Burns|1996|p=417}}

However, the increased usage of paper was just as dependent on the rise of movable-type printing.<ref>{{harvnb|Febvre|Martin|1997|pp=41–44}}; {{harvnb|Burns|1996|p=419}}: "In the West, the only inhibiting expense in the production of writings for an increasingly literate market was the manual labor of the scribe himself. With his mechanization by movable-type printing in the 1440s, the manufacture of paper, until then relatively confined, began to spread very widely. The Paper Revolution of the thirteenth century thus entered a new era."</ref> Codices of parchment are superior in quality to any other [[writing material]],<ref>{{harvnb|Roberts|Skeat|1983|pp=7f.}}: "Despite all that has been said above, even the strongest supporters of papyrus would not deny that parchment of good quality is the finest writing material ever devised by man. It is immensely strong, remains flexible indefinitely under normal conditions, does not deteriorate with age, and possesses a smooth, even surface which is both pleasant to the eye and provides unlimited scope for the finest writing and illumination."</ref> and Gutenberg still made great use of them in his edition of the [[42-line Bible]].<ref>The ratio between paper and parchment copies is estimated at around 150 to 30 ({{harvnb|Hanebutt-Benz|2000|pp=158–189}}).</ref> After much experimentation, he concluded that the formula for an oil-based ink worked best for printing with metal type.{{sfn|Childress|2008|p=60}}

=== Gutenberg's press ===
{{See also|Letterpress printing}}
[[File:Printing press.jpg|thumb|alt=Engraving depicting a printing press with its screw, platen, and frame|Printing press, engraving by W Lowry after [[John Farey Jr.]], 1819]]
[[File:Printer in 1568-ce.png|thumb|alt=See caption|[[Woodcut]] depicting four printing press workers, 1568. The worker at front left collects a printed sheet from the press, the worker to his right inks another sheet, and two workers in the background work with metal movable type. shows the printer on the left removing a printed sheet while the printer on the right inks the type. In a working day, two men could perform 14,000 hand movements and produce {{circa|3,600}} impressions.<ref name="Wolf 1974, 67f."/>]]
Gutenberg began working on the printing press around 1436, when he partnered with the [[gemcutter]] Andreas Dritzehn and the paper miller Andreas Heilmann.{{sfn|Meggs|1998|pp=58–69}} The first known mention of Gutenberg's work is in a 1439 [[lawsuit]] against him which describes his types, type molds, and collection of metals.{{sfn|Meggs|1998|pp=58–69}} Gutenberg had formerly worked as a professional goldsmith, and had obtained knowledge of metals from that craft. He was the first to produce type from an alloy of [[lead]], [[tin]], and [[antimony]]. This alloy produced a particularly durable type suitable for high-quality printing. To create these lead types, Gutenberg used a special matrix that allowed him to rapidly and precisely mold new type blocks from a uniform template.{{sfn|Meggs|1998|pp=58–69}} His type case is estimated to have contained 290 separate letter boxes including special characters, [[typographic ligature|ligatures]], and [[punctuation marks]].{{sfn|Mahnke|2009|p=290}}

Gutenberg is also credited with introducing an oil-based ink, which was more durable than the previously used water-based inks. He used both paper and [[vellum]] (high-quality parchment) in his printing. He created a trial of color printing for a few of the page headings in the [[Gutenberg Bible]], present only in some copies.{{sfn|Kapr|1996|p=172}} The [[Mainz Psalter]] of 1453, likely designed by Gutenberg, featured elaborate red and blue printed initials and was published by his successors [[Johann Fust]] and [[Peter Schöffer]].{{sfn|Kapr|1996|p=203}}

=== Operation ===
A classical printing press is a stationary machine about {{convert|5|to|7|ft}} long, {{convert|3|ft}} wide, and {{convert|7|ft}} tall.{{sfn|Childress|2008|p=56}} A compositor set the type, the small individual metal letters, into the desired lines of text. Several lines were arranged at once and inserted into a wooden frame, the galley. Once the correct number of pages was composed, the galleys were laid face up in another frame called a forme, which rested on a flat stone, the bed.{{sfn|Lyons|2011|p=59}}

The type was inked using two pads of leather called [[ink ball]]s and mounted on wooden handles. The ink balls were stuffed with wool or horsehair, and the leather was usually sheepskin, but sometimes also calfskin and dogskin. The compositor pressed the ink balls together to distribute the ink evenly, and then applied the balls to the type. A sheet of dampened paper was held together by various small pins and two thin frames, the [[tympan]] and the [[frisket]]. The paper was placed on the tympan, and the frisket, which contained cut-out openings matching the type, was folded over the sheet to protect the margins from ink.{{sfn|Lyons|2011|p=59}}

The tympan and frisket were then folded down so that the paper rested on the inked type. The rounce (a small handle) and the [[windlass]] (a winch) were used to wind the bed under the platen. The compositor pulled a long lever, the bar, which drove a screw that pressed the platen onto the paper, and the elastic nature of the machine caused the bar to spring back after each pull. The rounce was then rotated in the opposite direction to move the bed away from the platen, the tympan and frisket were lifted, and the printed sheet was removed.{{sfn|Lyons|2011|p=59}} Human hand worked the entire process until the development in the early 19th century of iron presses, some of which could be operated by [[steam power]].{{sfn|Meggs|1998|pp=130–133}}

=== Mass production and spread in Europe ===
{{See also|List of early modern newspapers}}
[[File:Printing towns incunabula.svg|thumb|alt=Map of Europe with dots marking cities where printing presses were established by the end of the fifteenth century|The spread of printing in the 15th century from [[Mainz]], Germany]]
[[File:European Output of Printed Books ca. 1450–1800.svg|thumb|alt=Line graph showing European printed book output rising from near zero around 1450 to approximately one billion by 1800|European book output rose from a few million to around one billion copies within a span of less than four centuries{{sfn|Buringh|van Zanden|2009|loc=p. 417, table 2}}]]

Gutenberg's mechanical movable-type printing press, alongside consumer demand for printed copies of Bibles and other religious works, precipitated the widespread growth of the printing industry across Europe.{{sfn|Febvre|Martin|1997|pp=248–261}} Gutenberg's print shop in [[Mainz]] was originally the only one in Europe, but by the end of the 15th century around 270 European cities were involved in printing.<ref name="ISTC">{{cite web |url=http://www.bl.uk/catalogues/istc/index.html |title=Incunabula Short Title Catalogue |publisher=[[British Library]] |access-date=2 March 2011 |archive-date=12 March 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110312185857/http://www.bl.uk/catalogues/istc/index.html |url-status=live }}</ref> As early as 1480, there were printers active in 110 different places in Germany, Italy, France, Spain, the Netherlands, Belgium, Switzerland, England, Bohemia and Poland.{{sfn|Febvre|Martin|1997|pp=182–183}} The historians [[Lucien Febvre]] and [[Henri-Jean Martin]] conclude that by this date, the printed book was used throughout Europe.{{sfn|Febvre|Martin|1997|p=182}}

In Italy, a center of early printing, print shops existed in 77 cities and towns by 1500, while 151 locations in Italy had hosted printing at some point by 1600. In 1600, nearly 3,000 printers are known to have been active in Italy. However, printing centers soon emerged, and one third of the Italian printers published in [[Venice]].<ref>{{harvnb|Borsa|1976|p=314}}; {{harvnb|Borsa|1977|pp=166–169}}</ref>

By 1500, printing presses throughout Western Europe had produced over 20 million copies.{{sfn|Buringh|van Zanden|2009|p=417}} Their output grew to an estimated 150–200 million copies by 1600.{{sfn|Buringh|van Zanden|2009|p=417}} European printing presses {{circa|1600}} could produce between 1,500{{sfn|Pollak|1972}} and 3,600 impressions per workday.<ref name="Wolf 1974, 67f.">{{harvnb|Wolf|1974|pp=67f.}}: {{blockquote|From old price tables it can be deduced that the capacity of a printing press around 1600, assuming a fifteen-hour workday, was between 3,200 and 3,600 impressions per day.}}</ref> By comparison, with manual [[woodblock printing]],<ref>{{harvnb|Needham|1965|p=211}}: {{blockquote|The outstanding difference between the two ends of the Old World was the absence of screw-presses from China, but this is only another manifestation of the fact that this basic mechanism was foreign to that culture.}} {{harvnb|Widmann|1974|loc=p. 34, fn. 14}}: {{blockquote|In East Asia, both woodblock and movable type printing were manual reproduction techniques, that is hand printing.}} {{harvnb|Duchesne|2006|p=83}}; {{harvnb|Man|2002|pp=112–115}}: {{blockquote|Chinese paper was suitable only for calligraphy or block-printing; there were no screw-based presses in the east, because they were not wine-drinkers, didn't have olives, and used other means to dry their paper.}} Encyclopædia Britannica 2006: "Printing": {{blockquote|The second necessary element was the concept of the printing press itself, an idea that had never been conceived in the Far East.}}</ref> a skilled printer could print 1,500 to 2,000 double sheets per day. A printing block could be used for up to 25,000 prints with repairs.<ref>{{harvnb|Tsien|1985|p=201}}</ref> The Korean ''Kabin'' font metal movable type developed in 1434 could print 40 sheets per day.{{sfn|Oh|2013|p=108}} At least 750,000 copies of [[Erasmus]]'s works were sold during his lifetime (1469–1536),{{sfn|Issawi|1980|p=492}} while [[Martin Luther]] became Europe's most published author {{circa|1520}}, at the start of the [[Reformation]]. Printers across Germany reprinted 291 editions of Luther's 45 original works, and between 1518 and 1520 they distributed 300,000 printed copies of his works, with the widespread printing surprising both [[Pope Leo X|the pope]] and secular rulers.{{sfn|Pettegree|2015|p=104}}{{sfn|Duchesne|2006|p=83}}

Newspapers arose due to faster typographical production and falling costs (see ''[[Relation (journal)|Relation]]''), and provided a new means of conveying current information to the public.{{sfn|Weber|2006|pp=387f.}} The historian [[Andrew Pettegree]] argues that the Reformation directly contributed to the market for printed news. Printers who had gained readers from Luther's pamphlets kept them by producing news sheets discussing current events. These news pamphlets closely resembled the Reformation ''[[Flugschriften]]'' (printed pamphlets) in format, typically running to four or eight pages in [[quarto]]. In the early seventeenth century, a German publisher issued news bulletins on a regular schedule, creating the first weekly newspaper, and after the format spread it remained the principal news medium in northern Europe for over a century.{{sfn|Pettegree|2015|pp=336–337}} Many libraries in Europe and North America contain works printed before 1501, known as [[incunabula]].<ref name="ISTC"/><ref>The Incunabula Short Title Catalogue listed 29,777 separate ''editions'' (not copies) as of 8 January 2008, a total that includes some items printed after 1500. Bettina Wagner gives 28,107 editions published before 1501: {{cite book |last=Wagner |first=Bettina |chapter=Das Second-Life der Wiegendrucke. Die Inkunabelsammlung der Bayerischen Staatsbibliothek |editor1-last=Griebel |editor1-first=Rolf |editor2-last=Ceynowa |editor2-first=Klaus |title=Information, Innovation, Inspiration. 450 Jahre Bayerische Staatsbibliothek |publisher=K. G. Saur |location=Munich |year=2008 |isbn=978-3-598-11772-5 |pages=207–224 |language=de}} (figure at pp. 207–208).</ref>

=== Global spread ===
{{Main|Global spread of the printing press}}
The printing press spread rapidly across Europe largely because the equipment was portable, making censorship efforts difficult. When [[Theocracy|religious]] or government entities attempted to curtail the technology in one city, the printers would relocate to neighboring cities, further accelerating the press's spread across Europe.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Assange |first=Julian |url=http://archive.org/details/cypherpunksfreed0000assa |title=Cypherpunks : freedom and the future of the internet |date=2012 |publisher=[India] : Times Group Books |others=Internet Archive |isbn=978-93-82299-37-0}}</ref> Colonial and missionary networks spread the European-style printing press even farther, as [[Jesuit]] missionaries established a press at [[Old Goa|Goa]] in 1556 with João de Bustamante as its first printer.{{sfn|Lent|1980|pp=129–130}}<ref>{{cite book |last=Priolkar |first=Anant Kakba |title=The Printing Press in India: Its Beginnings and Early Development |year=1958 |publisher=Marathi Samshodhana Mandala |location=Bombay |pages=3–4}}</ref> The Portuguese Jesuit [[Diogo de Mesquita]] acquired a press during a visit to Europe in 1586 and maintained it at [[Nagasaki]], producing religious works in Japanese until his death in 1614.{{sfn|Lent|1980|p=119}} The [[Dominican Order|Dominicans]] set up the first press in the Philippines, publishing the ''[[Doctrina Christiana]]''.{{sfn|Lent|1980|p=120}} In the [[Ottoman Empire]], [[Sephardi Jews]] quickly established a Hebrew press in [[Constantinople]] in 1493, an Armenian press was established in 1567, and a Greek press in 1627, but [[İbrahim Müteferrika]] established the first Arabic-script press for a Muslim readership in 1727. [[Esad of Ioannina]] assisted Müteferrika in the development of his press, which produced seventeen works before 1742.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Watson |first=William J. |title=İbrāhīm Müteferriḳa and Turkish Incunabula |journal=Journal of the American Oriental Society |volume=88 |issue=3 |year=1968 |pages=435–441 |doi=10.2307/596868 |jstor=596868}}</ref> In the Americas, [[Juan Pablos]] established the first press in [[Mexico City]] in 1539, working on behalf of the Seville-based publisher Juan Cromberger, while British colonists established another press at [[Cambridge, Massachusetts]], in 1638.<ref>{{cite book |last=McMurtrie |first=Douglas C. |title=The Book: The Story of Printing & Bookmaking |publisher=Oxford University Press |year=1943 |edition=3rd |pages=141–143}}</ref>

=== Industrial printing presses ===
The overall design of the wooden handpress was largely consistent throughout its long history, but its construction and performance improved considerably over three centuries, with metal screws replacing wooden ones {{circa|1550}} and the tympan and frisket becoming standard fittings.{{sfn|Pollak|1972|pp=227–228}} Around 1620, the Dutch cartographer [[Willem Blaeu]] introduced a press with a more advanced hose arrangement and a more reliable mechanism for moving the type form into position beneath the platen,{{sfn|Pollak|1972|p=228}} and printers introduced further changes over the next two centuries. As new metal components were introduced, the straight lever bar was curved to facilitate its movement, and screw dimensions were adjusted to suit particular press sizes. By the closing years of the wooden-press era, the Ramage press enhanced the speed of printing by incorporating a mechanism that returned the platen automatically after each impression.{{sfn|Pollak|1972|pp=228–229}} According to one estimate, these improvements raised press productivity by a factor of three or four between the mid-15th and late-16th centuries.{{sfn|Pollak|1972|p=228}}

Several more innovations and improvements followed before the start of the Industrial Revolution. By 1800, [[Charles Stanhope, 3rd Earl Stanhope|Lord Stanhope]] had built the first iron printing press, which maintained the screw of the wooden hand press but increased the pressure from a single pull through a new arrangement of bar and spindle. To allow greater force on the frame, Stanhope cast the structure in iron.{{sfn|Moran|1973|pp=46–47}} The Stanhope press could print a whole sheet in one pull, its chief advantage over the wooden press, and did so with far less effort on the lever.{{sfn|Moran|1973|p=53}} It could print 480 pages per hour, double the output of the old press.{{sfn|Bolza|1967|p=80}}

The use of steam power for running the machinery and the rotary motion of cylinders also drastically altered the design of the printing press, and the German printer [[Friedrich Koenig]] successfully introduced both elements in his press designs developed between 1802 and 1818.{{sfn|Bolza|1967|p=88}} Koenig moved to London in 1806, where the printers [[Thomas Bensley]], [[George Woodfall]], and [[Richard Taylor (editor)|Richard Taylor]] financed his experiments.{{sfn|Moran|1973|p=105}} In 1810, Koenig patented a press in 1810 that operated on both a [[steam engine]] and the old platen. A machine made to this design entered operation in Bensley's office in April 1811, with the engineer [[Andreas Friedrich Bauer]] assisting.{{sfn|Moran|1973|p=105}} He patented his first cylinder machine in October 1811.{{sfn|Moran|1973|pp=105–106}}{{clarify|date=September 2026|reason=Who patented the machine?}} [[John Walter (editor, born 1776)|John Walter]] of ''[[The Times]]'' ordered two steam-driven double machines built under Koenig's patent of 1813, with ''The Times'' printing 1,100 sheets an hour on them from 29 November 1814.{{sfn|Moran|1973|pp=107–108}} A further patent of 1814 covered a perfecting machine that printed both sides of a sheet in one operation; the first example was completed in 1816.{{sfn|Moran|1973|pp=109–110}}

==== Rotary press ====
In the United States, [[Richard M. Hoe]] invented the steam-powered [[rotary printing press]] in 1843,{{sfn|Meggs|1998|p=147}} which could produce millions of copies of a page in a single day. The transition to rolled paper, with continuous feed, greatly increased the rate of the presses.<ref>{{Cite journal |date=1854-08-05 |title=Printing Press |url=https://doi.org/10.1038/scientificamerican08051854-372a |journal=Scientific American |volume=9 |issue=47 |pages=372–372 |doi=10.1038/scientificamerican08051854-372a |issn=0036-8733|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Hoe's original design produced up to 8,000 pages per, with 2,000 revolutions per hour each printing four page images.<ref>{{cite web |title=Richard March Hoe {{!}} American inventor and manufacturer |url=https://www.britannica.com/biography/Richard-March-Hoe |website=Encyclopedia Britannica |language=en |access-date=28 June 2020 |archive-date=25 July 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200725071617/https://www.britannica.com/biography/Richard-March-Hoe |url-status=live }}</ref> By 1891, ''[[The New York World]]'' and the ''Philadelphia Item'' were operating presses that produced either 90,000 four-page sheets per hour or 48,000 eight-page sheets.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Peck |first1=Harry Thurston |title=The International Cyclopædia A Compendium of Human Knowledge, Revised with Large Additions · Volume 12 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=9YpRAAAAYAAJ |year=1895 |publisher=Dodd, Mead & Company |access-date=28 June 2020 |page=168}}</ref>

In the mid-19th century, a separate class of [[jobbing presses]] emerged for small-format commercial work such as cards, [[billhead]]s, and leaflets. [[Stephen P. Ruggles]] pioneered the platen jobber in Boston from the 1830s, and [[George Phineas Gordon]] refined it. Gordon's Franklin press was so influential that by 1894 at least eleven firms were manufacturing Gordon-type presses, and James Moran estimates that between 1840 and 1940, no fewer than 123 different kinds of treadle-driven jobbers were made in the United States alone. The quick pace of the platen jobber made it a significant force in reshaping the printing trade during the 19th century.{{sfn|Moran|1973|pp=148–153}}

==== Machine composition ====
Type continued to be set by hand long after the press itself had been mechanized. Two hot-metal systems automated composition toward the end of the nineteenth century.<ref>{{Cite journal |date=1857-11-14 |title=Printing Press |url=https://doi.org/10.1038/scientificamerican11141857-75o |journal=Scientific American |volume=13 |issue=10 |pages=75–75 |doi=10.1038/scientificamerican11141857-75o |issn=0036-8733|url-access=subscription }}</ref> [[Ottmar Mergenthaler]]'s [[Linotype machine|Linotype]] operated on a keyboard and assembled matrices to cast a whole line of type at once, and it became widely used, while [[Tolbert Lanston]]'s 1887 [[Monotype System|Monotype]] cast single characters from hot metal. As most text was now machine set, hand-set foundry type went into decline, and machine composition remained standard until [[phototypesetting]] and [[Digital printing|digital]] methods displaced it in the later 20th century.{{sfn|Meggs|1998|p=134}}

=== Later developments ===
{{Main|Offset printing|Phototypesetting|Digital printing}}
During the 20th century, printing technology moved beyond the letterpress principle. [[Offset printing]], developed in the early 1900s, transfers an image from a plate to a rubber blanket and then to paper, and its speed and high quality made it the dominant commercial printing method by mid-century.<ref>{{cite encyclopedia |title=Printing - The 20th Century |url=https://www.britannica.com/topic/printing-publishing/The-20th-century |encyclopedia=Encyclopædia Britannica |access-date=27 March 2026 |archive-date=8 December 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251208051632/https://www.britannica.com/topic/printing-publishing/The-20th-century |url-status=live }}</ref> The introduction of phototypesetting in the 1960s and 1970s replaced hot-metal type composition with photographic methods, and the spread of [[desktop publishing]] software from the mid-1980s shifted much of the typesetting process to personal computers.<ref>{{cite book |last=Romano |first=Frank J. |title=Machine Writing and Typesetting |publisher=Graphic Arts Research Center, Rochester Institute of Technology |year=1986 |isbn=978-0-89938-016-2 |pages=xi–xii}}</ref> By the early 21st century, digital printing had made short-run and on-demand production commercially viable, while offset remained the standard for high-volume work.<ref>{{cite book |last=Kipphan |first=Helmut |title=Handbook of Print Media: Technologies and Production Methods |publisher=Springer |year=2001 |isbn=978-3-540-67326-2 |pages=6–12}}</ref>

== Impact ==
{{See also|Scientific Revolution#Printing|The Gutenberg Galaxy}}
The wide circulation of information and ideas due to the printing press has been called the "printing revolution", and the historian [[Elizabeth Eisenstein]] described the press as an "agent of change" across various societies. After its invention, books were produced and sold in greater numbers, authors were more closely associated with their works, reading became a more individualistic affair, and Latin declined as a scholarly language.{{sfn|Eisenstein|1980|pp=xv–xvi}} In 1997, [[Time Life]] selected Gutenberg's invention of the printing press as the most important event of the second millennium.<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://archive.org/details/lifemillennium1000frie/mode/1up |title=The Life Millennium: The 100 Most Important Events & People of the Past 1000 Years |date=1998 |publisher=Life Books, Time Inc.; distributed by Bulfinch Press |isbn=978-0-8212-2557-8 |editor=Friedman, Robert |page=[https://archive.org/details/lifemillennium1000frie/page/165/mode/1up 166] |access-date=20 March 2024}}</ref>

=== Authorship and reading ===
The printing press resulted in a greater association between authors and their texts, and the production of identical copies allowed for the precise citation of references and attached greater importance to individual authors and their exact words. For many works produced before the printing press, the name of the author has been entirely lost.{{sfn|Eisenstein|1980|pp=80–88}} The consistency of the printed page gave authors new encouragement to number pages and include [[tables of contents]] and [[Index (publishing)|indices]] in their books.{{sfn|Eisenstein|1980|pp=88–92}}

Reading habits also shifted, due to the lower cost and wider availability of printed texts compared to manuscripts. Individuals shifted away from communal oral recitation toward silent and private reading, marking what Eisenstein describes as a transition "from a hearing public to a reading public".{{sfn|Eisenstein|1980|pp=129–131}} A sermon or speech had required listeners to gather in one place at one time, whereas people scattered across a continent could read a printed text. The reading public was therefore highly individualistic, and its members often did not know each other.{{sfn|Eisenstein|1980|pp=131–133}} After the printing press was invented, wider availability of texts contributed to increasing adult literacy rates across Europe in the next two centuries, although the growth of literacy differed regionally.{{sfn|Febvre|Martin|1997|pp=262–265}}

By the end of the 15th century, printers had circulated editions of major classical works across Europe, and the printed book had come to play a central role in the diffusion of classical literature.{{sfn|Febvre|Martin|1997|pp=262, 265}} Many Greek scholars came to Italy after the collapse of the [[Byzantine Empire]], and between 1495 and 1515 the Venetian printer [[Aldus Manutius]] drew on their knowledge and published many Greek works in printed editions. Without the press, the equivalent recovery of Latin texts had taken over a century.{{sfn|Barker|1978|p=74}} Book production became increasingly commercial, and the first [[copyright]] laws were passed.{{sfn|Febvre|Martin|1997|pp=160–164}}

=== Science ===
The press also changed how [[natural philosophers]] worked. Although Latin scientific treatises rarely became bestsellers, the shift from script to print preceded the conceptual revolutions of the sixteenth century rather than following them. [[Ptolemy]]'s ''[[Almagest]]'', published in the 2nd century AD, remained authoritative as an astronomical text for some 1400 years before [[Copernicus]]'s ''[[De revolutionibus]]'' surpassed it in 1543, but ''De revolutionibus'' was surpassed in less than 100 years.{{clarify|date=September 2026|reason=Which work surpassed De revolutionibus}} According to Eisenstein, the shift emerged largely not due to the genius of the later investigators but the introduction of printing. Scholars had previously circulated discoveries individually through manuscript letters, but could now circulate them with printing to more people,<ref>{{cite book | last= Grant | first = Edward | author-link=Edward Grant | year = 2007 | chapter = The Transformation of Medieval Natural Philosophy from the Early Modern Period to the End of the Nineteenth Century |quote="Numerous...significant books...appeared in the late sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. Because they were produced by the printing press, these books were rapidly disseminated throughout Europe. Scholars in different countries studied the same mathematical and scientific diagrams and illustrations and read the same texts of a given author. Science was thus standardized in a way that was unimaginable before the 1450s."| title= A History of Natural Philosophy | url= https://archive.org/details/historynaturalph00gran | url-access= limited | page = 287 | location = New York | publisher = Cambridge University Press | isbn= 978-0-521-68957-1}}</ref> communicate faster with each other,<ref>{{cite book |last=Wootton |first=David |author-link=David Wootton (historian) |title=The Invention of Science: A New History of the Scientific Revolution |year=2015 |publisher=Harper |location=New York |isbn=978-0-06-175952-9 |pages=197–198 |quote=Printing made it possible for Brahe to survey a wide range of publications (there were over a hundred on the comet of 1577, though many were merely astrological prognostications) and demonstrate that the four best observers had produced results compatible with his own. It also ensured that Brahe's new system was quickly known throughout Europe, so that his arguments could be tested against the nova of 1604 and the comets of 1618. Printing created a community of astronomers working on common problems with common methods and reaching agreed solutions.}}</ref> and reach a wider geographical range.{{sfn|Eisenstein|1980|pp=453–455, 462–466}}

Printing also enabled the establishment of communities of scientists across Europe who could collaborate using shared methods. These communities had first appeared in the era of [[incunabula]], well before the first learned journals of the late 17th century. They incorporated the serial publication of new findings, allowed for data to survive across generations, and moved away from professional secrecy to encourage the public to read the written works and discuss them with authors and editors.{{sfn|Eisenstein|1980|p=462}} Hand-copied medical and botanical illustrations gradually degenerated, while printed copies of these illustrations preserved the detail. Observers such as [[Andreas Vesalius]] could now correct the visual record by circulating well-drawn illustrations alongside their texts.{{sfn|Eisenstein|1980|pp=469–470, 484–486}}

=== Politics, state and church ===
Governments adapted quickly to printing, using it to publish policies including treaties and declarations of war in pamphlet form.{{sfn|Eisenstein|1980|p=135}} In the 1530s, the English politician [[Thomas Cromwell]]'s campaign supporting [[Henry VIII]]'s break with the [[Catholic Church]] marked the first time a European government sought to exploit the press for propaganda. Cromwell got printers and publicists to issue vernacular tracts defending royal supremacy, while Parliament approved the religious split.{{sfn|Eisenstein|1980|p=312}} The French monarchy also printed tracts to evoke the [[homeland|patrie]] as the realm of France personified by the king. Printing thus allowed early modern states to carry out "psychological war" alongside military operations.{{sfn|Eisenstein|1980|p=135}}

Various Catholic clergy attempted to curtail the political reach of print provoked sustained efforts at control, starting with the Mainz archbishop's licensing edict of 1485 and followed by a 1515 papal decree requiring all translations to be vetted by bishops or inquisitors. The Counter-Reformation papacy expanded these restrictions, as [[Index Librorum Prohibitorum|Papal Indexes]] forbade lay Catholics to read certain books, including vernacular Bibles. Secular governments also introduced licensing systems for printing, and some jurisdictions banned imported books.{{sfn|Eisenstein|1980|pp=347–350}} These measures were only partially successful, as printed material easily crossed borders and many cities had secret presses. Over the next three centuries, authorities seeking to regulate the press often came into conflict with those seeking to circulate forbidden material.{{sfn|Eisenstein|1980|pp=347–350}} Pettegree argues that print was especially important in 16th-century religious conflicts such as [[French Wars of Religion]] and the [[Dutch Revolt]]. In territories which suppressed open Protestant proselytism, Reformed ideas reached the public through pamphlets, broadsheets and clandestine printing, and Catholics also used these mediums.{{sfn|Pettegree|2005}} Printed newspapers, pamphlets and bulletins later played a major ideological role in the events before the [[English Civil War]] and the [[American Revolution|American]] and [[French Revolution]]s, through.{{sfn|Bailyn|Hench|1981|pp=1–3}}

Quantitative work in economics has tested some of these claims. [[Jeremiah Dittmar]] has shown that over the 16th century, cities which had established presses by 1500 grew around 60 percent faster than comparable cities which had not. Separate regressions using distance from Mainz as an instrument for press adoption support that finding.{{sfn|Dittmar|2011|p=1133}} Also analyzing distance, Jared Rubin estimates that cities with presses before 1500 were 52 percent more likely to have adopted Protestantism by 1530, 42 percent more likely by 1560, and 29 percent by 1600. The declining effect suggests that the press mattered most in the early Reformation, before politics and the wider diffusion of printing took over.{{sfn|Rubin|2014|pp=270–271, 281}}

Sascha Becker, Steven Pfaff, and Jared Rubin distinguish between supply-side and demand-side accounts of the Reformation. Supply-side accounts emphasize institutional or technological factors such as the press; demand-side accounts emphasize the religious, political, and economic grievances that drew populations and rulers toward reform.{{sfn|Becker|Pfaff|Rubin|2016|pp=1–4}} However, Davide Cantoni finds that the religious policies of German princes were influenced by those of their immediate neighbors, rather than by print exposure alone.{{sfn|Cantoni|2012|p=502}} Another report notes that 36 percent of cities with documented contact with Luther had adopted the Reformation by 1530, compared with 6 percent of cities without contact. Its authors argue that personal ties and trade-route diffusion also contributed to religious conversions.{{sfn|Becker|Hsiao|Pfaff|Rubin|2020|p=861}} The press is now generally treated as one of several causes rather than the only one.{{sfn|Becker|Pfaff|Rubin|2016|pp=16–18}}

[[Benedict Anderson]] places printing in a longer arc of political change. He notes that in many states, people believed in a sacred script, the [[divine right of kings]], and the inseparability of time and cosmology. For Anderson, print-capitalism was crucial in challenging these beliefs. It replaced sacred languages with vernaculars and accustomed readers to news in homogeneous calendrical time.{{sfn|Anderson|2006|pp=36, 39–46}}

=== Contemporary criticism ===
Some contemporaries were critical of printing. Dominican friar Filippo de Strata, writing {{circa|1473}}, called the press a "whore" (''meretrix'') compared to the "virgin" pen, and argued that printers valued profit over accuracy and scholarship.{{sfn|Lee|2022}} In ''De laude scriptorum manualium'' (1492), Benedictine abbot [[Johannes Trithemius]] argued that printing would discourage books and that paper books were fragile compared to parchment manuscripts. He also stated that mechanical production of sacred text could not replace the spiritual discipline of hand-copying.{{sfn|Trithemius|Behrendt|1974}} In 1470, Florentine humanist Niccolò Perotti claimed that many printed books were inaccurate, while a decade later Gerolamo Squarzafico claimed that most printers were illiterate and Giorgio Merula worried that printing could harm classical scholarship. The Swiss physician [[Paracelsus]] promoted direct observation over book learning, although he made full use of print to broadcast his views.{{sfn|Eisenstein|1980|pp=474, 484–486}} Some critics were concerned that untrained readers might develop heretical ideas as they gained access to religious texts.{{sfn|Lee|2022}}

=== Language ===
As printing spread, Latin ceased to be the dominant language of publication. Authors wrote more frequently in the [[vernacular]] language of each region, and printed texts helped to standardize the spelling and syntax of these languages, reducing their variability. Febvre and Martin argue that printing contributed more than any other factor to the development of national languages. They also view printing as contributing to the rise of nationalism in Europe.{{sfn|Febvre|Martin|1997|pp=319–332}}

ARTICLE: Radio
WIKIPEDIA REVISION TEXT

{{short description|Use of radio waves for communication}}
{{About|the general technology|the audio application|Radio broadcasting|the device commonly known as a "radio"|Radio receiver|other uses}}
{{pp-move|small=yes}}
[[File:Radio towers on Sandia Peak - closeup.jpg|thumb|An [[antenna farm]] hosting various [[Antenna (radio)|radio antennas]] on [[Sandia Mountains|Sandia Peak]] near [[Albuquerque, New Mexico]], United States]]

'''Radio''' is the technology of [[telecommunication|communicating]] using [[radio wave]]s.<ref name="OED">{{Cite web |date=2019 |title=Radio |url=https://en.oxforddictionaries.com/definition/radio |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190324025858/https://en.oxforddictionaries.com/definition/radio |archive-date=24 March 2019 |access-date=26 February 2019 |website=Oxford Living Dictionaries |publisher=Oxford University Press}}</ref><ref name="PCMag">{{Cite encyclopedia |title=Definition of radio |encyclopedia=Encyclopedia |publisher=PCMagazine website, Ziff-Davis |url=https://www.pcmag.com/encyclopedia/term/50130/radio |access-date=26 February 2019 |date=2018 |archive-date=24 March 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190324025857/https://www.pcmag.com/encyclopedia/term/50130/radio |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="Ellingson-2016">{{Cite book |last=Ellingson |first=Steven W. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=QMKSDQAAQBAJ&pg=PA1 |title=Radio Systems Engineering |date=2016 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-1316785164 |pages=1–4}}</ref> Radio waves are [[electromagnetic wave]]s of [[frequency]] between 3&nbsp;[[hertz]] (Hz) and 300&nbsp;[[gigahertz]] (GHz). They are generated by an [[electronic device]] called a [[transmitter]] connected to an [[antenna (radio)|antenna]] which radiates the waves. They can be received by other antennas connected to a [[radio receiver]]; this is the fundamental principle of radio communication. In addition to communication, radio is used for [[radar]], [[radio navigation]], [[radio control|remote control]], [[remote sensing]], and other applications.

In '''radio communication''', used in radio and [[television broadcasting]], cell phones, [[two-way radio]]s, [[wireless network]]ing, and [[satellite communication]], among numerous other uses, radio waves are used to carry information across space from a transmitter to a receiver, by [[Modulation|modulating]] the radio signal (impressing an information signal on the radio wave by varying some aspect of the wave) in the transmitter. In radar, used to locate and track objects like aircraft, ships, spacecraft and missiles, a beam of radio waves emitted by a radar transmitter reflects off the target object, and the reflected waves reveal the object's location to a receiver that is typically colocated with the transmitter. In radio navigation systems such as [[GPS]] and [[VHF omnidirectional range|VOR]], a mobile navigation instrument receives radio signals from multiple [[radio beacon|navigational radio beacons]] whose position is known, and by precisely measuring the arrival time of the radio waves the receiver can calculate its position on Earth. In wireless [[radio control|radio remote control]] devices like [[drone (aircraft)|drone]]s, [[garage door opener]]s, and [[keyless entry system]]s, radio signals transmitted from a controller device control the actions of a remote device.

The existence of radio waves was first proven by German physicist [[Heinrich Hertz]] on 11 November 1886.<ref name="KIT" /> In the mid-1890s, building on techniques physicists were using to study electromagnetic waves, Italian physicist [[Guglielmo Marconi]] developed the first apparatus for long-distance radio communication,<ref name="ieeexplore.ieee.org">Bondyopadhyay, Prebir K.  (1995) "[https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/4137304/?tp=&arnumber=4137304 Guglielmo Marconi – The father of long distance radio communication – An engineer's tribute"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221014032424/https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/4137304?tp=&arnumber=4137304 |date=2022-10-14 }}, ''25th European Microwave Conference: Volume 2'', pp. 879–85</ref> sending a wireless [[Morse Code]] message to a recipient over a kilometer away in 1895,<ref name="1890s – 1930s: Radio">{{Cite web |title=1890s – 1930s: Radio |url=https://www.elon.edu/u/imagining/time-capsule/150-years/back-1890-1930/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220608035814/https://www.elon.edu/u/imagining/time-capsule/150-years/back-1890-1930/ |archive-date=8 June 2022 |access-date=14 July 2022 |publisher=[[Elon University]] |language=en-US}}</ref> and the first transatlantic signal on 12 December 1901.<ref name="IEEEatlantic">{{Cite web |last=Belrose |first=John S. |date=5–7 September 1995 |title=Radio's First Message -- Fessenden and Marconi |url=https://ewh.ieee.org/reg/7/millennium/radio/radio_differences.html |access-date=6 November 2022 |website=[[Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers]]}}</ref>  The first commercial radio broadcast was transmitted on 2 November 1920, when the live returns of the [[1920 United States presidential election]] were broadcast by Westinghouse Electric and Manufacturing Company in Pittsburgh, under the call sign [[KDKA (AM)|KDKA]].<ref name="History of Commercial Radio">{{Cite web |date=23 October 2020 |title=History of Commercial Radio |url=https://www.fcc.gov/media/radio/history-of-commercial-radio |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220101085855/https://www.fcc.gov/media/radio/history-of-commercial-radio |archive-date=1 January 2022 |access-date=14 July 2022 |publisher=[[Federal Communications Commission]] |language=en-US}}</ref>

The emission of radio waves is regulated by law, coordinated by the [[International Telecommunication Union]] (ITU), which allocates frequency bands in the [[radio spectrum]] for various uses.

==Etymology==
The word ''radio'' is derived from the Latin word ''radius'', meaning "spoke of a wheel, beam of light, ray." It was first applied to communications in 1881 when, at the suggestion of French scientist {{ill|Ernest Mercadier|fr}}, [[Alexander Graham Bell]] adopted ''radiophone'' (meaning "radiated sound") as an alternate name for his [[photophone]] optical transmission system.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=radio (n.) |url=https://www.etymonline.com/word/radio |access-date=13 July 2022 |website=Online Etymology Dictionary |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite magazine |last=Bell |first=Alexander Graham |date=July 1881 |title=Production of Sound by Radiant Energy |magazine=Popular Science Monthly |pages=329–330 |quote="[W]e have named the apparatus for the production and reproduction of sound in this way the "photophone", ''because an ordinary beam of light contains the rays which are operative.'' To avoid in future any misunderstandings upon this point, we have decided to adopt the term "''radiophone''", proposed by M. Mercadier, as a general term signifying the production of sound by any form of radiant energy..." |authorlink=Alexander Graham Bell}}</ref>

Following Hertz's discovery of the existence of [[radio waves]] in 1886, the term ''Hertzian waves'' was initially used for this radiation.<ref name=":2">{{Cite book |last=Manning |first=Trevor |title=Microwave Radio Transmission Design Guide |date=2009 |publisher=Artech House |page=2}}</ref> The first practical radio communication systems, developed by [[Marconi]] in 1894–1895, transmitted [[telegraph]] signals by radio waves,<ref name="KIT" /> so radio communication was first called ''[[wireless telegraphy]]''. Up until about 1910 the term ''wireless telegraphy'' also included a variety of other experimental systems for transmitting telegraph signals without wires, including [[electrostatic induction]], [[electromagnetic induction]] and [[Electrical conductor|aquatic and earth conduction]], so there was a need for a more precise term referring exclusively to electromagnetic radiation.<ref name="Maver">{{Cite book |last=Maver |first=William Jr. |url=https://archive.org/details/americantelegra02mavegoog |title=American Telegraphy and Encyclopedia of the Telegraph: Systems, Apparatus, Operation |date=1903 |publisher=Maver Publishing Co. |location=New York |page=[https://archive.org/details/americantelegra02mavegoog/page/n391 333] |quote=wireless telegraphy.}}</ref><ref name="Steuart">{{Cite book |last=Steuart |first=William Mott |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=x-cpAAAAYAAJ&q=%22wireless+telegraphy&pg=PA118 |title=Special Reports: Telephones and Telegraphs 1902 |date=1906 |publisher=U.S. Bureau of the Census |location=Washington D.C. |pages=118–119 |display-authors=etal}}</ref>

The French physicist [[Édouard Branly]], who in 1890 developed the radio wave detecting [[coherer]], called it in French a ''[[:fr:radioconducteur|radio-conducteur]]''.<ref name="earlyradiohistory.us">https://earlyradiohistory.us/sec022.htm {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191115034734/http://earlyradiohistory.us/sec022.htm |date=2019-11-15 }} Thomas H. White, United States Early Radio History, Section 22</ref><ref name=":3">{{Cite magazine |last=Collins |first=A. Frederick |date=10 May 1902 |title=The Genesis of Wireless Telegraphy |magazine=Electrical World and Engineer |page=811 |authorlink=Archie Frederick Collins}}</ref> The ''radio-'' prefix was later used to form additional descriptive compound and hyphenated words, especially in Europe. For example, in early 1898 the British publication ''The Practical Engineer'' included a reference to ''the radiotelegraph'' and ''radiotelegraphy''.<ref name="earlyradiohistory.us" /><ref>{{Cite magazine |date=25 February 1898 |title=Wireless Telegraphy |magazine=The Practical Engineer |page=174 |quote=" Dr. O. J. Lodge, who preceded Marconi in making experiments in what may be called "ray" telegraphy or radiotelegraphy by a year or two, has devised a new method of sending and receiving the messages. The reader will understand that in the radiotelegraph, electric waves forming the signals of the message start from the sending instrument and travel in all directions like rays of light from a lamp, only they are invisible."}}</ref>

The use of ''radio'' as a standalone word dates back to at least 30 December 1904, when instructions issued by the British Post Office for transmitting telegrams specified that "The word 'Radio'... is sent in the Service Instructions."<ref name="earlyradiohistory.us" /><ref>"Wireless Telegraphy", ''The Electrical Review'' (London), 20 January 1905, page 108, quoting from the British Post Office's 30 December 1904 ''Post Office Circular''.</ref> This practice was universally adopted, and the word "radio" introduced internationally, by the 1906 Berlin Radiotelegraphic Convention, which included a Service Regulation specifying that "Radiotelegrams shall show in the preamble that the service is 'Radio{{'"}}.<ref name="earlyradiohistory.us" />

The switch to ''radio'' in place of ''wireless'' took place slowly and unevenly in the English-speaking world. [[Lee de Forest]] helped popularize the new word in the United States—in early 1907, he founded the DeForest Radio Telephone Company, and his letter in the 22 June 1907 ''Electrical World'' about the need for legal restrictions warned that "Radio chaos will certainly be the result until such stringent regulation is enforced."<ref>"Interference with Wireless Messages", ''Electrical World'', 22 June 1907, page 1270.</ref> The United States Navy would also play a role. Although its translation of the 1906 Berlin Convention used the terms ''wireless telegraph'' and ''wireless telegram'', by 1912 it began to promote the use of ''radio'' instead. The term started to become preferred by the general public in the 1920s with the introduction of broadcasting.

==History==
{{main|History of radio}}
{{further|Invention of radio|Timeline of radio|History of broadcasting}}

[[Electromagnetic wave]]s were predicted by [[James Clerk Maxwell]] in his 1873 theory of [[electromagnetism]], now called [[Maxwell's equations]], who proposed that a coupled oscillating [[electric field]] and [[magnetic field]] could travel through space as a wave, and proposed that light consisted of electromagnetic waves of short [[wavelength]].  On 11 November 1886, German physicist [[Heinrich Hertz]], attempting to confirm Maxwell's theory, first observed radio waves he generated using a primitive [[spark-gap transmitter]].<ref name="KIT">{{Cite web |date=16 May 2022 |title=125 Years Discovery of Electromagnetic Waves |url=https://www.kit.edu/kit/english/pi_2011_8434.php |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220714163329/https://www.kit.edu/kit/english/pi_2011_8434.php |archive-date=14 July 2022 |access-date=14 July 2022 |publisher=[[Karlsruhe Institute of Technology]] |language=en-US}}</ref> Experiments by Hertz and physicists [[Jagadish Chandra Bose]], [[Oliver Lodge]], [[Lord Rayleigh]], and [[Augusto Righi]], among others, showed that radio waves like light demonstrated reflection, [[refraction]], [[diffraction]], [[Polarization (waves)|polarization]], [[standing wave]]s, and traveled at the same speed as light, confirming that both light and radio waves were electromagnetic waves, differing only in [[frequency]].<ref>Sungook Hong (2001), ''Wireless: From Marconi's Black-box to the Audion'', MIT Press, pp. 5–10</ref> In 1895, [[Guglielmo Marconi]] developed the first radio communication system, using a spark-gap transmitter to send [[Morse code]] over long distances.  By December 1901, he had transmitted across the Atlantic Ocean.<ref name="KIT" /><ref name="ieeexplore.ieee.org" /><ref name="1890s – 1930s: Radio" /><ref name="IEEEatlantic" />  Marconi and [[Karl Ferdinand Braun]] shared the 1909 Nobel Prize in Physics "for their contributions to the development of wireless telegraphy".<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023 |title=The Nobel Prize in Physics 1909 |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1909/summary/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260422044852/https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1909/summary/ |archive-date=22 April 2026 |access-date=31 July 2023 |publisher=[[NobelPrize.org]] |language=en}}</ref>

During radio's first two decades, called the [[radiotelegraphy]] era, the primitive radio transmitters could only transmit pulses of radio waves, not the continuous waves which were needed for audio [[modulation]], so radio was used for person-to-person commercial, diplomatic and military text messaging.  Starting around 1908, industrial countries built worldwide networks of powerful transoceanic transmitters to exchange [[telegram]] traffic between continents and communicate with their colonies and naval fleets.  During [[World War I]] the development of [[continuous wave]] radio transmitters, [[rectifying]] electrolytic, and crystal [[detector (radio)|radio receiver detectors]] enabled [[amplitude modulation]] (AM) [[radiotelephony]] to be achieved by [[Reginald Fessenden]] and others, allowing [[audio signal|audio]] to be transmitted. On 2 November 1920, the first commercial radio broadcast was transmitted by Westinghouse Electric and Manufacturing Company in Pittsburgh, under the call sign [[KDKA (AM)|KDKA]]. The broadcast featured live coverage of the [[1920 United States presidential election]].<ref name="History of Commercial Radio" />

==Principles==
Radio waves are radiated by [[electric charge]]s undergoing [[acceleration]].<ref name="Kraus">{{Cite book |last=Kraus |first=John D. |url=https://archive.org/details/Antennas2ndbyjohnD.Kraus1988/page/n75 |title=Antennas |date=1988 |publisher=Tata-McGraw Hill |isbn=0074632191 |edition=2nd |page=50}}</ref><ref name="Serway">{{Cite book |last1=Serway |first1=Raymond |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=CX0u0mIOZ44C&q=%22electromagnetic+wave%22+charge+acceleration&pg=PA714 |title=College Physics, 8th Ed. |last2=Faughn |first2=Jerry |last3=Vuille |first3=Chris |date=2008 |publisher=Cengage Learning |isbn=978-0495386933 |page=714}}</ref> They are generated artificially by time-varying [[electric current]]s, consisting of [[electron]]s flowing back and forth in a metal conductor called an [[antenna (radio)|antenna]].<ref name="Balanis">{{Cite book |last=Balanis |first=Constantine A. |url=https://archive.org/details/Antenna.Theory.Analysis.and.Design3rd.Edition |title=Antenna theory: Analysis and Design, 3rd Ed. |date=2005 |publisher=John Wiley and Sons |isbn=978-1118585733 |page=[https://archive.org/details/Antenna.Theory.Analysis.and.Design3rd.Edition/page/n22 10]}}</ref><ref name="Ellingson-2016a">{{Cite book |last=Ellingson |first=Steven W. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=QMKSDQAAQBAJ&q=%22radio+wave%22+time+varying+electric+current&pg=PA16 |title=Radio Systems Engineering |date=2016 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-1316785164 |pages=16–17}}</ref>

As they travel farther from the transmitting antenna, radio waves spread out so their [[signal strength]] ([[intensity (physics)|intensity]] in watts per square meter) decreases (see [[Inverse-square law]]), so radio transmissions can only be received within a limited range of the transmitter, the distance depending on the transmitter power, the antenna [[radiation pattern]], receiver sensitivity, [[Electromagnetic interference|background noise]] level, and presence of [[Line-of-sight propagation|obstructions between transmitter and receiver]].  An [[omnidirectional antenna]] transmits or receives radio waves in all directions, while a [[directional antenna]] transmits radio waves in a beam in a particular direction, or receives waves from only one direction.<ref name="Visser">{{Cite book |last=Visser |first=Hubregt J. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=rEs5dz1Zu7AC&q=radio+antenna+theory |title=Antenna Theory and Applications |publisher=[[John Wiley & Sons]] |year=2012 |isbn=978-1119990253 |access-date=29 August 2022}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Zainah Md Zain |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=t_LvDwAAQBAJ |title=Proceedings of the 11th National Technical Seminar on Unmanned System Technology 2019: NUSYS'19 |last2=Hamzah Ahmad |last3=Dwi Pebrianti |last4=Mahfuzah Mustafa |last5=Nor Rul Hasma Abdullah |last6=Rosdiyana Samad |last7=Maziyah Mat Noh |publisher=Springer Nature |year=2020 |isbn=978-9811552816 |page=535 |access-date=2022-08-27 |archive-date=2024-10-03 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003154123/https://books.google.com/books?id=t_LvDwAAQBAJ |url-status=live }} [https://books.google.com/books?id=t_LvDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA535 Extract of pp. 535–536] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003154112/https://books.google.com/books?id=t_LvDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA535#v=onepage&q&f=false |date=2024-10-03 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Hurley |first1=Chris |title=WarDriving and Wireless Penetration Testing |last2=Rogers |first2=Russ |last3=Thornton |first3=Frank |last4=Connelly |first4=Daniel |last5=Baker |first5=Brian |date=2007 |isbn=978-1-59749-111-2 |pages=31–61 |chapter=Understanding Antennas and Antenna Theory |doi=10.1016/B978-159749111-2/50027-1}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Neely |first1=Matthew |title=Wireless Reconnaissance in Penetration Testing |last2=Hamerstone |first2=Alex |last3=Sanyk |first3=Chris |date=2013 |isbn=978-1-59749-731-2 |pages=7–43 |chapter=Basic Radio Theory and Introduction to Radio Systems |doi=10.1016/B978-1-59-749731-2.00002-8}}</ref>

Radio waves travel at the [[speed of light]] in vacuum<ref>{{Cite web |title=Electromagnetic Radiation |url=https://lambda.gsfc.nasa.gov/product/suborbit/POLAR/cmb.physics.wisc.edu/tutorial/light.html#:~:text=Generally%20speaking%2C%20we%20say%20that,than%20the%20speed%20of%20light. |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160523101442/https://lambda.gsfc.nasa.gov/product/suborbit/POLAR/cmb.physics.wisc.edu/tutorial/light.html |archive-date=23 May 2016 |access-date=18 August 2022 |publisher=[[NASA]] |language=en-US}}</ref> and at slightly lower velocity in air.<ref name="Podesta">{{Cite book |last=de Podesta |first=M. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=h8BNvnR050cC&pg=PA131 |title=Understanding the Properties of Matter |publisher=CRC Press |year=2002 |isbn=978-0-415-25788-6 |page=131 |access-date=2024-09-23 |archive-date=2024-10-03 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003154115/https://books.google.com/books?id=h8BNvnR050cC&pg=PA131 |url-status=live }}</ref>

The other types of [[electromagnetic wave]]s besides radio waves, [[infrared]], [[visible light]], [[ultraviolet]], [[X-ray]]s and [[gamma rays]], can also carry information and be used for communication.  The wide use of radio waves for telecommunication is mainly due to their desirable [[radio propagation|propagation]] properties stemming from their longer wavelength.<ref name="Ellingson-2016a" /> Radio waves have the ability to pass through the atmosphere in any weather, foliage, and at longer wavelengths through most building materials.  By [[diffraction]], longer wavelengths can bend around obstructions, and unlike other electromagnetic waves, they tend to be scattered rather than absorbed by objects larger than their wavelength.

==Communication systems==
[[File:Signal processing system.png|thumb|upright=1.4|Radio communication.  Information such as sound is converted by a transducer, such as a [[microphone]], to an electrical signal, which modulates a [[radio wave]] produced by the [[transmitter]]. A receiver intercepts the radio wave and extracts the information-bearing modulation signal, which is converted back to a human-usable form with another transducer, such as a [[loudspeaker]].]]
[[File:Amfm3-en-de.gif|thumb|Comparison of AM and FM modulated radio waves]]

In radio communication systems, information is carried across space using radio waves.  At the sending end, the information to be sent is converted by some type of [[transducer]] to a time-varying [[electrical signal]] called the modulation signal.<ref name="Ellingson-2016a" /><ref name="HowStuffWorks">{{Cite web |last=Brain |first=Marshall |date=7 December 2000 |title=How Radio Works |url=http://electronics.howstuffworks.com/radio8.htm |access-date=11 September 2009 |publisher=HowStuffWorks.com |archive-date=2 October 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091002050151/http://electronics.howstuffworks.com/radio8.htm |url-status=live }}</ref> The modulation signal may be an [[audio signal]] representing sound from a [[microphone]], a [[video signal]] representing moving images from a [[video camera]], or a [[digital signal]] consisting of a sequence of [[bit]]s representing binary data from a computer.  The modulation signal is applied to a [[radio transmitter]].  In the transmitter, an [[electronic oscillator]] generates an [[alternating current]] oscillating at a [[radio frequency]], called the ''[[carrier wave]]'' because it serves to generate the radio waves that ''carry'' the information through the air.  The modulation signal is used to [[modulation|modulate]] the carrier, varying some aspect of the carrier wave, impressing the information in the modulation signal onto the carrier. Different radio systems use different modulation methods:<ref name="Faruque-2016">{{Cite book |last=Faruque |first=Saleh |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=AT3ADAAAQBAJ&q=radio+types+of+modulation |title=Radio Frequency Modulation Made Easy |publisher=[[Springer Publishing]] |year=2016 |isbn=978-3319412023 |access-date=29 August 2022 |archive-date=3 October 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003154100/https://books.google.com/books?id=AT3ADAAAQBAJ&q=radio+types+of+modulation#v=snippet&q=radio%20types%20of%20modulation&f=false |url-status=live }}</ref>
* [[Amplitude modulation]] (AM) – in an AM transmitter, the [[amplitude]] (strength) of the radio carrier wave is varied by the modulation signal;<ref name="Faruque-2016" />{{rp|3}}
* [[Frequency modulation]] (FM) – in an FM transmitter, the frequency of the radio carrier wave is varied by the modulation signal;<ref name="Faruque-2016" />{{rp|33}}
* [[Frequency-shift keying]] (FSK) – used in wireless digital devices to transmit [[digital signal]]s, the frequency of the carrier wave is shifted between frequencies.<ref name="Faruque-2016" />{{rp|58}}
* [[Orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing]] (OFDM) – a family of [[digital modulation]] methods widely used in high-bandwidth systems such as [[Wi-Fi]] networks, cellphones, [[digital television]] broadcasting, and [[digital audio broadcasting]] (DAB) to transmit digital data using a minimum of [[radio spectrum]] bandwidth.  It has higher [[spectral efficiency]] and more resistance to [[fading]] than AM or FM.  In OFDM, multiple radio carrier waves closely spaced in frequency are transmitted within the radio channel, with each carrier modulated with bits from the incoming [[bitstream]], so multiple bits are being sent simultaneously, in parallel.  At the receiver, the carriers are demodulated and the bits are combined in the proper order into one bitstream.<ref name="Ergen-2009">{{Cite book |last=Ergen |first=Mustafa |title=Mobile Broadband |date=2009 |isbn=978-0-387-68189-4 |doi=10.1007/978-0-387-68192-4}}{{pn|date=September 2024}}</ref>

Many other types of modulation are also used. In some types, the carrier wave is suppressed, and only one or both modulation [[sideband]]s are transmitted.<ref>Tony Dorbuck (ed.), ''The Radio Amateur's Handbook, Fifty-Fifth Edition'', American Radio Relay League, 1977, p. 368</ref>

The modulated carrier is [[amplifier|amplified]] in the transmitter and applied to a transmitting [[antenna (radio)|antenna]] which radiates the energy as radio waves.  The radio waves carry the information to the receiver location.<ref>John Avison, The World of Physics, Nelson · 2014, page 367</ref> At the receiver, the radio wave induces a tiny oscillating [[voltage]] in the receiving antenna{{snd}}a weaker replica of the current in the transmitting antenna.<ref name="Ellingson-2016a" /><ref name="HowStuffWorks" /> This voltage is applied to the [[radio receiver]], which [[amplifier|amplifies]] the weak radio signal so it is stronger, then [[demodulate]]s it, extracting the original modulation signal from the modulated carrier wave.  The modulation signal is converted by a [[transducer]] back to a human-usable form: an audio signal is converted to [[sound wave]]s by a loudspeaker or earphones, a [[video signal]] is converted to images by a [[display device|display]], while a digital signal is applied to a computer or microprocessor, which interacts with human users.<ref name="Faruque-2016" />

The radio waves from many transmitters pass through the air simultaneously without interfering with each other because each transmitter's radio waves oscillate at a different frequency, measured in [[hertz]] (Hz), [[kilohertz]] (kHz), [[megahertz]] (MHz) or [[gigahertz]] (GHz).  The receiving antenna typically picks up the radio signals of many transmitters.  The receiver uses ''[[tuned circuit]]s'' to select the desired radio signal out of all the signals picked up by the antenna and reject the others.  A tuned circuit acts like a [[resonator]], similar to a [[tuning fork]].<ref name="HowStuffWorks" /> It has a natural [[resonant frequency]] at which it oscillates.  The resonant frequency of the receiver's tuned circuit is adjusted by the user to the frequency of the desired radio station; this is called ''tuning''.  The oscillating radio signal from the desired station causes the tuned circuit to oscillate in sympathy, and it passes the signal on to the rest of the receiver.  Radio signals at other frequencies are blocked by the tuned circuit and not passed on.<ref>''C-W and A-M Radio Transmitters and Receivers'', United States. Department of the Army – 1952, pp. 167–168</ref>

===Bandwidth===
[[File:Modulated radio signal frequency spectrum.svg|thumb|[[Frequency spectrum]] of a typical modulated AM or FM radio signal.  It consists of a component ''C'' at the [[carrier wave]] frequency <math>f_c</math> with the [[modulated]] information contained in two narrow bands of frequencies called [[sideband]]s (''SB'') just above and below the carrier frequency. The bandwidth (''BW'') is the amount of spectrum occupied by the sidebands.]]

A modulated radio wave, carrying an information signal, occupies a range of frequencies. The information in a radio signal is usually concentrated in narrow frequency bands called [[sideband]]s (''SB'') just above and below the [[carrier wave|carrier]] frequency. The width in [[hertz]] of the frequency range that the radio signal occupies, the highest frequency minus the lowest frequency, is called its [[bandwidth (signal processing)|bandwidth]] (''BW'').<ref name="Faruque-2016" /><ref name="Spectrum101">{{Cite web |date=February 2016 |title=Spectrum 101 |url=https://www.nasa.gov/sites/default/files/atoms/files/spectrum_101.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170211001857/https://www.nasa.gov/sites/default/files/atoms/files/spectrum_101.pdf |archive-date=11 February 2017 |access-date=2 December 2019 |publisher=US National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)}}, p. 6</ref> For any given [[signal-to-noise ratio]], a given bandwidth can carry the same amount of information regardless of where in the radio frequency spectrum it is located; bandwidth is a measure of [[channel capacity|information-carrying capacity]]. The bandwidth required by a radio transmission depends on the data rate of the information being sent, and the [[spectral efficiency]] of the modulation method used; how much data it can transmit in each unit of bandwidth.  Different types of information signals carried by radio have different data rates.  For example, a television signal has a greater data rate than an [[audio signal]].<ref name="Faruque-2016" /><ref name="Pogorel-Girard">{{Cite book |last1=Pogorel |first1=Girard |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=BGjfWBG33t4C&q=radio+spectrum+management |title=The Radio Spectrum: Managing a Strategic Resource |last2=Chaduc |first2=Jean-Marc |publisher=[[Wiley (publisher)|Wiley]]) |year=2010 |isbn=978-0470393529 |access-date=29 August 2022 |archive-date=3 October 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003154057/https://books.google.com/books?id=BGjfWBG33t4C&q=radio+spectrum+management#v=snippet&q=radio%20spectrum%20management&f=false |url-status=live }}</ref>

The [[radio spectrum]], the total range of radio frequencies that can be used for communication in a given area, is a limited resource.<ref name="Spectrum101" /><ref name="Ellingson-2016" /> Each radio transmission occupies a portion of the total spectrum available.  Radio spectrum is regarded as an [[economic good]] which has a monetary cost and is in increasing demand.  In some parts of the radio spectrum, the right to use a frequency band or even a single radio channel is bought and sold for millions of dollars.  So there is an incentive to employ technology to minimize the spectrum used by radio services.<ref name="Pogorel-Girard" />

A slow transition from analog to [[digital radio]] transmission technologies began in the late 1990s.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Norberg, Bob |date=27 November 2022 |title=Digital Radio Is Coming, But Analog Isn't Dead Yet |url=https://www.theledger.com/story/news/2002/11/28/digital-radio-is-coming-but-analog-isnt-dead-yet/26029858007/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220903133917/https://www.theledger.com/story/news/2002/11/28/digital-radio-is-coming-but-analog-isnt-dead-yet/26029858007/ |archive-date=3 September 2022 |access-date=3 September 2022 |language=en-US |newspaper=[[The Ledger]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=13 October 2005 |title=Analogue To Digital: Radio Slow To Tune Into Transition |url=https://www.financialexpress.com/archive/analogue-to-digital-radio-slow-to-tune-into-transition/96138/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220903133628/https://www.financialexpress.com/archive/analogue-to-digital-radio-slow-to-tune-into-transition/96138/ |archive-date=3 September 2022 |access-date=3 September 2022 |language=en |newspaper=[[The Financial Express (India)|Financial Express]]}}</ref>  Part of the reason for this is that [[digital modulation]] can transmit more information in a given bandwidth than [[analog modulation]]; the modulation itself is more efficient and [[loss compression]] further improves efficiency. Digital modulation also has greater [[noise immunity]] than analog, associated [[digital signal processor]]s have more power and flexibility than analog circuits, and a wide variety of information can be transmitted using the same digital modulation.<ref name="Faruque-2016" />

Because it is a fixed resource which is in demand by an increasing number of users, the [[radio spectrum]] has become increasingly congested in recent decades, and the need to use it more effectively is driving many additional radio innovations such as [[trunked radio system]]s, [[spread spectrum]] (ultra-wideband) transmission, [[frequency reuse]], [[dynamic spectrum management]], frequency pooling, and [[cognitive radio]].<ref name="Pogorel-Girard" />

===ITU frequency bands===
The [[ITU]] arbitrarily divides the [[radio spectrum]] into 12 bands, each beginning at a wavelength which is a power of ten (10<sup>n</sup>)&nbsp;metres, with corresponding frequency of 3 times a power of ten, and each covering a decade of frequency or wavelength.<ref name="Ellingson-2016" /><ref name="ITU2016">{{Cite web |date=3 November 2016 |title=Radio Regulations, 2016 Edition |url=https://www.itu.int/dms_pub/itu-r/opb/reg/R-REG-RR-2016-ZPF-E.zip |access-date=9 November 2019 |publisher=International Telecommunication Union |format=PDF |archive-date=13 December 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211213121728/https://www.itu.int/dms_pub/itu-r/opb/reg/R-REG-RR-2016-ZPF-E.zip |url-status=live }} Article 2, Section 1, p.27</ref>  Each of these bands has a traditional name:<ref name="Nomenclature">{{Cite report |url=https://www.itu.int/dms_pubrec/itu-r/rec/v/R-REC-V.431-8-201508-I!!PDF-E.pdf |title=Nomenclature of the frequency and wavelength bands used in telecommunications |date=2015 |publisher=International Telecommunications Union |location=Geneva |docket=ITU-R V.431-8 |access-date=6 April 2023 |archive-date=3 October 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003154101/https://www.itu.int/dms_pubrec/itu-r/rec/v/R-REC-V.431-8-201508-I!!PDF-E.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref>
