| [[Ultra high frequency|Ultra<br />high frequency]] || UHF || 300–3,000&nbsp;MHz || 100–10&nbsp;cm
|- style="text-align:center;"
| [[Super high frequency|Super<br />high frequency]] || SHF || 3–30&nbsp;GHz || 10–1&nbsp;cm
|- style="text-align:center;"
| [[Extremely high frequency|Extremely<br />high frequency]] || EHF || 30–300&nbsp;GHz || 10–1&nbsp;mm
|- style="text-align:center;"
| [[Tremendously high frequency|Tremendously<br />high frequency]] || THF || 300–3,000&nbsp;GHz<br />(0.3–3.0&nbsp;THz) || 1.0–0.1&nbsp;mm
|}</div>
It can be seen that the [[bandwidth (signal processing)|bandwidth]], the absolute range of frequencies, contained in each band is not equal but increases exponentially as the frequency increases; each band contains ten times the bandwidth of the preceding band.<ref>{{Cite report |title=Communications-electronics Management of the Electromagnetic Spectrum |publisher=United States Department of the Army |page=2 |series=Headquarters, Department of the Army |year=1973}}</ref>

Though not defined by the ITU,<ref name="Nomenclature" /> the term ''tremendously low frequency'' (TLF) has been used for wavelengths from 1–3&nbsp;Hz (300,000–100,000&nbsp; km).<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Duncan |first1=Christopher |title=Advances in Computer Vision and Computational Biology |last2=Gkountouna |first2=Olga |last3=Mahabir |first3=Ron |date=2021 |publisher=Springer International Publishing |isbn=978-3030710507 |editor-last=Arabnia |editor-first=Hamid R. |series=Transactions on Computational Science and Computational Intelligence |location=Cham |pages=235–247 |language=en |chapter=Theoretical Applications of Magnetic Fields at Tremendously Low Frequency in Remote Sensing and Electronic Activity Classification |doi=10.1007/978-3-030-71051-4_18 |editor-last2=Deligiannidis |editor-first2=Leonidas |editor-last3=Shouno |editor-first3=Hayaru |editor-last4=Tinetti |editor-first4=Fernando G. |editor-last5=Tran |editor-first5=Quoc-Nam |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/10.1007/978-3-030-71051-4_18 |s2cid=238934419 |access-date=2023-04-06 |archive-date=2024-10-03 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003154056/https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-030-71051-4_18 |url-status=live }}</ref>

==Regulation==
{{further|Radio regulation}}
The airwaves are a resource shared by many users.  Two radio transmitters in the same area that attempt to transmit on the same frequency will interfere with each other, causing garbled reception, often to the extent that neither transmission may be received clearly.<ref name="Spectrum101" /> [[radio frequency interference|Interference]] with radio transmissions can not only have a high economic cost, but it can also be life-threatening (for example, in the case of interference with emergency communications or [[air traffic control]]).<ref name="CISA">{{Cite web |title=Radio Frequency Interference Best Practices Guidebook - CISA - Feb. 2020 |url=https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/publications/safecom-ncswic_rf_interference_best_practices_guidebook_2.7.20_-_final_508c.pdf |access-date=29 August 2022 |website=Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency SAFECOM/National Council of Statewide Interoperability Coordinators |publisher=USDepartment of Homeland Security}}</ref><ref name="Mazar">{{Cite book |last=Mazar (Madjar) |first=Haim |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ysqOCQAAQBAJ&q=radio+spectrum+management |title=Radio Spectrum Management: Policies, Regulations and Techniques |publisher=[[Wiley (publisher)|Wiley]] |year=2016 |isbn=978-1118511794 |access-date=29 August 2022 |archive-date=3 October 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003154124/https://books.google.com/books?id=ysqOCQAAQBAJ&q=radio+spectrum+management#v=snippet&q=radio%20spectrum%20management&f=false |url-status=live }}</ref>

To prevent interference between different users, the emission of radio waves is strictly regulated by national laws and coordinated by an international body, the [[International Telecommunication Union]] (ITU), which allocates bands in the [[radio spectrum]] for different uses.<ref name="Spectrum101" /><ref name="Ellingson-2016" /> Radio transmitters must be licensed by governments, under a variety of license classes depending on use, and are restricted to certain frequencies and power levels.  In some classes, such as radio and television broadcasting stations, the transmitter is given a unique identifier consisting of a string of letters and numbers called a ''[[call sign]]'', which must be used in all transmissions.<ref name="ITU1">{{Cite web |title=ARTICLE 19 Identification of stations |url=https://life.itu.int/radioclub/rr/art19.pdf |access-date=29 August 2022 |publisher=International Telecommunication Union |archive-date=3 October 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003154542/https://life.itu.int/radioclub/rr/art19.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref> In order to adjust, maintain, or internally repair radio transmitters, individuals must hold a government license, such as the [[general radiotelephone operator license]] in the US, obtained by taking a test demonstrating adequate technical and legal knowledge of safe radio operation.<ref name="FCC2">{{Cite web |date=6 May 2016 |title=Commercial Radio Operator Types of Licenses |url=https://www.fcc.gov/wireless/bureau-divisions/mobility-division/commercial-radio-operator-license-program/commercial-0 |access-date=29 August 2022 |website=Federal Communications Commission |archive-date=8 August 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210808110250/https://www.fcc.gov/wireless/bureau-divisions/mobility-division/commercial-radio-operator-license-program/commercial-0 |url-status=live }}</ref>

Exceptions to the above rules allow the unlicensed operation by the public of low power short-range transmitters in consumer products such as cell phones, [[cordless phone]]s, [[wireless device]]s, [[walkie-talkie]]s, [[citizens band radio]]s, [[wireless microphone]]s, [[garage door opener]]s, and [[baby monitor]]s. In the US, these fall under [[Part 15]] of the [[Federal Communications Commission]] (FCC) regulations.  Many of these devices use the [[ISM band]]s, a series of frequency bands throughout the radio spectrum reserved for unlicensed use.  Although they can be operated without a license, like all radio equipment, these devices generally must be [[Type approval|type-approved]] before the sale.<ref name="FCC4">{{Cite web |last=Dichoso |first=Joe |date=October 9, 2007 |title=FCC Basics of Unlicensed Transmitters |url=https://transition.fcc.gov/oet/ea/presentations/files/oct07/Oct_07-Basics_of_Unlicensed_Trans-JD.pdf |access-date=29 August 2022 |website=Federal Communications Commission |archive-date=29 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220829182256/https://transition.fcc.gov/oet/ea/presentations/files/oct07/Oct_07-Basics_of_Unlicensed_Trans-JD.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref>

[[Radio jamming]] is the deliberate radiation of radio signals designed to interfere with the reception of other radio signals.  Jamming devices are called ''signal suppressors'' or ''interference generators'' or just ''jammers''.<ref name=":0" /> During wartime, militaries use jamming to interfere with enemies' tactical radio communication. Since radio waves can pass beyond national borders, some [[totalitarian]] countries that practice censorship use jamming to prevent their citizens from listening to broadcasts from radio stations in other countries. Jamming is usually accomplished by a powerful transmitter that generates noise on the same frequency as the target transmitter.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" /> US Federal law prohibits the nonmilitary operation or sale of any type of jamming devices, including ones that interfere with GPS, cellular, Wi-Fi and police radars.<ref name=":3" />

==Applications==
{{main|Applications of radio}}
{{see also|Radio spectrum#Applications|Radio receiver#Applications}}
Radio has many practical applications, which include broadcasting, voice communication, data communication, radar, radiolocation, and remote control.

{{History of Italy}}
The '''Roman Empire''' was a state that dominated the [[Mediterranean]] and much of [[Europe]], [[Western Asia]], and [[North Africa]] during the [[classical antiquity|classical period]]. The [[Roman Republic]] had previously conquered most of these territories, which later came under permanent single-person rule following [[Octavian]]'s [[Rise of Augustus|rise to power]] and the establishment of the [[Principate|Augustan Principate]] in 27 BC. By the late 3rd century AD, the empire had been divided many times. The [[Fall of the Western Roman Empire|Western Roman Empire collapsed]] in 476 AD, whereas the [[Eastern Roman Empire]] (also known as the [[Byzantine Empire]]) persisted until the [[fall of Constantinople]] in 1453.<!-- Do not change link from Octavian to Augustus per [[WP:NOTBROKEN]]. His name was Octavian when he was made Roman Emperor. -->

By 100 BC, the [[city of Rome]] had [[Ancient Rome|expanded its rule]] from the [[Italian peninsula]] to most of the Mediterranean and beyond. However, it was severely destabilised by [[List of Roman civil wars and revolts|civil wars and political conflicts]], which culminated in the [[War of Actium|victory of Octavian]] over [[Mark Antony]] and [[Cleopatra]] at the [[Battle of Actium]] in 31 BC, and the subsequent conquest of the [[Ptolemaic Kingdom]] in Egypt. In 27 BC, the [[Roman Senate]] granted Octavian overarching military power ({{lang|la|[[imperium]]}}) and the new title of ''[[Augustus (title)|Augustus]]'', marking [[Constitutional reforms of Augustus|his accession]] as the [[Reign of Augustus|first Roman emperor]]. The vast [[Roman people|Roman]] territories were organized into [[senatorial province]]s, governed by [[proconsul]]s who were appointed by lot annually, and [[Imperial province|imperial]] provinces, which belonged to the emperor but were [[Legatus Augusti pro praetore|governed]] by [[legates]].

The [[History of the Roman Empire|first two centuries of the Empire]] saw unprecedented stability and prosperity known as the {{lang|la|[[Pax Romana]]}} ({{Literal translation|Roman Peace}}). Rome reached its [[Borders of the Roman Empire|greatest territorial extent]] under [[Trajan]] ({{Reign|98|117|era=AD}}), but increasing trouble and decline began under [[Commodus]] ({{Reign|180|192}}). In the 3rd century, the Empire underwent a [[Crisis of the Third Century|50-year crisis]] that threatened its existence due to civil war, [[Plague of Cyprian|plagues]] and barbarian invasions. The [[Gallic Empire|Gallic]] and [[Palmyrene Empire|Palmyrene]] empires broke away and a series of [[Barracks emperor|short-lived emperors]] led the Empire, which was later reunified under [[Aurelian]] ({{Reign|270|275}}). The civil wars ended with the victory of [[Diocletian]] ({{Reign|284|305}}), who set up two different imperial courts in the [[Greek East and Latin West]]. [[Constantine the Great]] ({{Reign|306|337}}), the first [[Constantine the Great and Christianity|Christian emperor]], moved the imperial seat from Rome to [[Names of Istanbul|Byzantium]] in 330, and renamed it [[Constantinople]]. The [[Migration Period]], involving [[Germanic–Roman contacts|large invasions by Germanic peoples]] and the [[Huns]], led to the decline of the [[Western Roman Empire]]. With the [[fall of Ravenna]] to the [[Heruli|Germanic Herulians]] and the [[deposition of Romulus Augustus]] in 476 by [[Odoacer]], the Western Empire finally collapsed. The [[Byzantine (Eastern Roman) Empire]] survived for another millennium with Constantinople as its [[Centres of governance in the Roman Empire|sole capital]], until [[Fall of Constantinople|the city's fall]] in 1453.{{efn|"After the capture of Constantinople, the capital of the Byzantine Empire became the capital of the Ottoman Empire. The Osmanli Turks called their empire the Empire of [[Rum]] (Rome) ({{Langx|ota|دولت علنإه روم|lit=Exalted State of Rome}})."<ref>{{Cite book |last=Roy |first=Kaushik |date=2015 |title=Military Transition in Early Modern Asia, 1400–1750: Cavalry, Guns, Government and Ships |series=Bloomsbury Studies in Military History Series |publisher=[[Bloomsbury Publishing|Bloomsbury]] |page=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=dSVnAwAAQBAJ&pg=PA37 37] |isbn=9781474264037 }}</ref>  In this sense, it could be argued that a "Roman" Empire survived until the early 20th century.}}

Due to the Empire's extent and endurance, its institutions and culture had [[legacy of the Roman Empire|a lasting influence]] on the development of [[history of Latin|language]], [[religion in ancient Rome|religion]], [[Roman art|art]], [[Ancient Roman architecture|architecture]], [[Latin literature|literature]], [[Ancient Roman philosophy|philosophy]], [[Roman law|law]], and [[Roman magistrate|forms of government]] across its territories. The rediscovery of [[Science in classical antiquity|classical science]] and [[Ancient Roman technology|technology]] (which formed the basis for [[Islamic science]]) in medieval Europe contributed to the [[Scientific Renaissance]] and [[Scientific Revolution]]. Rome's republican institutions have influenced the [[Maritime republics|Italian city-state republics]] of the medieval period, the early [[United States]], and modern democratic [[republic]]s.

[[File:Roman Empire map.ogv|thumb|Animated overview of the Roman territorial history from the [[Roman Republic|Republic]] until the fall of its last remnant (the [[Byzantine Empire]]) in 1453]]

===Transition from Republic to Empire===
{{Further|Roman Republic|Roman Kingdom}}
[[File:Augustus of Prima Porta (inv. 2290).jpg|thumb|upright|''[[Augustus of Prima Porta]]'']]
Rome had begun expanding shortly after the founding of the [[Roman Republic]] in the 6th century BC, though not outside the [[Italian Peninsula]] until the 3rd century BC. The Republic was not a nation-state in the modern sense, but a network of self-ruled towns (with varying degrees of independence from the [[Roman Senate|Senate]]) and provinces administered by military commanders. It was governed by annually elected [[Roman magistrate|magistrates]] ([[Roman consul]]s above all) in conjunction with the Senate{{r|n=Potter2009_179|r={{harvp|Potter|2009|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=g4ZmqsyC5kEC&pg=PA179 179]}}.}} The 1st century BC was a time of political and military upheaval, which ultimately led to rule by [[Roman emperor|emperors]].{{sfnp|Nicolet|1991|pp=1, 15}}{{sfnp|Hekster|Kaizer|2011|p=viii}}<ref>{{Cite book |last=Lintott |first=Andrew |author-link=Andrew Lintott |date=1999 |title=The Constitution of the Roman Republic |publisher=[[OUP]] |page=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=yaFPohP2lB8C&pg=PA114 114] |isbn=0198150687 }}{{br}} ^ {{Cite book |last=Eder |first=Walter |date=1993 |chapter=Augustus and the Power of Tradition: the Augustan Principate as Binding Link between Republic and Empire |editor-last1=Raaflaub |editor-first1=Kurt A. |editor-link1=Kurt Raaflaub |editor-last2=Toher |editor-first2=Mark |title=Between Republic and Empire: Interpretations of Augustus and His Principate |publisher=[[University of California Press|UCP]] |page=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=f6i6EAAAQBAJ&pg=PA98 98] |isbn=0-5200-8447-0 }}</ref> The consuls' military power rested in the Roman legal concept of ''[[imperium]]'', meaning "command" (typically in a military sense).<ref>{{Cite book |last=Richardson |first=John |title=Fines Provinciae |postscript=none }} in {{harvp|Hekster|Kaizer|2011|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=5eN5DwAAQBAJ&pg=PA10 10]}}.</ref> Occasionally, successful consuls or generals were given the honorary title ''[[imperator]]'' (commander); this is the origin of the word ''emperor'', since this title was always bestowed to the early emperors.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Richardson |first=John |title=Fines Provinciae |postscript=none }} in {{harvp|Hekster|Kaizer|2011|pp=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=5eN5DwAAQBAJ&pg=PA1 1-2]}}.</ref>{{efn|[[Augustus]] avoided any association with the ancient [[kings of Rome]]. Augustus had replaced his first name with ''Imperator'', a title regularly used by [[Julius Caesar]], thus becoming ''Imperator Caesar Augustus'', which further linked the title with his position. ''Imperator'' did not acquire the meaning of "ruler" until the late 1st century.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Morpurgo |first1=Arnaldo |last2=Cornell |first2=Tim |author-link2=Tim Cornell |title="imperator" |date=1999 |url=https://archive.org/details/the-oxford-classical-dictionary-simon-hornblower-antony-spawforth-1999_202405/page/750/mode/1up}} In {{harvp|''The Oxford Classical Dictionary'' (1999)||}}.</ref> Both ''[[Caesar (title)|Caesar]]'' and ''[[Augustus (title)|Augustus]]'' evolved into formal titles, the former denoting the heir and the latter the monarch. In some languages, ''Caesar'' became the origin of the word "[[emperor]]", such as in German (''[[Kaiser]]'') and some Slavic languages (''[[Tsar]]'').}}

Rome suffered a long series of internal conflicts, conspiracies, and [[Roman civil wars|civil wars]] from the late second century BC, (see [[Crisis of the Roman Republic]]) while greatly extending its power beyond Italy. In 44 BC [[Julius Caesar]] was briefly [[perpetual dictator]] before being [[Assassination of Julius Caesar|assassinated]] by a faction that opposed his concentration of power. This faction was driven from Rome and defeated at the [[Battle of Philippi]] in 42 BC by [[Mark Antony]] and Caesar's adopted son [[Octavian]]. Antony and Octavian [[Second Triumvirate|divided the Roman world]] between them, but this [[Rise of Augustus|did not last long]]. Octavian's forces defeated those of Mark Antony and [[Cleopatra]] at the [[Battle of Actium]] in 31 BC. In 27 BC the [[Roman Senate|Senate]] gave him the title ''[[Augustus (title)|Augustus]]'' ("venerated") and made him ''[[princeps]]'' ("foremost") with [[proconsul]]ar ''[[imperium]]'', thus beginning the [[Principate]], the first epoch of Roman imperial history. Although the republic stood in name, Augustus had all meaningful authority.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Syme |first=Ronald |author-link=Ronald Syme |date=1960 |orig-date=1939 |title=The Roman Revolution |publisher=[[OUP]] |pages=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=87M1DwAAQBAJ&pg=PA3 3–4] }}</ref> During his [[Reign of Augustus|40-year rule]], a new constitutional order emerged so that, upon his death, [[Tiberius]] would succeed him as the new ''[[de facto]]'' monarch.<ref>{{cite book |last=Eck |first=Werner |author-link=Werner Eck |date=2007 |translator=Deborah Lucas Schneider |title=The Age of Augustus |edition=2nd |publisher=[[Wiley-Blackwell]] |pages=[https://books.google.mn/books?id=QziqEAAAQBAJ&pg=PA148 148-58] |isbn=9781405151498 }}</ref>

===''Pax Romana''===
{{Main|Pax Romana}}

{{Multiple image
| total_width = 500
| header      = The so-called "[[Five Good Emperors]]" of 96–180 AD
| image1      = Bust of Emperor Nerva in lorica military cloak and paludamentum, Greek marble, 96 - 98 AD, Galleria degli Uffizi, Florence (19243236348).jpg
| caption1    = [[Nerva]] ({{R.|96|98}})
| image2      = Traianus Glyptothek Munich 72.jpg
| caption2    = [[Trajan]] ({{R.|98|117}})
| image3      = Bust Hadrian Musei Capitolini MC817.jpg
| caption3    = [[Hadrian]] ({{R.|117|138}})
| image4      = Antoninus Pius (Museo del Prado) 01.jpg
| caption4    = [[Antoninus Pius]] ({{R.|138|161}})
| image5      = (Toulouse) Buste cuirassé de Marc Aurèle agè - Musée Saint-Raymond Ra 61 b.jpg
| caption5    = [[Marcus Aurelius]] ({{R.|161|180}})
}}

The 200 years that began with Augustus's rule are traditionally regarded as the {{lang|la|[[Pax Romana]]}} ("Roman Peace"). The cohesion of the empire was furthered by a degree of social stability and economic prosperity that Rome had never before experienced. Uprisings in the provinces were infrequent and put down "mercilessly and swiftly".<ref>{{Cite book |last=Boatwright |first=Mary T. |author-link=Mary T. Boatwright |date=2000 |title=Hadrian and the Cities of the Roman Empire |publisher=[[Princeton University Press|PUP]] |pages=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=YmKmSTzToCMC&pg=PA4 4] |isbn=0691094934 }}</ref> The success of Augustus in establishing principles of dynastic succession was limited by his outliving a number of talented potential heirs. The [[Julio-Claudian dynasty]] lasted for four more emperors—[[Tiberius]], [[Caligula]], [[Claudius]], and [[Nero]]—before it yielded in 69 AD to the strife-torn [[Year of the Four Emperors]], from which [[Vespasian]] emerged as the victor. Vespasian became the founder of the brief [[Flavian dynasty]], followed by the [[Nerva–Antonine dynasty]] which produced the "[[Five Good Emperors]]": [[Nerva]], [[Trajan]], [[Hadrian]], [[Antoninus Pius]], and [[Marcus Aurelius]].<ref>{{cite EBO |short=yes |last1=Roy |first1=Gitanjali |last2=Rodriguez |first2=Emily |date=2007–2026 |title=Five Good Emperors |url=https://www.britannica.com/topic/Five-Good-Emperors |display-authors=1 }}</ref>

Among the so-called "Five Good Emperors", Hadrian ({{Reign|117|138}}) is particularly noted for consolidating the empire's frontiers and embarking on ambitious building projects throughout the provinces.{{r|n=EBO_Hudson2025|r={{cite EBO |short=yes |last=Hudson |first=Myles |date=2025 |title=What was Hadrian's relationship with his Jewish subjects? |url=https://www.britannica.com/story/what-was-hadrians-relationship-with-his-jewish-subjects }}}} In Judaea, which had long been the center of Jewish national and religious life, his reign marked a decisive turning point. After earlier Jewish resistance to Roman rule, Hadrian visited the region in 129/130 AD and refounded Jerusalem as the Roman colony Aelia Capitolina, naming it after his family (Aelius) and the Capitoline Triad.{{r|n=EBO_Aelia1998|r={{cite EBO |short=yes |last1=Zeidan |first1=Adam |last2=Young |first2=Grace |date=1998–2024 |title=Aelia Capitolina |url=https://www.britannica.com/place/Aelia-Capitolina |display-authors=1 }}}} The refoundation overlaid the destroyed Jewish city with a new Roman urban plan, and included the construction of a Temple to Jupiter on the site of the former Jewish Temple.{{r|EBO_Aelia1998}} Later tradition and archaeological evidence also indicate a Temple of Venus near the site of the [[Holy Sepulchre]].<ref>{{cite EBO |short=yes |last1=Dumper |first1=Michael |last2=Prawer |first2=Joshua |date=2026 |title=History of Jerusalem |url=https://www.britannica.com/place/Jerusalem/History |display-authors=1 }}</ref>

Hadrian's measures, combined with restrictions on Jewish practices, helped spark the [[Bar Kokhba Revolt]] (132–135 AD). After crushing the uprising, Roman forces expelled most Jews from Jerusalem, barring their entry except on certain days, and rebuilt the city as a statement of imperial power and domination.{{r|EBO_Hudson2025}} Most scholars consider Hadrianic Aelia to have been unwalled, with free-standing gate complexes (such as the northern gate beneath today's Damascus Gate) rather than a continuous defensive circuit.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Magness |first1=Jodi |author-link1=Jodi Magness |last2=Davies |first2=Gwyn |date=2023 |title=Jerusalem's Northern Defences Under Hadrian |journal=Palestine Exploration Quarterly |volume=155 |issue=3 |pages=204–216 |doi=10.1080/00310328.2022.2030609 |url=https://doi.org/10.1080/00310328.2022.2030609 }}</ref>

===Transition from classical to late antiquity===
{{Main|Later Roman Empire|Fall of the Western Roman Empire}}

{{See also|Barbarian kingdoms|Byzantine Empire}}
[[File:Invasions of the Roman Empire 1.png|upright=1.35|thumb|The [[Migration Period|Barbarian invasions]] consisted of the movement of (mainly) ancient [[Germanic peoples]] into Roman territory. Historically, this event marked the transition between [[classical antiquity]] and the [[Middle Ages]].]]

In the view of contemporary Greek historian [[Cassius Dio]], the accession of [[Commodus]] in 180 marked the descent "from a kingdom of gold to one of rust and iron",{{sfnp|Dio's Roman History||loc=Vol. 9, [https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Cassius_Dio/72*.html#ref25 Epitome of Book 72, 36.4] (pp. 67-9)}} a comment which has led some historians, notably [[Edward Gibbon]], to take Commodus' reign as the beginning of the [[Historiography of the fall of the Western Roman Empire|Empire's decline]].{{sfnp|Gibbon|1836|loc=Volume 1 - [https://www.gutenberg.org/files/25717/25717-h/25717-h.htm#chap04.2 Chapter 4: The Cruelty, Follies And Murder Of Commodus. Part II]}}{{sfnp|Goldsworthy|2009|p=[https://archive.org/details/howromefelldeath0000gold/page/50/mode/1up?q=involuntary 50]}}

In 212, during the reign of [[Caracalla]], [[Roman citizenship]] was granted to all freeborn inhabitants of the empire. The [[Severan dynasty]] was tumultuous; an emperor's reign was ended routinely by his murder or execution and, following its collapse, the Empire was engulfed by the [[Crisis of the Third Century]], a period of [[invasion]]s, [[civil strife]], [[Economic collapse|economic disorder]], and [[Plague of Cyprian|plague]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Brown |first=Peter |author-link=Peter Brown (historian) |date=1989 |orig-date=1971 |title=[[The World of Late Antiquity|The World of Late Antiquity - AD 150-750]] |publisher=[[W. W. Norton & Company|Norton]] |isbn=0393958035 |page=22 }}</ref> In defining [[periodization|historical epochs]], this crisis sometimes marks the transition from [[Classical Antiquity|classical]] to [[late antiquity]]. [[Aurelian]] ({{R.|270|275}}) stabilised the empire militarily and [[Diocletian]] reorganised and restored much of it in 285.{{sfnp|Goldsworthy|2009|pp=405–15}} Diocletian's reign brought the empire's most concerted effort against the perceived threat of [[early Christianity|Christianity]], the "[[Great Persecution]]".<ref>{{cite EBO |short=yes |last1=Cousin |first1=Jean |last2=Lotha |first2=Gloria |date=2001–2026 |title=Reorganization of the empire of Diocletian |url=https://www.britannica.com/biography/Diocletian/Reorganization-of-the-empire |display-authors=1 }}</ref>

Diocletian divided the empire into four regions, each ruled by a separate [[Tetrarchy|tetrarch]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Potter |first=David S. |author-link=David Stone Potter |date=2004 |title=The Roman Empire at Bay - AD 180-395 |publisher=[[Routledge]] |pages=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=qDVXRO1CFXAC&pg=PA296 296–8] |isbn=0415100585 }}</ref> Confident that he fixed the disorder plaguing Rome, he abdicated along with his co-emperor, but the Tetrarchy [[Civil wars of the Tetrarchy|collapsed shortly after]]. Order was eventually restored by [[Constantine the Great]], who became the first emperor to [[Constantine the Great and Christianity|convert to Christianity]], and who established [[Constantinople]] as the new [[Centres of governance in the Roman Empire|capital]] of the Eastern Empire. During the decades of the [[Constantinian dynasty|Constantinian]] and [[Valentinian dynasty|Valentinian]] dynasties, the empire was divided along an east–west axis, with dual power centres in Constantinople and Rome. [[Julian (emperor)|Julian]], who under the influence of his adviser [[Mardonius (philosopher)|Mardonius]] attempted to restore [[Religion in ancient Rome|Classical Roman]] and [[Hellenistic religion]], only briefly interrupted the succession of Christian emperors. [[Theodosius I]], the last emperor to rule over both East and West, died in 395 after making Christianity the [[Christianity as the Roman state religion|state religion]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Starr |first=Chester G. |author-link=Chester G. Starr |date=1991 |orig-date=1965 |title=A History of the Ancient World |edition=4th |publisher=[[OUP]] |pages=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=bA3kgtZU1iMC&pg=PA670 670–8] |isbn=0195066286 }}</ref>
[[File:Western and Eastern Roman Empires 476AD(3).svg|thumb|The Roman Empire by 476, noting western and eastern divisions]] [[File:The Roman Empire, AD 395.png|right|thumb|upright=1.15|The administrative divisions of the Roman Empire in 395 AD]]

===Fall in the West and survival in the East===
The [[Western Roman Empire]] began to [[Fall of the Western Roman Empire|disintegrate]] in the early 5th century. The Romans fought off all invaders, most famously [[Attila]],{{sfnp|Bury|1958|pp=[https://archive.org/details/historyoflaterro01buryuoft/page/295/mode/1up 295–7]}} but the empire had [[Migration Period|assimilated so many Germanic peoples]] of dubious loyalty to Rome that the empire started to dismember itself.{{sfnp|Bury|1958|pp=[https://archive.org/details/historyoflaterro01buryuoft/page/312/mode/1up 312–3]}} Most chronologies place the end of the Western Roman Empire in 476, when [[Romulus Augustulus]] was [[Deposition of Romulus Augustulus|forced to abdicate]] to the [[Germanic peoples|Germanic]] warlord [[Odoacer]].{{efn|name=Scholl2017_32_cite|"Odoacer, who dethroned the last Roman emperor Romulus Augustulus in 476, used neither the imperial insignia nor the colour purple; they were used exclusively by the emperor in Byzantium."<ref>{{Cite book |editor-last1=Scholl |editor-first1=Christian |editor-last2=Gebhardt  |editor-first2=Torben R. |editor-last3=Clauß |editor-first3=Jan |date=2017 |title=Transcultural approaches to the concept of imperial rule in the Middle Ages |publisher=[[Peter Lang (publisher)|Peter Lang]] |page=32 |isbn=9783631662199 |url=https://www.peterlang.com/document/1067766 }}</ref>}}<ref name="The Fall of Rome">{{Cite web |last=Peter |first=Heather |author-link=Peter Heather |date=2011 |title=The Fall of Rome |website=BBC |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/history/ancient/romans/fallofrome_article_01.shtml |access-date=22 August 2026 }}</ref>{{efn|"The patrician Orestes had married the daughter of Count Romulus, of Petovio in Noricum: the name of Augustus, notwithstanding the jealousy of power, was known at Aquileia as a familiar surname; and the appellations of the two great founders, of the city and of the monarchy, were thus strangely united in the last of their successors ..... The life of this inoffensive youth was spared by the generous clemency of Odoacer; who dismissed him, with his whole family, from the Imperial palace.".{{sfnp|Gibbon|1836|loc=Volume 3 - [https://www.gutenberg.org/files/25717/25717-h/25717-h.htm#linknoteref-36.125 Chapter 36: Total Extinction Of The Western Empire. Part V para 5]}}}}

Odoacer ended the Western Empire by declaring [[Zeno (emperor)|Zeno]] sole emperor and placing himself as Zeno's nominal subordinate. In reality, Italy was ruled by Odoacer alone.{{efn|name=Scholl2017_32_cite}}<ref name="The Fall of Rome"/>{{efn|"The republic (they repeat that name without a blush) might safely confide in the civil and military virtues of Odoacer; and they humbly request, that the emperor would invest him with the title of Patrician, and the administration of the diocese of Italy. ..... His vanity was gratified by the title of sole emperor, and by the statues erected to his honor in the several quarters of Rome; ..... He entertained a friendly, though ambiguous, correspondence with the patrician Odoacer; and he gratefully accepted the Imperial ensigns."{{sfnp|Gibbon|1836|loc=Volume 3 - [https://www.gutenberg.org/files/25717/25717-h/25717-h.htm#linknote-36.123 Chapter 36:Total Extinction Of The Western Empire. Part V para 4]}}}} The Eastern Roman Empire, called the [[Byzantine Empire]] by later historians, continued until the reign of [[Constantine XI Palaiologos]], the last Roman emperor. He died in battle in 1453 against [[Mehmed II]] and his [[Ottoman Empire|Ottoman]] forces during the [[Fall of Constantinople|siege of Constantinople]]. Mehmed II adopted the title of ''[[Kayser-i Rûm|caesar]]'' in an attempt to claim a connection to the former Empire.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Ozgen |first=Korkut |title=Mehmet II |website=TheOttomans.org |url=http://www.theottomans.org/english/family/mehmet2.asp |access-date=3 April 2007 |archive-date=30 April 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150430145544/http://www.theottomans.org/english/family/mehmet2.asp |url-status=live}}{{br}}^ {{Cite web |last=Cartwright |first=Mark |date=23 January 2018 |title=1453: The Fall of Constantinople |url=https://www.worldhistory.org/article/1180/1453-the-fall-of-constantinople |access-date=11 February 2020 |website=World History Encyclopedia |archive-date=12 April 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210412192442/https://www.worldhistory.org/article/1180/1453-the-fall-of-constantinople/ |url-status=live}}{{br}}^ {{harvp|Nicolle|2000|p=85}}.</ref> His claim was soon recognized by the [[Patriarchate of Constantinople]], but not by European monarchs.

==Geography and demography==
{{Main|Demography of the Roman Empire|Borders of the Roman Empire}}

{{Further|Classical demography}}
The Roman Empire was [[List of largest empires|one of the largest]] in history, with contiguous territories throughout Europe, North Africa, and the Middle East.{{sfnp|Kelly|2006|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=nV4uwy-Q7wUC&pg=PA3 3]}} The Latin phrase {{lang|la|imperium sine fine}} ("empire without end"{{sfnp|Nicolet|1991|p=29}}) expressed the ideology that neither time nor space limited the Empire. In [[Virgil]]'s ''[[Aeneid]]'', limitless empire is said to be granted to the Romans by [[Jupiter (god)|Jupiter]].{{sfnp|Nicolet|1991|p=29}}{{efn|"The conquer'd war is due, and the vast world is theirs."<ref>{{harvp|Virgil's_Aeneid||loc=Book [https://classics.mit.edu/Virgil/aeneid.9.ix.html IX], 880}}.</ref>}}<ref>{{Cite book |last=Mattingly |first=David J. |author-link=David Mattingly (archaeologist) |date=2011 |title=Imperialism, Power, and Identity: Experiencing the Roman Empire |publisher=[[Princeton University Press|PUP]] |page=[https://archive.org/details/imperialismpower0000matt/page/15/mode/1up 15] |isbn=9780691146058 }}.{{br}}^ {{cite book |last=Moretti |first=G. |date=1994 |chapter=The Other World and the 'Antipodes': The Myth of Unknown Countries between Antiquity and the Renaissance |editor-last1=Haase |editor-first1=Wolfgang |editor-last2=Reinhold |editor-first2=Meyer |editor-link2=Meyer Reinhold |title=The Classical Tradition and the Americas |volume=1 - European Images of the Americas and the Classical Tradition. Part 1 |publisher=[[de Gruyter]]  |page=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=I1LEmKPgJ8MC&pg=PA257 257] |isbn=9783110115727 }}.</ref>{{r|n=Southern2015_14_6|r={{Cite book |last=Southern |first=Patricia |author-link=Pat Southern |date=2015 |orig-date=2001 |title=The Roman Empire from Severus to Constantine |publisher=[[Routledge]] |pages=[https://archive.org/details/romanempirefroms0000sout/page/14/mode/1up 14–6] |isbn=9780415738088 }}}} This claim of universal dominion was renewed when the Empire came under Christian rule in the 4th century.{{Efn|[[Prudentius]] (348–413) in particular Christianizes the theme in his poetry.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Mastrangelo |first=Marc |date=2008 |title=The Roman Self in Late Antiquity: Prudentius and the Poetics of the Soul |publisher=[[JHUP]] |pages=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=DLFJHVaYmbkC&pg=PA73 73], [https://books.google.ca/books?id=DLFJHVaYmbkC&pg=PA203 203] |isbn=9780801887222 }}</ref> [[St. Augustine]], however, distinguished between the secular and eternal "Rome" in ''[[The City of God]]''. See also {{Citation |last=Fears |first=J. Rufus |chapter=The Cult of Jupiter and Roman Imperial Ideology |date=1981 |title=Aufstieg und Niedergang der römischen Welt |volume=II |issue=17.1 |author-link=J. Rufus Fears |page=136}}, on how Classical Roman ideology influenced Christian Imperial doctrine, {{Citation |last=Bang |first=Peter Fibiger |chapter=The King of Kings: Universal Hegemony, Imperial Power, and a New Comparative History of Rome |date=2011 |title=The Roman Empire in Context: Historical and Comparative Perspectives |publisher=John Wiley & Sons}} and the Greek concept of globalism (''[[ecumene|oikouménē]]'').}} In addition to annexing large regions, the Romans directly altered their geography, for example [[Deforestation during the Roman period|cutting down entire forests]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Mosley |first=Stephen |date=2010 |title=The Environment in World History |publisher=[[Routledge]] |at=loc. 1851 |isbn=9780203859537 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=mIFiAgAAQBAJ }}</ref>

[[Roman expansion]] was mostly accomplished under the [[Roman Republic|Republic]], though parts of northern Europe were conquered in the 1st century, when Roman control in Europe, Africa, and Asia was strengthened. Under [[Augustus]], a "global map of the known world" was displayed for the first time in public at Rome, coinciding with the creation of the most comprehensive [[political geography]] that survives from antiquity, the ''[[Geographica|Geography]]'' of [[Strabo]].{{sfnp|Nicolet|1991|pp=7-8}} When Augustus died, the account of his achievements (''[[Res Gestae Divi Augusti|Res Gestae]]'') prominently featured the geographical cataloguing of the Empire.{{sfnp|Nicolet|1991|pp=9, 16}} Geography alongside meticulous written records were central concerns of [[#Central government|Roman Imperial administration]].{{sfnp|Nicolet|1991|pp=10-1}}

[[File:Milecastle 39 on Hadrian's Wall.jpg|thumb|A segment of the ruins of [[Hadrian's Wall]] in northern England, overlooking [[Crag Lough]]]]
The Empire reached its largest expanse under [[Trajan]] ({{R.|98|117}}),{{r|Southern2015_14_6}} encompassing 5 million km<sup>2</sup>.{{r|Taagepera1979_125|TurchinAdamsHall2006_222}} The traditional population estimate of {{Nowrap|55–60 million}} inhabitants{{r|n=Kelly2006_1|r={{harvp|Kelly|2006|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=nV4uwy-Q7wUC&pg=PA1 1]}}.}} accounted for between one-sixth and one-fourth of the world's total population{{r|n=MorrisScheidel2009_184|r={{harvp|Morris|Scheidel|2009|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=XnDtcvRwsrgC&pg=PA184 184]}}.}} and made it the most populous unified political entity in the West until the mid-19th century.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Goldsmith |first=Raymond W. |author-link=Raymond W. Goldsmith |date=September 1984 |title=An Estimate of the Size And Structure of the National Product of the Early Roman Empire |journal=Review of Income and Wealth |volume=30 |issue=3 |pages=263–288 |doi=10.1111/j.1475-4991.1984.tb00552.x |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1475-4991.1984.tb00552.x }}</ref> 21st-century [[Classical demography#Demography of the Roman Empire|demographic studies]] have argued for a population peak from {{Nowrap|70 million}} to more than {{Nowrap|100 million}}.<ref name="Population and demography">{{Cite book |last=Scheidel |first=Walter |author-link=Walter Scheidel |date=April 2006 |title=Population and demography |series=Princeton/Stanford Working Papers in Classics |page=9 |url=http://www.princeton.edu/~pswpc/pdfs/scheidel/040604.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181113015918/http://www.princeton.edu/~pswpc/pdfs/scheidel/040604.pdf |archive-date=13 November 2018 |access-date=25 August 2026 }}{{br}}^ {{Cite journal |last1=Hanson |first1=Jack W. |last2=Ortman |first2=Scott G. |date=2017 |title=A systematic method for estimating the populations of Greek and Roman settlements |journal=Journal of Roman Archaeology |volume=30 |pages=301–324 |doi=10.1017/S1047759400074134 |s2cid=165770409 |url=https://doi.org/10.1017/S1047759400074134 }}</ref> Each of the three largest cities in the Empire—Rome, [[Alexandria]], and [[Antioch]]—was almost twice the size of any European city at the beginning of the 17th century.{{r|n=BowmanEtal2000_721|r={{harvp|Bowman|Garnsey|Rathbone|2000|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=mhNUGgG2eacC&pg=PA721 721]}}.}}

As the historian [[Christopher Kelly (historian)|Christopher Kelly]] described it:

{{Blockquote|Then the empire stretched from [[Hadrian's Wall]] in drizzle-soaked [[northern England]] to the sun-baked banks of the [[Euphrates]] in Syria; from the great [[Rhine]]–[[Danube]] river system, which snaked across the fertile, flat lands of Europe from the [[Low Countries]] to the [[Black Sea]], to the rich plains of the North African coast and the luxuriant gash of the [[Nile Valley]] in Egypt. The empire completely circled the [[Mediterranean]]&nbsp;... referred to by its conquerors as ''[[mare nostrum]]''—'our sea'.{{r|Kelly2006_1}}}}

[[File:The cities of the Roman world in the Imperial period.jpg|thumb|Roman cities in the Imperial period<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hanson |first1=Jack W. |last2=Ortman |first2=S.G. |last3=Lobo |first3=J. |date=2017 |title=Urbanism and the division of labour in the Roman Empire |journal=Journal of the Royal Society, Interface |volume=14 |issue=136 |doi=10.1098/rsif.2017.0367 |pmid=29142013 |pmc=5721147 }}</ref>]]

Trajan's successor [[Hadrian]] adopted a policy of maintaining rather than expanding the empire. Borders (''fines'') were marked, and the frontiers (''[[Limes (Roman Empire)|limites]]'') patrolled.{{r|Southern2015_14_6}} The most heavily fortified borders were the most unstable.{{sfnp|Hekster|Kaizer|2011|p=viii}} [[Hadrian's Wall]], which separated the Roman world from what was perceived as an ever-present [[barbarian]] threat, is the primary surviving monument of this effort.<ref>{{Cite book |editor-last=Woolf |editor-first=Greg |editor-link=Greg Woolf |date=2003 |title=Cambridge Illustrated History of the Roman World |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press|CUP]] |page=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=qO54sAEvDL4C&pg=PA340 340] |isbn=0521827752 }}{{br}}^ {{Cite book |last=Opper |first=Thorsten |date=2008 |title=Hadrian: Empire and Conflict |publisher=[[Harvard University Press|HUP]] |page=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=PI94DTyNRLkC&pg=PA64 64] |isbn=978-0674030954 }}{{br}}^ {{Cite book |last=Fields |first=Nic |date=2003 |title=Hadrian's Wall AD 122–410, which was, of course, at the bottom of Hadrian's garden |publisher=[[Osprey Publishing|Osprey]] |page=[https://archive.org/details/hadrianswallad120000fiel/page/35/mode/1up?q=Ultimately 35] |isbn=1841764302 }}</ref> In the eastern provinces, rural administration often relied on [[Diocletian boundary stones|inscribed boundary stones]] to demarcate land and regulate taxation.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Marom |first=Roy |author-link=Roy Marom |date=2025 |title=A Toponymic Reassessment of the Abil al-Qamḥ Diocletianic Boundary Stone: Identifying Golgol at al-Zūq al-Fauqānī |journal=Jerusalem Journal of Archaeological Research |volume=8 |pages=[https://jjar.huji.ac.il/sites/default/files/jjar/files/jjar08_03_marom.pdf 51–59] |url=https://escholarship.org/uc/item/80b199p2 }}{{br}}^ {{Cite journal |last1=Ecker |first1=Avner |last2=Leibner |first2=Uzi |date=2026 |orig-date=2025 |title='Diocletian oppressed the inhabitants of Paneas' (ySheb. 9:2): A New Tetrarchic boundary stone from Abel Beth Maacah |journal=Palestine Exploration Quarterly |volume=158 |issue=1 |pages=35–47 |doi=10.1080/00310328.2024.2435218 |issn=0031-0328 |url=https://doi.org/10.1080/00310328.2024.2435218 }}</ref>

==Languages==
{{Main|Languages of the Roman Empire}}

{{See also|Jireček Line}}

Latin and Greek were the main languages of the Empire,{{Efn|name=diglossia|It has been called a state of bilingualism but that's only true of the educated and so Bruno Rochette suggests it's more appropriate as a [[diglossia]] but concedes this still does not adequately explain it, as Greek was "high" against Latin's "super-high".{{sfnp|Rochette|2018|p=123}}   Latin experienced a period of spreading from the second century BC, and especially in the western provinces, but not as much in the eastern provinces.{{sfnp|Rochette|2011|pp=562–3}} In the east, Greek was always the dominant language, a leftover influence from the [[Hellenistic period]] that predates the Empire.<ref>{{harvp|Rochette|2018|p=108}}.{{br}}^ {{Cite book |last=Millar |first=Fergus |author-link=Fergus Millar |date=2006 |title=A Greek Roman Empire: Power and Belief under Theodosius II (408–450) |publisher=[[University of California Press|UCP]] |pages=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=0bowDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA14 14-5] |isbn=9780520253919 }}</ref>{{r|n=Treadgold1997_5_7|r={{harvp|Treadgold|1997|pp=[https://archive.org/details/historyofbyzanti0000trea/page/5/mode/1up 5–7]}}.}}}} but the Empire was deliberately multilingual.{{sfnp|Rochette|2018|p=117}} [[Andrew Wallace-Hadrill]] says "The main desire of the Roman government was to make itself understood".<ref>{{Cite book |last=Wallace-Hadrill |first=Andrew |author-link=Andrew Wallace-Hadrill |date=2010 |title=Rome's cultural revolution |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press|CUP]] |isbn=9780521721608 |edition=Reprinted w/corr. |page=60}}</ref> At the start of the Empire, knowledge of Greek was useful to pass as educated nobility and knowledge of Latin was useful for a career in the military, government, or law.{{sfnp|Dickey|2023|loc=References on p. [https://books.google.ca/books?id=uNXBEAAAQBAJ&pg=PA4 4 n. 8]}} Bilingual inscriptions indicate the everyday interpenetration of the two languages.<ref>{{harvp|Rochette|2011|p=556}}. ^ {{harvp|Adams|2003|p=[https://archive.org/details/j.-n.-adams-romanitas-2003/page/200/mode/1up 200]}}.</ref>

Latin and Greek's mutual linguistic and cultural influence is a complex topic.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Feeney |first=Denis |author-link=Denis Feeney |date=2016 |title=Beyond Greek: The Beginnings of Latin Literature |publisher=[[Harvard University Press|HUP]] |pages=[https://books.google.com/books?id=YQRuCwAAQBAJ&pg=PA10 10-2] |isbn=9780674055230 }}</ref> Latin words incorporated into Greek were very common by the early imperial era, especially for military, administration, and trade and commerce matters.{{sfnp|Dickey|2023|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=uNXBEAAAQBAJ&pg=PA651 651]}} Greek grammar, literature, poetry and philosophy shaped Latin language and culture.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Batstone |first=William W. |date=2006 |chapter=Literature |editor-last1=Rosenstein |editor-first1=Nathan |editor2-last=Morstein-Marx |editor2-first=Robert |title=A Companion to the Roman Republic |edition=1 |publisher=[[Wiley-Blackwell]] |isbn=9781444334135 |pages=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=6BOQZirLCWgC&pg=PA543 543–564] }}{{br}}^ {{harvp|Freeman|2000|p=[https://archive.org/details/greekachievement0000free/page/438/mode/1up?q=Rawson 438]}}.</ref>

[[File:P.Ryl. I 61.tif|thumb|upright=1.4|left|A 5th-century [[papyrus]] showing a parallel Latin-Greek text of a speech by [[Cicero]]<ref>{{cite book |editor-last=Hunt |editor-first=Artur S. |date=1911 |chapter= |title=Catalogue of the Greek Papyri in the John Rylands Library, Manchester |volume=I - Literary Terxts 1-61 |publisher=[[Manchester University Press|MUP]] / [[Bernard Quaritch|Bernard Quaritch, and Sherratt and Huches]] |at=Plate 8 ([[recto]]), pa. 61. [[Cicero]]'s [[In Catilinam]] II.14-15, pp. [https://archive.org/details/catalogueofgreek01johnuoft/page/193/mode/1up 193-4] }}</ref>]]
There was never a legal requirement for Latin in the Empire, but it represented a certain status.<ref>{{Harvb|Adams|2003|pp=[https://archive.org/details/j.-n.-adams-romanitas-2003/page/188/mode/1up 188], [https://archive.org/details/j.-n.-adams-romanitas-2003/page/197/mode/1up 197]}}. ^ {{harvp|Freeman|2000|p=[https://archive.org/details/greekachievement0000free/page/394/mode/1up?q=interpreter 394]}}. ^ {{harvp|Rochette|2011|p=549}}.</ref> High standards of Latin, ''[[Classical Latin|Latinitas]]'', started with the advent of Latin literature.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Bloomer |first=W. Martin |date=1997 |title=Latinity and Literary Society at Rome |publisher=[[University of Pennsylvania Press|UPP]] |page=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=7PmACgAAQBAJ&pg=PA4 4] |isbn=9780812233902 }}</ref> Due to the flexible language policy of the Empire, a natural competition of language emerged that spurred ''Latinitas'', to defend Latin against the stronger cultural influence of Greek.{{sfnp|Rochette|2018|p=122}} Over time Latin usage was used to project power and a higher social class.<ref>{{Cite book |last=La Bua |first=Giuseppe |date=2019 |title=Cicero and Roman education: the reception of the speeches and ancient scholarship |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press|CUP]] |pages=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=r-GCDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA330 329 ff.] |isbn=9781107068582}}</ref>{{sfnp|Adams|2003|p=[https://archive.org/details/j.-n.-adams-romanitas-2003/page/205/mode/1up 205]}} Most of the emperors were bilingual but had a preference for Latin in the public sphere beginning during the [[Punic Wars]].{{sfnpm|Rochette|2023|1p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=i2HjEAAAQBAJ&pg=PA263 263], 268|Rochette|2018|2pp=114–5, 118}} Different emperors up until Justinian would attempt to require the use of Latin in the administration but there is no evidence that a linguistic imperialism existed during the early Empire.{{sfnp|Rochette|2018|p=107}}

After all freeborn inhabitants were universally [[wikt:enfranchise|enfranchised]] in [[Constitutio Antoniniana|212]], many Roman citizens lacked a knowledge of Latin.{{sfnp|Adams|2003|pp=[https://archive.org/details/j.-n.-adams-romanitas-2003/page/185/mode/1up 185–6], 205}} The wide use of [[Koine Greek]] was what enabled the spread of Christianity and reflects its role as the [[lingua franca]] of the Mediterranean during the time of the Empire.{{r|Treadgold1997_5_7}} Following Diocletian's reforms in the 3rd century AD, there was a decline in the knowledge of Greek in the west.{{sfnp|Rochette|2018|pp=108–9}} Spoken Latin later fragmented into the incipient [[romance languages]] in the 7th century AD following the collapse of the Empire's west.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Carlton |first=Charles Merritt |date=2017 |orig-date=1973 |title=A linguistic analysis of a collection of late Latin documents composed in Ravenna between A.D. 445–700. A quantitative approach |edition=Reprinted |publisher=[[De Gruyter]] |page=37 |doi=10.1515/9783111636221 |isbn=9783111254029 |access-date=17 August 2023 |url=https://doi.org/10.1515/9783111636221 }}</ref>{{efn|According to Mario Pei  (1976), the decisive moment came with the Islamic conquest of North Africa and Iberia, which was followed by numerous raids on land and by sea. All this had the effect of disrupting connections between the western Romance-speaking regions.<ref>{{cite book |last=Pei |first=Mario A. |author-link=Mario Pei |date=1976 |title=The Story of Latin and the Romance Languages |publisher=[[Harper (publisher)#Harper & Row (1962–1990)|Harper & Row]] |pages=76–81 |isbn=9780060133122 }}</ref>}}

The dominance of Latin and Greek among the literate elite obscures the continuity of other spoken languages within the Empire.{{r|n=Miles2000_58_60|r={{Cite book |last=Miles |first=Richard |chapter=Communicating Culture, Identity, and Power |date=2000 |editor=Janet Huskinson |title=Experiencing Power: Culture, Identity and Power in the Roman Empire |publisher=[[Routledge]] |pages=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=I3_1VjpbvKcC&pg=PA58 58–60] |isbn=0415212847 }}}} Latin, referred to in its spoken form as [[Vulgar Latin]], gradually replaced [[Celtic languages|Celtic]] and [[Italic languages]].<ref>{{harvp|Rochette|2011|p=550}}.{{br}}^ {{Cite book |last=Zimmer |first=Stefan |chapter=Celtic Languages |date=2006 |editor-last=Koch |editor-first=John T. |editor-link=John T. Koch |title=Celtic Culture: A Historical Encyclopedia |volume=1 of 5 (A-Celti) |publisher=[[ABC-Clio]] |page=[https://archive.org/details/celticculturehis0001unse/page/372/mode/1up 372 §4] |isbn=1851094407 }}</ref><ref name="curchin">{{Cite journal |last=Curchin |first=Leonard A. |date=Autumn 1995 |title=Literacy in the Roman Provinces: Qualitative and Quantitative Data from Central Spain |journal=The American Journal of Philology |volume=116 |issue=3 |pages=461–476 (464) |doi=10.2307/295333 |jstor=295333 }}</ref> References to interpreters indicate the continuing use of local languages, particularly in Egypt with [[Coptic language|Coptic]], and in military settings along the Rhine and Danube. Roman [[jurist]]s also show a concern for local languages such as [[Punic language|Punic]], [[Gaulish]], and [[Aramaic]] in assuring the correct understanding of laws and oaths.{{sfnp|Rochette|2011|pp=558–9}} In [[Africa (Roman province)|Africa]], Libyco-Berber and Punic were used in inscriptions into the 2nd century.{{r|Miles2000_58_60}} In [[Syria (Roman province)|Syria]], [[Palmyra|Palmyrene]] soldiers used their [[Palmyrene dialect|dialect of Aramaic]] for inscriptions, an exception to the rule that Latin was the language of the military.{{sfnp|Adams|2003|p=[https://archive.org/details/j.-n.-adams-romanitas-2003/page/199/mode/1up 199]}} The last reference to Gaulish was between 560 and 575.{{efn|"''Veniens vero Arvernos, delubrum illud, quod Gallica lingua Vasso Galatæ vocant, incendit, diruit, atque subvertit.'' And coming to Clermont [to the [[Arverni]]] he [ [[Chrocus]]] set on fire, overthrew and destroyed that shrine which they call Vasso Galatæ in the Gallic tongue."<ref>{{cite book |last=Gregory of Tours |author-link=Gregory of Tours |date=1927 |orig-date=c. 590 |title=The History of the Franks |volume=2 |translator=O. M. Dalton |translator-link=O. M. Dalton |publisher=[[The Clarendon Press]] |at=[https://archive.org/details/historyoffranks0002greg/page/22/mode/1up Book I, 32] }}</ref>}}{{efn|Le déclin du Gaulois et sa disparition ne s'expliquent pas seulement par des pratiques culturelles spécifiques: Lorsque les Romains conduits par César envahirent la Gaule, au 1er siecle avant J.-C., celle-ci romanisa de manière progressive et profonde. Pendant près de 500 ans, la fameuse période gallo-romaine, le gaulois et le latin parlé coexistèrent; au VIe siècle encore; le temoignage de Grégoire de Tours atteste la survivance de la langue gauloise.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Hélix |first=Laurence |date=2011 |title=Histoire de la langue française |language=fr |location=[[Paris]] |publisher=Ellipses |page=7 |isbn=9782729864705 }}</ref>}} The emergent [[Gallo-Romance languages]] would then be shaped by Gaulish.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Guiter |first=Henri |date=1995 |chapter=Sur le substrat gaulois dans la Romania |language=fr |editor-last=Bochnakowa |editor-first=Anna |editor-last2=Widlak |editor-first2=Stanislan |title=Munus amicitae. Studia linguistica in honorem Witoldi Manczak septuagenarii |publisher=Jagiellonian University |pages=61–67 |isbn=8323309272 |chapter-url=https://archive.org/details/munusamicitiaest0000unse/page/61/mode/1up?q=actual }}{{br}}^ {{Cite book |last=Roegiest |first=Eugeen |date=2006 |title=Vers les sources des langues romanes: Un itinéraire linguistique à travers la Romania |language=fr |location=[[Leuven]] |publisher=Acco |page=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=hMdz09HGd8kC&pg=PA83 83] |isbn=9033460947 }}{{br}}^ {{Cite book |last=Savignac |first=Jean-Paul |date=2004 |title=Dictionnaire français-gaulois |publisher=La Différence |page=26 |edition=French |isbn=2729115293 }}{{br}}^ {{Cite book |last=Matasović |first=Ranko |author-link=Ranko Matasović |date=2007 |chapter=Insular Celtic as a Language Area |editor=Hildegard L. C. Tristram |title=The Celtic Languages in Contact Papers from the Workshop Within the Framework of the XIII International Congress of Celtic Studies, Bonn, 26-27 July 2007 |publisher=[[University of Potsdam]] Verlag |page=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=VgBtaDT-evYC&pg=PA106 106] |isbn=9783940793072 }}{{br}}^ {{Cite book |last=Adams |first=J. N. |date=2007 |chapter=Ch. V – Regionalisms in provincial texts: Gaul |title=The Regional Diversification of Latin 200 BC – AD 600 |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press|CUP]] |pages=[https://archive.org/details/regionaldiversif0000adam/page/279/mode/1up?q=1526A 279]–289 |isbn=9780521881494 }}</ref> [[Proto-Basque]] or [[Aquitanian language|Aquitanian]] evolved with Latin loan words to modern [[Basque language|Basque]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Trask |first=Robert L. |author-link=R. L. Trask |date=1997 |title=The history of Basque |publisher=[[Routledge]] |page=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=lbLbAAAAQBAJ&pg=PA411 411] |isbn=0415131162 |oclc=34514667}}</ref> The [[Thracian language]], as were several now-extinct languages in Anatolia, are attested in Imperial-era inscriptions.{{r|Treadgold1997_5_7|Miles2000_58_60}}

==Society==
{{Further|Ancient Roman society}}
[[File:Pompeii family feast painting Naples.jpg|thumb|A multigenerational banquet depicted on a wall painting from [[Pompeii]] (1st century AD)]]

The Empire was multicultural, with "astonishing cohesive capacity" to create shared identity while encompassing diverse peoples.{{sfnp|Peachin|2011|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=RDSI1V12ueIC&pg=PA12 12]}} Public monuments and communal spaces open to all—such as [[Forum (Roman)|forums]], [[List of Roman amphitheatres|amphitheatres]], [[Roman circus|racetracks]] and [[thermae|baths]]—helped foster a sense of "Romanness".{{sfnp|Peachin|2011|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=RDSI1V12ueIC&pg=PA16 16]}}

Roman society had multiple, overlapping [[Social class in ancient Rome|social hierarchies]].{{sfnp|Peachin|2011|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=RDSI1V12ueIC&pg=PA9 9]}} The civil war preceding Augustus caused upheaval,{{r|n=GarnseySaller2015_107_11|r={{Cite book |last1=Garnsey |first1=Peter |author-link1=Peter Garnsey |last2=Saller |first2=Richard P. |author-link2=Richard Saller |date=2015 |title=The Roman Empire: Economy, Society and Culture |publisher=[[University of California Press|UCP]] |pages=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=h6owDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA107 107–11] |isbn=9780520285989 }}}} but did not effect an immediate [[redistribution of wealth]] and social power. From the perspective of the lower classes, a peak was merely added to the social pyramid.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Noreña |first=Carlos F. |date=2011 |title=Imperial Ideals in the Roman West: Representation, Circulation, Power |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press|CUP]] |page=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=kyiQIv_ZvJYC&pg=PA7 7] |isbn=9781107005082 }}</ref> Personal relationships—[[Patronage in ancient Rome|patronage]], friendship (''amicitia''), [[Family in ancient Rome|family]], [[Marriage in ancient Rome|marriage]]—continued to influence politics.{{sfnp|Peachin|2011|pp=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=RDSI1V12ueIC&pg=PA4 4–5]}} By the time of [[Nero]], however, it was not unusual to find a former slave who was richer than a freeborn citizen, or an [[equestrian order|equestrian]] who exercised greater power than a senator.{{sfnp|Winterling|2009|pp=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=_35eZH6_vT8C&pg=PA11 11], [https://books.google.ca/books?id=_35eZH6_vT8C&pg=PA21 21]}}

The blurring of the Republic's more rigid hierarchies led to increased [[social mobility]],<ref>{{Cite book |last=Saller |first=Richard P. |author-link=Richard Saller |date=2002 |orig-date=1982 |title=Personal Patronage under the Early Empire |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press|CUP]] |pages=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=E7RayowC-IQC&pg=PA123 123], 176, 183 |isbn=0521893925 }}{{br}}^ {{Cite book |last=Duncan |first=Anne |date=2006 |title=Performance and Identity in the Classical World |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press|CUP]] |page=164 |isbn=9780521852821 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=y6gZBAAAQBAJ }}</ref> both upward and downward, to a greater extent than all other well-documented ancient societies.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Reinhold |first=Meyer |author-link=Meyer Reinhold |date=2002 |title=Studies in Classical History and Society |publisher=[[OUP]] |pages=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=KdcJCAAAQBAJ&pg=PA25 25 ff.], 42 |isbn=9780195145434 }}</ref> Women, freedmen, and slaves had opportunities to profit and exercise influence in ways previously less available to them.{{sfnp|Bowman|Garnsey|Rathbone|2000|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=mhNUGgG2eacC&pg=PA18 18]}} Social life, particularly for those whose personal resources were limited, was further fostered by a proliferation of [[associations in Ancient Rome|voluntary associations]] and [[confraternities]] (''[[collegia]]'' and ''[[Sodales|sodalitates]]''): professional and trade guilds, veterans' groups, religious sodalities, drinking and dining clubs,{{sfnp|Peachin|2011|pp=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=RDSI1V12ueIC&pg=PA17 17, 20]}} performing troupes,{{sfnp|Millar|1983|pp=81–2}} and [[burial societies]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Carroll |first=Maureen |author-link=Maureen Carroll |date=2006 |title=Spirits of the Dead: Roman Funerary Commemoration in Western Europe |publisher=[[OUP]] |page=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=D3ITDAAAQBAJ&pg=PA45 45–6] |isbn=9780199291076 }}</ref>

===Legal status===
{{Main|Status in Roman legal system|Roman citizenship}}

According to the [[jurist Gaius]], the essential distinction in the Roman "[[legal personality|law of persons]]" was that all humans were either free (''liberi'') or slaves (''servi'').<ref>{{harvp|Frier|McGinn|2004|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=f19bw1D9s6gC&pg=PA14 14]}}.{{br}}^ {{harvp|Gaius' Institutiones||loc=Book 1 § 9 p. [https://archive.org/details/gaiinstitutiones00gaiuuoft/page/18/mode/1up 18]}}.{{br}}^ {{harvp|Justinian's Digest||loc=Book 1 V.3, p. [https://archive.org/details/digestofjustinia01char/page/24/mode/1up 24]}}.</ref> The legal status of free persons was further defined by their citizenship. Most citizens held limited rights (such as the ''[[ius Latinum]]'', "Latin right"), but were entitled to legal protections and privileges not enjoyed by non-citizens. Free people not considered citizens, but living within the Roman world, were ''[[peregrini]]'', non-Romans.{{sfnp|Frier|McGinn|2004|pp=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=f19bw1D9s6gC&pg=PA31 31–2]}} In 212, the ''[[Constitutio Antoniniana]]'' extended citizenship to all freeborn inhabitants of the empire. This legal egalitarianism required a far-reaching revision of existing laws that distinguished between citizens and non-citizens.{{sfnp|Potter|2009|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=g4ZmqsyC5kEC&pg=PA177 177]}}

====Women in Roman law====
{{Main|Women in ancient Rome}}

{{Multiple image
| align  = right
| image1 = Fanciulla intenta alla lettura (IV stile), I sec, da pompei, MANN 8946.JPG
| width1 = 160
| image2 = Bronze young girl reading CdM Paris.jpg
| width2 = 136
| footer = Left: Fresco of an [[Auburn hair|auburn]] maiden reading a text, [[Pompeian Styles|Pompeian Fourth Style]] (60–79 AD), [[Pompeii]], Italy<br />Right: Bronze statuette (1st century AD) of a young woman reading, based on a [[Hellenistic art|Hellenistic]] original
}}

Freeborn Roman women were considered citizens, but did not vote, hold political office, or serve in the military. A mother's citizen status determined that of her children, as indicated by the phrase ''ex duobus civibus Romanis natos'' ("children born of two Roman citizens").{{Efn|The ''civis'' ("citizen") stands in explicit contrast to a ''[[Peregrinus (Roman)|peregrina]]'', a foreign or non-Roman woman<ref>{{cite book |last=Sherwin-White |first=Adrian N. |author-link=A. N. Sherwin-White |date=1979 |orig-date=1939 |title=Roman Citizenship |edition=2nd |publisher=[[Clarendon Press]] |pages=[https://archive.org/details/romancitizenship0000sher/page/211/mode/1up?q=suffragii 211], 268 }}{{br}}^ {{harvp|Frier|McGinn|2004|pp=31–2, [https://books.google.ca/books?id=f19bw1D9s6gC&pg=PA457 457]}}.</ref> In the form of legal marriage called ''conubium'', the father's legal status determined the child's, but ''conubium'' required that both spouses be free citizens. A soldier, for instance, was banned from marrying while in service, but if he formed a long-term union with a local woman while stationed in the provinces, he could marry her legally after he was discharged, and any children they had would be considered the offspring of citizens—in effect granting the woman retroactive citizenship. The ban was in place from the time of Augustus until it was rescinded by [[Septimius Severus]] in 197 AD.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Phang |first=Sara Elise |date=2001 |title=The Marriage of Roman Soldiers (13 B.C.–A.D. 235): Law and Family in the Imperial Army |publisher=[[Brill Publishers|Brill]] |page=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=jyFdUxqYZ48C&printsec=frontcover&pg=PA2 2] |isbn=9004121552 }}{{br}}^ {{Cite book |last=Southern |first=Pat |author-link=Pat Southern |date=2007 |title=The Roman Army: A Social and Institutional History |publisher=[[OUP]] |page=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=LzLRCwAAQBAJ&pg=PA144 144] |isbn=9780195328783 }}</ref>}} A Roman woman kept her own [[Roman naming conventions|family name]] (''nomen'') for life. Children most often took the father's name, with some exceptions.{{sfnp|Rawson|1992|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=85Gdul_43DEC&pg=PA18 18]}} Women could own property, enter contracts, and engage in business.<ref>{{harvp|Frier|McGinn|2004|p=461}}. ^ {{harvp|Bowman|Garnsey|Rathbone|2000|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=mhNUGgG2eacC&pg=PA733 733]}}.</ref> Inscriptions throughout the Empire honour women as benefactors in funding public works, an indication they could hold considerable fortunes.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Woodhull |first=Margaret L. |date=2004 |chapter=Matronly Patrons in the Early Roman Empire: The Case of Salvia Postuma |editor1=Fiona McHardy |editor-link1=Fiona McHardy |editor2=Eireann Marshall |title=Women's Influence on Classical Civilization |publisher=[[Routledge]] |page=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=RUSAAgAAQBAJ&pg=PA77 77] |isbn=0415309581 }}</ref>

The archaic [[manus marriage|''manus'' marriage]] in which the woman was subject to her husband's authority was largely abandoned by the Imperial era, and a married woman retained ownership of any property she brought into the marriage. Technically she remained under her father's legal authority, even though she moved into her husband's home, but when her father died she became legally emancipated.{{sfnp|Frier|McGinn|2004|pp=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=f19bw1D9s6gC&pg=PA19 19–20]}} This arrangement was a factor in the degree of independence Roman women enjoyed compared to many other cultures up to the modern period:<ref>{{Cite book |last=Cantarella |first=Eva |author-link=Eva Cantarella |date=1987 |orig-date=1981 |title=Pandora's Daughters: The Role and Status of Women in Greek and Roman Antiquity |translator=Maureen B. Fant |publisher=[[JHUP]] |pages=[https://archive.org/details/pandorasdaughter00cant/page/140/mode/1up 140–1] |isbn=080183385X }}{{br}}^ {{Cite journal |last=Sullivan |first=J.P. |date=1979 |title=Martial's Sexual Attitudes |journal=Philologus |volume=123 |issue=1–2 |pages=288–302 (296) |doi=10.1524/phil.1979.123.12.288 |s2cid=163347317 |url=https://philpapers.org/rec/SULMSA-2 }}</ref> although she had to answer to her father in legal matters, she was free of his direct scrutiny in daily life,{{sfnp|Rawson|1992|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=85Gdul_43DEC&pg=PA15 15]}} and her husband had no legal power over her.{{sfnp|Frier|McGinn|2004|pp=19–20, [https://books.google.ca/books?id=f19bw1D9s6gC&pg=PA22 22]}} Although it was a point of pride to be a "one-man woman" (''univira'') who had married only once, there was little stigma attached to [[Marriage in ancient Rome#Divorce|divorce]], nor to speedy remarriage after being widowed or divorced.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Treggiari |first=Susan |author-link=Susan Treggiari |date=1993 |orig-date=1991 |title=Roman Marriage: 'Iusti Coniuges' from the Time of Cicero to the Time of Ulpian |publisher=[[Clarendon Press]] |pages=[https://archive.org/details/romanmarriageius0000treg/page/258/mode/1up 258–9], 500–2 |isbn=0198149395 }}</ref> Girls had equal inheritance rights with boys if their father died without leaving a will.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Johnston |first=David |date=1999 |chapter=Ch. 3.3 - Succession |title=Roman Law in Context |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press|CUP]] |pages=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=6aN9XVKUYdMC&pg=PA44 44 ff.] |isbn=0521639611 }}{{br}}^ {{harvp|Frier|McGinn|2004|loc=Ch. IV - Succession (p. 323 ff.)}}.{{br}}^ {{Cite book |last=Thomas |first=Yan |date=1992 |chapter=The Division of the Sexes in Roman Law |editor1=Pauline Schmitt Pantel |editor2=Georges Duby |editor3=Michelle Perrot |title=A History of Women |volume=1 - From Ancient Goddesses to Christian Saints |publisher=[[Belknap Press]] |page=134 |isbn=9780674403697 }}</ref> A mother's right to own and dispose of property, including setting the terms of her will, gave her enormous influence over her sons into adulthood.{{sfnp|Severy|2003|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=Wa8DldoTnuYC&pg=PA12 12]}}
[[File:Wall painting - mistress and three maids - Herculaneum (insula orientalis II - palaestra - room III) - Napoli MAN 9022.jpg|thumb|300px|right|Dressing of a priestess or bride, Roman fresco from [[Herculaneum]], Italy (30–40 AD)]]

As part of the Augustan programme to restore traditional morality and social order, [[Leges Iuliae|moral legislation]] attempted to regulate conduct as a means of promoting "[[family values]]". [[Marriage in ancient Rome#Adultery|Adultery]] was criminalized,{{sfnp|Severy|2003|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=Wa8DldoTnuYC&pg=PA4 4]}} and defined broadly as an illicit sex act (''[[stuprum]]'') between a male citizen and a married woman, or between a married woman and any man other than her husband. That is, a [[double standard]] was in place: a married woman could have sex only with her husband, but a married man did not commit adultery if he had sex with a prostitute or person of marginalized status.{{efn|"...the earlier [pre-Augustan] custom allowed much latitude for personal negotiation and gradual social change"<ref>{{Cite book |last=Mussbaum |first=Martha C. |author-link=Martha C. Nussbaum |date=2002 |chapter=The Incomplete Feminism of Musonius Rufus, Platonist, Stoic, and Roman |editor1=Martha C. Nussbaum |editor2=Juha Sihvola |editor-link2=Juha Sihvola |title=The Sleep of Reason: Erotic Experience and Sexual Ethics in Ancient Greece and Rome |publisher=[[University of Chicago Press|UCP]] |page=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=ZAiNHQVPlaMC&pg=PA305 305] |isbn=0226609154 }}</ref>}}<ref>{{Cite journal |last=McGinn |first=Thomas A.J. |date=1991 |title=Concubinage and the Lex Iulia on Adultery |journal=Transactions of the American Philological Association |volume=121 |pages=335–375 (342) |doi=10.2307/284457 |jstor=284457 }}{{br}}^ {{Cite book |last=Fantham |first=Elaine |author-link=Elaine Fantham |date=2011 |chapter=''Stuprum'': Public Attitudes and Penalties for Sexual Offences in Republican Rome |title=Roman Readings: Roman Response to Greek Literature from Plautus to Statius and Quintilian |publisher=[[de Gruyter]] |page=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=qH9AyrTUguAC&pg=PA124 124] |isbn=9783110229332 }} The author mentions [[Papinian]], ''De adulteriis'' I and [[Modestinus]], ''Liber Regularum'' I.{{br}}^ {{Cite book |last=Cantarella |first=Eva |author-link=Eva Cantarella |date=2002 |orig-date=1988 |title=Bisexuality in the Ancient World |translator=Cormac Ó Cuilleanáin |publisher=[[Yale University Press|YUP]] |page=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=clZgThbI5yIC&pg=PA104 104] }}{{br}}^ {{harvp|Edwards|2007|pp=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=Ioq6GmIyLQIC&pg=PA34 34–5]}}.</ref> Childbearing was encouraged: a woman who had given birth to three children was granted symbolic honours and greater legal freedom (the ''[[ius trium liberorum]]'').<ref>{{Cite thesis |last=Hug |first=Angela Grace |date=December 2014 |title=Fecunditas, Sterilitas, and the Politics of Reproduction at Rome |publisher=[[York University]]  |url=https://www.academia.edu/64387404 }}</ref>

====Slaves and the law====
{{Main|Slavery in ancient Rome}}
At the time of Augustus, it is estimated that the percentage of the population in [[Roman Italy]] reduced to slavery was around 20-30%, or one to two millions slaves,{{efn|"Recent studies of Italian demography have further increased doubts about a rapid expansion of the peninsula's servile population in this era. No direct evidence exists for the number of slaves in Italy at any time. Brunt has little trouble showing that Beloch's estimate of 2 million during the reign of Augustus is without foundation. Brunt himself suggests that there were about 3 million slaves out of a total population in Italy of about 7.5 million at this date, but he readily concedes that this is no more than a guess. As Lo Cascio has cogently noted, that guess in effect is a product of Brunt's low estimate of the free population."<ref>{{Cite book |last=Rosenstein |first=Nathan |date=2004 |title=Rome at War: Farms, Families, And Death in the Middle Republic |publisher=[[UNC Press]] |isbn=9780807828397 |page=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=iPJECQAAQBAJ&pg=PA185 185] }}</ref>}}{{efn|Scheidel (2005) has estimated between 1 and 1.5&nbsp;million slaves in the 1st&nbsp;century&nbsp;BC.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Scheidel |first=Walter |author-link=Walter Scheidel |date=2005 |title=Human Mobility in Roman Italy, II: The Slave Population |journal=Journal of Roman Studies |volume=95 |pages=64–79 |doi=10.3815/000000005784016270 |url=http://piketty.pse.ens.fr/files/Scheidel2005.pdf }}</ref>}}{{efn|Jason Paul Wickham notes in his thesis the difficulty in estimating the size of the slave population and the supply needed to maintain and grow the population.<ref>{{cite thesis |last=Wickham |first=Jason P. |date=2014 |title=The Enslavement of War Captives by the Romans to 146&nbsp;BC |publisher=[[University of Liverpool]] |page=198 |url=https://livrepository.liverpool.ac.uk/17893/}}</ref>}}<ref>{{cite book |editor-last=Goldhill |editor-first=Simon |editor-link=Simon Goldhill |date=2001 |title=Being Greek Under Rome: Cultural Identity, The Second Sophistic and the Development of Empire |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press|CUP]] |isbn=9780521030878 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=rbwCTL507fsC }}</ref>{{page needed|date=September 2026}}{{r|n=Bradley2002_12|r={{harvp|Bradley|2002|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=xu3rkG9dVY8C&pg=PA12 12]}}.}} making Rome one of five historical "slave societies" in which slaves constituted at least a fifth of the population and played a major role in the economy.{{Efn|The others are [[Slavery in ancient Greece|ancient Athens]], and in the modern era [[Slavery in Brazil|Brazil]], the [[Slavery in the British and French Caribbean|Caribbean]], and the [[Slavery in the United States|United States]]}}{{r|Bradley2002_12}} In urban settings, slaves might be professionals such as teachers, physicians, chefs, and accountants; the majority of slaves provided trained or unskilled labour. [[Agriculture in ancient Rome|Agriculture]] and industry, such as milling and mining, relied on the exploitation of slaves. Outside Italy, slaves were on average an estimated 10 to 20% of the population, sparse in [[Roman Egypt]] but more concentrated in some Greek areas. Expanding Roman ownership of arable land and industries affected preexisting practices of slavery in the provinces.{{sfnp|Harris|1999|pp=62–75}}<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Taylor |first=Timothy |author-link=Timothy Taylor (archaeologist)
 |date=2001 |title=Believing the ancients: Quantitative and qualitative dimensions of slavery and the slave trade in later prehistoric Eurasia |journal=World Archaeology |volume=33 |issue=1 |pages=27–43 |doi=10.1080/00438240120047618 |jstor=827887 |s2cid=162250553 |issn=0043-8243 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/827887 |url-access=limited }}</ref> Although slavery has often been regarded as waning in the 3rd and 4th centuries, it remained an integral part of Roman society until gradually ceasing in the 6th and 7th centuries with the disintegration of the complex Imperial economy.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Harper |first=Kyle |author-link=Kyle Harper |date=2011 |title=Slavery in the Late Roman World, AD 275–425 |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press|CUP]] |pages=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=IPU8ZAcrOtIC&pg=PA10 10–6] |isbn=9780521198615 }}</ref>

[[File:Sarcofago avvocato Valerius Petrnianus-optimized.jpg|thumb|Slave holding writing tablets for his master ([[relief]] from a 4th-century sarcophagus)]]
Laws pertaining to slavery were "extremely intricate".{{sfnp|Frier|McGinn|2004|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=f19bw1D9s6gC&pg=PA7 7]}} Slaves were considered property and had no [[legal personhood]]. They could be subjected to forms of corporal punishment not normally exercised on citizens, [[Sexuality in ancient Rome#Master-slave relations|sexual exploitation]], torture, and [[summary execution]]. A slave could not as a matter of law be raped; a slave's rapist had to be prosecuted by the owner for property damage under the [[Lex Aquilia|Aquilian Law]].<ref>{{harvp|McGinn|2003|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=BmH31IK-OgEC&pg=PA314 314]}}.{{br}}^ {{Cite book |last=Gardner |first=Jane F. |author-link=Jane F. Gardner |date=1991 |orig-date=1986 |title=Women in Roman Law and Society |publisher=[[Indiana University Press|IUP]] |page=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=CTzKESIH1mQC&pg=PA119 119] |isbn=0253206359 }}</ref> Slaves had no right to the form of legal marriage called ''[[conubium]]'', but their unions were sometimes recognized.{{sfnp|Frier|McGinn|2004|pp=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=f19bw1D9s6gC&pg=PA31 31–3]}} Technically, a slave could not own property,{{sfnp|Frier|McGinn|2004|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=f19bw1D9s6gC&pg=PA21 21]}} but a slave who conducted business might be given access to an individual fund (''peculium'') that he could use, depending on the degree of trust and co-operation between owner and slave.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Gamauf |first=Richard |date=2009 |title=Slaves doing business: The role of Roman law in the economy of a Roman household |journal=European Review of History / Revue européenne d'histoire |volume=16 |issue=3 |pages=331–346 |doi=10.1080/13507480902916837 |s2cid=145609520 |url=https://doi.org/10.1080/13507480902916837 }}</ref> Within a household or workplace, a hierarchy of slaves might exist, with one slave acting as the master of others.{{sfnp|Bradley|2002|pp=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=xu3rkG9dVY8C&pg=PA2 2–3]}} Talented slaves might accumulate a large enough ''peculium'' to justify their freedom, or be [[manumitted]] for services rendered. Manumission had become frequent enough that in 2 BC a law (''[[Lex Fufia Caninia]]'') limited the number of slaves an owner was allowed to free in his will.{{sfnp|Bradley|2002|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=xu3rkG9dVY8C&pg=PA10 10]}}

Following the [[Servile Wars]] of the Republic, legislation under Augustus and his successors shows a driving concern for controlling the threat of rebellions through limiting the size of work groups, and for hunting down fugitive slaves.{{sfnp|Fuhrmann|2012|pp=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=yspXtgPVoJQC&pg=PA21 21–41]}} Over time slaves gained increased legal protection, including the right to file complaints against their masters.
