A bill of sale might contain a clause stipulating that the slave could not be employed for prostitution, as [[prostitutes in ancient Rome]] were often slaves.{{sfnp|McGinn|2003|pp=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=BmH31IK-OgEC&pg=PA288 288 ff]}} The burgeoning trade in [[eunuch]]s in the late 1st century prompted legislation that prohibited the [[Sexuality in ancient Rome#Castration and circumcision|castration]] of a slave against his will "for lust or gain".<ref>{{Cite book |last=Abusch |first=Ra'anan |date=2003 |chapter=Circumcision and Castration under Roman Law in the Early Empire |editor=Elizabeth Wyner Mark |title=The Covenant of Circumcision: New Perspectives on an Ancient Jewish Rite |publisher=[[Brandeis University Press]] |pages=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=nAfUF2_ClqgC&pg=PA77 77–8] |isbn=158465306X }}{{br}}^ {{Cite book |last=Schäfer |first=Peter |author-link=Peter Schäfer |date=2003 |orig-date=1983 |title=The History of the Jews in the Greco-Roman World |edition=Revised |publisher=[[Routledge]] |page=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=YBarWAR2qVkC&pg=PA150 150] |isbn=0415305853  }}</ref>

Roman slavery was not based on [[Race (human categorization)|race]].{{efn|"Roman slavery was a nonracist and fluid system".<ref>{{Cite book |last=Goodwin |first=Stefan |date=2009 |title=Africa in Europe |volume=1 - Antiquity into the Age of Global Exploration |publisher=[[Lexington Books]] |page=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=QUA5AAAAQBAJ&pg=PA41 41] |isbn=9780739117262 }}</ref>}}{{sfnp|Frier|McGinn|2004|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=f19bw1D9s6gC&pg=PA15 15]}} Generally, slaves in Italy were indigenous Italians,<ref>{{Cite book |last=Santosuosso |first=Antonio |author-link=Antonio Santosuosso |date=2018 |orig-date=2001 |title=Storming the Heavens: Soldiers, Emperors and Civilians in the Roman Empire |publisher=[[Routledge]] |pages=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=N__EDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA43 43–4] |isbn=9780813341606 }}</ref> with a minority of foreigners (including both slaves and freedmen) estimated at 5% of the total in the capital at its peak, where their number was largest. Foreign slaves had higher mortality and lower birth rates than natives and were sometimes even subjected to mass expulsions.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Noy |first=David |date=2000 |title=Foreigners at Rome: Citizens and Strangers |publisher=[[Duckworth Books|Duckworth]] |pages=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=rRctEAAAQBAJ&pg=PA39 39-40] |isbn=0715629522 }}</ref> The average recorded age at death for the slaves of the city of Rome was seventeen and a half years (17.2 for males; 17.9 for females).<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Harper |first=James |date=1972 |title=Slaves and Freedmen in Imperial Rome |journal=American Journal of Philology |volume=93 |issue=2 |pages=341–342 |doi=10.2307/293259 |jstor=293259 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/293259 }}</ref>

During the period of republican expansionism when slavery had become pervasive, war captives were a main source of slaves. The range of ethnicities among slaves to some extent reflected that of the armies Rome defeated in war, and the [[Greece in the Roman era|conquest of Greece]] brought a number of highly skilled and educated slaves. Slaves were also traded in markets and sometimes sold by [[Cilician pirates|pirates]]. [[Child abandonment|Infant abandonment]] and self-enslavement among the poor were other sources.{{sfnp|Harris|1999|pp=62–75}} ''[[Slavery in ancient Rome#Vernae|Vernae]]'', by contrast, were "homegrown" slaves born to female slaves within the household, estate or farm. Although they had no special legal status, an owner who mistreated or failed to care for his ''vernae'' faced social disapproval, as they were considered part of the family household and in some cases might actually be the children of free males in the family.<ref>{{harvp|Rawson|1992|pp=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=85Gdul_43DEC&pg=PA186 186]–8, 190}}. ^ {{harvp|Bradley|2002|pp=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=xu3rkG9dVY8C&pg=PA34 34], 48–50}}.</ref>

====Freedmen====
[[File:DM Tiberius Claudius Chryseros.jpg|thumb|[[Urn#Cremation urns|Cinerary urn]] for the freedman Tiberius Claudius Chryseros and two women, probably his wife and daughter]]
Rome differed from [[Greek city-states]] in allowing freed slaves to become citizens; any future children of a freedman were born free, with full rights of citizenship. After manumission, a slave who had belonged to a Roman citizen enjoyed active political freedom (''libertas''), including the right to vote.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Millar |first=Fergus |author-link=Fergus Millar |date=2002 |orig-date=1998 |title=The Crowd in Rome in the Late Republic |publisher=[[University of Michigan Press|UMP]] |isbn=0472088785 |pages=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=YVBNzYQy5vYC&pg=PA23 23], 209 }}</ref> His former master became his patron (''[[Patronage in ancient Rome|patronus]]''): the two continued to have customary and legal obligations to each other.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Mouritsen |first=Henrik |date=2011 |title=The Freedman in the Roman World |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press|CUP]] |page=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=sOWxzU66-7sC&pg=PA36 36] |isbn=9780521856133 }}</ref>{{r|n=Berger2002_564|r={{Cite book |last=Berger |first=Adolf |date=2002 |orig-date=1953 |chapter=Libertus |title=Encyclopedic Dictionary of Roman Law |publisher=The Lawbook Exchange |page=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=iklePELtR6QC&pg=PA564 564] |isbn=1584771429 }}}} During the early Empire, freedmen held key positions in the government bureaucracy, so much so that [[Hadrian]] limited their participation by law.{{r|Berger2002_564}} The rise of successful freedmen—through political influence or wealth—is a characteristic of early Imperial society. The prosperity of a high-achieving group of freedmen is attested by [[:Commons:Category:Liberti and libertae in Ancient Roman inscriptions|inscriptions throughout the Empire]].

===Census rank===
{{See also|Senate of the Roman Empire|Equestrian order|Decurion (administrative)}}
The Latin word {{lang|la|ordo}} (plural {{lang|la|ordines}}) is translated variously and inexactly into English as "class, order, rank". One purpose of the [[Roman census]] was to determine the {{lang|la|ordo}} to which an individual belonged.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Dolganov |first=Anna |date=2021 |chapter=Documenting Roman Citizenship |editor-last1=Lavan |editor-first1=Myles |editor-last2=Ando |editor-first2=Clifford  |title=Roman and Local Citizenship in the Long Second Century CE |publisher=[[OUP]] |page=[https://books.google.com/books?id=PbNLEAAAQBAJ&pg=PA191 191] |isbn=9780197573884 }}</ref> Two of the highest {{lang|la|ordines}} in Rome were the senatorial and equestrian. Outside Rome, cities or colonies were led by [[decurion (administrative)|decurions]], also known as ''[[curiales]]''.<ref>{{cite EBO |short=yes |last1=Rodriguez |first1=Emily |last2=Chauhan |first2=Yamini |date=2019 |title=decurio |url=https://www.britannica.com/topic/decurio |display-authors=1 }}</ref>

[[File:0 Sarcophage d'Acilia - Pal. Massimo alle Terme.JPG|thumb|left|Fragment of a sarcophagus depicting [[Gordian III]] and senators (3rd century)]]
"Senator" was not itself an elected office in ancient Rome; an individual gained admission to the Senate after he had been elected to and served at least one term as an [[Executive magistrates of the Roman Empire|executive magistrate]]. A senator also had to meet a minimum property requirement of 1 million ''[[sestertii]]''.<ref>{{harvp|Bowman|Garnsey|Rathbone|2000|pp=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=mhNUGgG2eacC&pg=PA217 217–8]}}.{{br}}^ {{Cite book |last=Syme |first=Ronald |author-link=Ronald Syme |date=1999 |title=Provincial at Rome, and, Rome and the Balkans 80 BC – AD 14 |publisher=[[University of Exeter Press|UEP]] |pages=12–3 |isbn=0859896323 }}</ref> Not all men who qualified for the ''ordo senatorius'' chose to take a Senate seat, which required [[legal domicile]] at Rome. Emperors often filled vacancies in the 600-member body by appointment.{{sfnp|Bowman|Garnsey|Rathbone|2000|pp=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=mhNUGgG2eacC&pg=PA215 215], 221–2}}{{efn|"The standard complement of 600 was flexible; twenty [[quaestor]]s, for instance, held office each year and were thus admitted to the Senate regardless of whether there were "open" seats."{{sfnp|Millar|1983|p=88}}}} A senator's son belonged to the ''ordo senatorius'', but he had to qualify on his own merits for admission to the Senate. A senator could be removed for violating moral standards.{{sfnp|Millar|1983|p=88}}

In the time of Nero, senators were still primarily from [[Italy (Roman Empire)|Italy]], with some from the Iberian peninsula and southern France; men from the Greek-speaking provinces of the East began to be added under Vespasian.{{sfnp|Bowman|Garnsey|Rathbone|2000|pp=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=mhNUGgG2eacC&pg=PA218 218–9]}} The first senator from the easternmost province, [[Cappadocia (Roman province)|Cappadocia]], was admitted under Marcus Aurelius.{{Efn|That senator was Tiberius Claudius Gordianus{{sfnp|Bowman|Garnsey|Rathbone|2000|p=219}}}} By the [[Severan dynasty]] (193–235), Italians made up less than half the Senate.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=MacMullen |first=Ramsay |author-link=Ramsay MacMullen |date=January 1966 |title=Provincial Languages in the Roman Empire |journal=The American Journal of Philology |volume=87 |issue=1 |pages=1–17 |doi=10.2307/292973 |jstor=292973 |url=https://ia800108.us.archive.org/view_archive.php?archive=/24/items/wikipedia-scholarly-sources-corpus/10.2307%252F291187.zip&file=10.2307%252F292973.pdf }}</ref> During the 3rd century, domicile at Rome became impractical, and inscriptions attest to senators who were active in politics and munificence in their homeland (''patria'').{{sfnp|Millar|1983|p=88}}

Senators were the traditional governing class who rose through the {{lang|la|[[cursus honorum]]}}, the political career track, but equestrians often possessed greater wealth and political power. Membership in the equestrian order was based on property; in Rome's early days, ''equites'' or knights had been distinguished by their ability to serve as mounted warriors, but cavalry service was a separate function in the Empire.{{Efn|The relation of the equestrian order to the "public horse" and Roman cavalry parades and demonstrations (such as the ''[[Lusus Troiae]]'') is complex, but those who participated in the latter seem, for instance, to have been the ''equites'' who were accorded the high-status (and quite limited) seating at the theatre by the ''[[Lex Roscia theatralis]]''. Senators could not possess the "public horse".{{sfnp|Wiseman|1970|pp=78–9}}}} A census valuation of 400,000 sesterces and three generations of free birth qualified a man as an equestrian.{{sfnp|Wiseman|1970|pp=71–2, 76}} The census of 28 BC uncovered large numbers of men who qualified, and in 14 AD, a thousand equestrians were registered at [[Cádiz]] and [[Padua]] alone.{{Efn|Ancient Gades, in Roman Spain (now [[Cádiz]]), and Patavium, in the Celtic north of Italy (now [[Padua]]), were atypically wealthy cities, and having 500 equestrians in one city was unusual.{{sfnp|Strabo's Geography||loc=Vol. 2 - Book 3 5.3, [https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.57226/page/131/mode/2up p. 131]; Book 5 1.7, [https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.57226/page/313/mode/2up p. 313]}}}}{{sfnp|Wiseman|1970|pp=75–6, 78}} Equestrians rose through a military career track (''[[tres militiae]]'') to become highly placed [[prefect]]s and [[procurator (Roman)|procurators]] within the Imperial administration.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Fear |first=Andrew |chapter=War and Society |date=2007 |editor1=Philip Sabin |editor-link1=Philip Sabin |editor2=Hans van Wees |editor-link2=Hans van Wees |editor3=Michael Whitby |editor-link3=Michael Whitby |title=The Cambridge History of Greek and Roman Warfare |volume=2 - Rome from the Late Republic to the Late Empire |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press|CUP]] |pages=[https://archive.org/details/the-cambridge-history-of-greek-and-roman-warfare-volume-2-rome-from-the-late-republic-to-the-late/page/214/mode/1up 214–5] |isbn=9780521782746 }}{{br}}^ {{harvp|Bennett|1997|p=[https://archive.org/details/trajanoptimuspri0000benn/page/5/mode/1up?q=equestrians 5]}}.</ref>

The rise of provincial men to the senatorial and equestrian orders is an aspect of social mobility in the early Empire. Roman aristocracy was based on competition, and unlike later [[European nobility]], a Roman family could not maintain its position merely through hereditary succession or having title to lands.<ref>{{harvp|Morris|Scheidel|2009|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=XnDtcvRwsrgC&pg=PA188 188]}}. ^ {{harvp|Millar|1983|pp=87–8}}.</ref> Admission to the higher {{lang|la|ordines}} brought distinction and privileges, but also responsibilities. In antiquity, a city depended on its leading citizens to fund public works, events, and services ({{lang|la|[[Munera (ancient Rome)|munera]]}}). Maintaining one's rank required massive personal expenditures.{{sfnp|Millar|1983|p=96}} Decurions were so vital for the functioning of cities that in the later Empire, as the ranks of the town councils became depleted, those who had risen to the Senate were encouraged to return to their hometowns, in an effort to sustain civic life.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Liebeschuetz |first=Wolfgang |author-link=Wolf Liebeschuetz |date=1992 |chapter=The End of the Ancient City |editor=John Rich |title=The City in Late Antiquity |publisher=[[Routledge]] |pages=[https://archive.org/details/cityinlateantiqu0003unse/page/26/mode/1up 26–7] |isbn=041506855X }}</ref>

In the later Empire, the ''[[Dignitas (Roman concept)|dignitas]]'' ("worth, esteem") that attended on senatorial or equestrian rank was refined further with titles such as ''[[vir illustris]]'' ("illustrious man").{{sfnp|Millar|1983|p=90|loc=calls them "status-appellations"}} The appellation ''clarissimus'' (Greek ''lamprotatos'') was used to designate the ''dignitas'' of certain senators and their immediate family, including women.{{sfnp|Millar|1983|p=91}} "Grades" of equestrian status proliferated.{{sfnp|Millar|1983|p=90}}

====Unequal justice====
[[File:Tunisia-3363 - Amphitheatre Spectacle.jpg|thumb|Condemned man attacked by a leopard in the arena (3rd-century mosaic from Tunisia)]]
As the republican principle of citizens' equality under the law faded, the symbolic and social privileges of the upper classes led to an informal division of Roman society into those who had acquired greater honours (''honestiores'') and humbler folk (''humiliores''). In general, ''honestiores'' were the members of the three higher "orders", along with certain military officers.{{r|n=Verboven_Peachin|r={{Cite journal |last=Verboven |first=Koenraad |date=2007 |title=The Associative Order: Status and Ethos among Roman Businessmen in Late Republic and Early Empire |journal=Athenaeum |volume=95 |pages=870–872 |hdl=1854/LU-395187  |url=https://biblio.ugent.be/publication/395187/file/6799583 }}{{br}}^ {{harvp|Peachin|2011|loc=(Dennis P. Kehoe, Law and Social Foundation in the Roman Empire), pp. 153–4}}.}} The granting of universal citizenship in 212 seems to have increased the competitive urge among the upper classes to have their superiority affirmed, particularly within the justice system.{{r|n=Peachin2011_153_4|r={{harvp|Peachin|2011|loc=(Dennis P. Kehoe, Law and Social Foundation in the Roman Empire), pp. [https://books.google.ca/books?id=RDSI1V12ueIC&pg=PA153 153–4]}}.}}<ref>{{Cite book |last=Perkins |first=Judith |author-link=Judith Perkins |date=2009 |chapter=Early Christian and Judicial Bodies |editor1=Thorsten Fögen |editor2=Mireille M. Lee |title=Bodies and Boundaries in Graeco-Roman Antiquity |publisher=Walter de Gruyter |pages=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=Y972uaq36SgC&pg=PA245 245–6] |isbn=9783110212525 }}{{br}}^{{harvp|Peachin|2011|loc=([[Garrett G. Fagan]], Violence in Roman Social Relations), p. 475}}.</ref> Sentencing depended on the judgment of the presiding official as to the relative "worth" (''dignitas'') of the defendant: an ''honestior'' could pay a fine for a crime for which an ''humilior'' might receive a [[scourging]].{{r|Peachin2011_153_4}}

Execution, which was an infrequent legal penalty for free men under the Republic,<ref>{{Cite book |last=Gaughan |first=Judy E. |date=2010 |title=Murder Was Not a Crime: Homicide and Power in the Roman Republic |publisher=[[University of Texas Press|UTP]] |page=[https://archive.org/details/murderwasnotcrim00gaug_0/page/91/mode/1up 91]|isbn=9780292721111 }}{{br}}^ {{Cite book |last=Kelly |first=Gordon P. |date=2006a |title=A History of Exile in the Roman Republic |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press|CUP]] |page=[https://archive.org/details/historyofexilein0000kell/page/8/mode/1up 8] |isbn=0521848601 }}</ref> could be quick and relatively painless for ''honestiores'', while ''humiliores'' might suffer the kinds of torturous death previously reserved for slaves, such as [[crucifixion]] and [[damnatio ad bestias|condemnation to the beasts]].{{r|n=Coleman1990|r={{Cite journal |last=Coleman |first=Kathleen M. |date=1990 |title=Fatal Charades: Roman Executions Staged as Mythological Enactments |journal=Journal of Roman Studies |volume=80 |pages=44–73 |doi=10.2307/300280 |jstor=300280 |s2cid=163071557}}}} In the early Empire, those who converted to Christianity could lose their standing as ''honestiores'', especially if they declined to fulfil religious responsibilities, and thus became subject to punishments that created the conditions of [[Christian martyrs|martyrdom]].{{r|Peachin2011_153_4}}<ref>{{Cite book |last=Robinson |first=Olivia F. |author-link=Olivia F.  Robinson |date=2007 |title=Penal Practice and Penal Policy in Ancient Rome |publisher=[[Routledge]] |page=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=0PF9AgAAQBAJ&pg=PA108 108] |isbn=9780415416511 }}</ref>

==Government and military==
{{Main|Constitution of the Roman Empire}}

[[File:Jerash BW 12.JPG|thumbnail|Forum of Gerasa ([[Jerash]] in present-day [[Jordan]]), with columns marking a covered walkway ''([[stoa]])'' for vendor stalls, and a semicircular space for public speaking]]

The three major elements of the Imperial state were the central government, the military, and the provincial government.{{sfnp|Bohec|2001|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=r2hBqYtZWNEC&pg=PA8 8]}} The military established control of a territory through war, but after a city or people was brought under treaty, the mission turned to policing: protecting Roman citizens, agricultural fields, and religious sites.{{sfnp|Bohec|2001|pp=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=r2hBqYtZWNEC&pg=PA14 14–5]}} The Romans lacked sufficient manpower or resources to rule through force alone. [[Local government (ancient Roman)|Cooperation with local elites]] was necessary to maintain order, collect information, and extract revenue. The Romans often exploited internal political divisions.<ref>{{harvp|Plutarch's Moralia||loc=813c (p. [https://archive.org/details/plutarchsmoralia10plut_0/page/234/mode/2up 235]), 814c (pp. [https://archive.org/details/plutarchsmoralia10plut_0/page/238/mode/2up 239-41])}}.{{br}} ^ {{harvp|Potter|2009|pp=181–2}}.{{br}} ^ {{Cite book |last=Luttwak |first=Edward |author-link=Edward Luttwak |date=2016 |orig-date=1976 |title=The Grand Strategy of the Roman Empire. From the First Century CE to the Third |edition=Revised and updated |publisher=[[JHUP]] |pages=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=A3z_CwAAQBAJ&pg=PA38 38-9] |isbn=9781421419459 }}</ref>

Communities with demonstrated loyalty to Rome retained their own laws, could collect their own taxes locally, and in exceptional cases were exempt from Roman taxation. Legal privileges and relative independence incentivized compliance.{{sfnp|Potter|2009|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=g4ZmqsyC5kEC&pg=PA184 184]}} Roman government was thus [[limited government|limited]], but efficient in its use of available resources.{{sfnp|Potter|2009|p=181}}

===Central government===
{{See also|Roman emperor|Senate of the Roman Empire}}
[[File:Antoninus Pius Hermitage.jpg|thumb|left|[[Antoninus Pius]] ({{R.|138|161}}) wearing a [[toga]] ([[Hermitage Museum]])|311x311px]]
The [[Imperial cult of ancient Rome]] identified [[Roman emperor|emperors]] and some members of their families with [[Divine right of kings|divinely sanctioned]] authority (''[[auctoritas]]''). The rite of [[apotheosis]] (also called ''consecratio'') signified the deceased emperor's deification.<ref>{{Cite book |editor-last=Smith |editor-first=William |editor-link=William Smith (lexicographer) |date=1875 |chapter=Apotheosis |title=A Dictionary of Greek and Roman Antiquities |publisher=[[John Murray (publishing house)|John Murray]] |at=pp.[https://books.google.ca/books?id=WByCBGN_-4YC&pg=PA105 105–6]. Online text at [https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/secondary/SMIGRA*/Apotheosis.html penelope.uchicago.edu]  }}</ref> The dominance of the emperor was based on the consolidation of powers from several republican offices.{{sfnp|Abbott|1901|p=[https://archive.org/details/ahistoryanddesc04abbogoog/page/354/mode/1up 354]}} The emperor made himself the central religious authority as ''[[pontifex maximus]]'', and centralized the right to declare war, ratify treaties, and negotiate with foreign leaders.{{sfnp|Abbott|1901|p=[https://archive.org/details/ahistoryanddesc04abbogoog/page/345/mode/1up 345]}} While these functions were clearly defined during the [[Principate]], the emperor's powers over time became less constitutional and more monarchical, culminating in the [[Dominate]].{{sfnp|Abbott|1901|p=[https://archive.org/details/ahistoryanddesc04abbogoog/page/341/mode/1up 341]}} The emperor was the ultimate authority in policy- and decision-making, but in the early Principate, he was expected to be accessible and deal personally with official business and petitions. A bureaucracy formed around him only gradually.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Millar |first=Fergus |author-link=Fergus Millar |date=2004 |chapter=Emperors at Work |editor1=Hannah M. Cotton |editor-link1=Hannah Cotton |editor2=Guy MacLean Rogers |title=Rome, the Greek World, and the East |volume=2 - Government, Society, and Culture in the Roman Empire |publisher=[[University of North Carolina Press|UNCP]] |isbn=0807855200 |at=pp. 3–22, especially pp. [https://books.google.ca/books?id=Gq3qCQAAQBAJ&pg=PA4 4], 20 }}</ref> The Julio-Claudian emperors relied on an informal body of advisors that included not only senators and equestrians, but trusted slaves and freedmen.{{sfnp|Bowman|Garnsey|Rathbone|2000|pp=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=mhNUGgG2eacC&pg=PA195 195 ff]}} After Nero, the influence of the latter was regarded with suspicion, and the emperor's council (''consilium'') became subject to official appointment for greater [[Open government|transparency]].{{sfnp|Bowman|Garnsey|Rathbone|2000|pp=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=mhNUGgG2eacC&pg=PA205 205–9]}} Though the Senate took a lead in policy discussions until the end of the [[Antonine dynasty]], equestrians played an increasingly important role in the ''consilium''.{{sfnp|Bowman|Garnsey|Rathbone|2000|pp=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=mhNUGgG2eacC&pg=PA202 202–3], 205, 210}} The women of the emperor's family often intervened directly in his decisions.{{sfnp|Bowman|Garnsey|Rathbone|2000|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=mhNUGgG2eacC&pg=PA211 211]}}

Access to the emperor might be gained at the daily reception (''salutatio''), a development of the traditional homage a client paid to his patron; public banquets hosted at the palace; and religious ceremonies. The common people who lacked this access could manifest their approval or displeasure as a group at [[#Spectacles|games]].{{sfnp|Bowman|Garnsey|Rathbone|2000|p=212}} By the 4th century, the Christian emperors became remote figureheads who issued general rulings, no longer responding to individual petitions.{{sfnp|Millar|1983|p=76}} Although the Senate could do little short of assassination and open rebellion to contravene the will of the emperor, it retained its symbolic political centrality.{{sfnp|Bowman|Garnsey|Rathbone|2000|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=mhNUGgG2eacC&pg=PA215 215]}} The Senate legitimated the emperor's rule, and the emperor employed senators as legates (''[[legati]]''): generals, diplomats, and administrators.{{r|BowmanEtal2000_721}}{{r|n=Winterling2009_16|r={{harvp|Winterling|2009|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=_35eZH6_vT8C&pg=PA16 16]}}.}}

The practical source of an emperor's power and authority was the military. The [[legionaries]] were paid by the Imperial treasury, and swore an annual [[Sacramentum (oath)|oath of loyalty]] to the emperor.{{sfnp|Goldsworthy|2003|p=80}} Most emperors chose a successor, usually a close family member or [[Adoption in ancient Rome|adopted]] heir. The new emperor had to seek a swift acknowledgement of his status and authority to stabilize the political landscape. No emperor could hope to survive without the allegiance of the [[Praetorian Guard]] and the legions. To secure their loyalty, several emperors paid the ''[[donativum]]'', a monetary reward. In theory, the Senate was entitled to choose the new emperor, but did so mindful of acclamation by the army or Praetorians.{{r|Winterling2009_16}}

===Military===
{{Main|Imperial Roman army|Late Roman army|Structural history of the Roman military}}

[[File:Palestra grande di pompei, affreschi di Moregine, terzo triclinio, IV stile, epoca neroniana, 07 vittoria con tripode.jpg|thumb|upright|Winged [[Victoria (mythology)|Victory]], ancient Roman fresco of the Neronian era from [[Pompeii]]]]
[[File:Roman Empire 125.png|thumb|upright=1.35|The Roman Empire under [[Hadrian]] (ruled 117–138) showing the location of the Roman legions deployed in 125 AD]]

After the [[Punic Wars]], the Roman army comprised professional soldiers who volunteered for 20 years of active duty and five as reserves. The transition to a professional military began during the late Republic and was one of the many profound shifts away from republicanism, under which an army of [[conscripts|conscript citizens]] defended the homeland against a specific threat. The Romans expanded their war machine by "organizing the communities that they conquered in Italy into a system that generated huge reservoirs of manpower for their army".<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Tignor |first1=Robert |last2=Adelman |first2=Jeremy |date=2014 |title=Worlds Together, Worlds Apart: A History of the World |volume=1 - Beginnings through the Fifteenth Century |edition=4th |publisher=[[W. W. Norton & Company]] |isbn=9780393922080 |page=257 |display-authors=1 |url-access=limited |url=https://archive.org/details/worldstogetherwo0001tign/mode/1up }}</ref> By Imperial times, military service was a full-time career.{{sfnp|Edmondson|1996|pp=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=PpKop1jpJnwC&pg=PA111 111–2]}} The pervasiveness of military garrisons throughout the Empire was a major influence in the process of [[Romanization (cultural)|Romanization]].{{sfnp|Bohec|2001|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=r2hBqYtZWNEC&pg=PA9 9]}}

The primary mission of the military of the early empire was to preserve the {{lang|la|[[Pax Romana]]}}.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Hekster |first=Olivier J. |date=2007 |chapter=Fighting for Rome: The Emperor as a Military Leader |editor1=Lukas de Blois |editor2=Elio Lo Cascio  |editor-link2=Elio Lo Cascio |title=Impact of the Roman Army (200 BC–AD 476) |publisher=[[Brill Publishers|Brill]] |page=96 |isbn=9789004160446 |url=https://archive.org/details/oapen-20.500.12657-38152 }}</ref> The three major divisions of the military were:
* the garrison at Rome, comprising the [[Praetorian Guard]], the ''[[cohortes urbanae]]'' and the ''[[vigiles]]'', who functioned as police and firefighters;
* the provincial army, comprising the [[Roman legions]] and the auxiliaries provided by the provinces (''[[auxilia]]'');
* the [[Roman navy|navy]].
[[File:042 Conrad Cichorius, Die Reliefs der Traianssäule, Tafel XLII.jpg|thumb|upright=1.6|Relief panel from [[Trajan's Column]] in Rome, showing the building of a fort and the reception of a [[Dacia]]n embassy]]

Through his military reforms, which included consolidating or disbanding units of questionable loyalty, Augustus regularized the legion. A legion was organized into ten [[Cohort (military unit)|cohorts]], each of which comprised six [[centuria|centuries]], with a century further made up of ten squads (''[[Contubernium (Roman army unit)|contubernia]]''); the exact size of the Imperial legion, which was likely determined by [[military logistics|logistics]], has been estimated to range from 4,800 to 5,280.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Roth |first=Jonathan |date=1994 |title=The Size and Organization of the Roman Imperial Legion |journal=Historia: Zeitschrift für Alte Geschichte |volume=43 |issue=3 |pages=346–362 |jstor=4436338 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/4436338 }}</ref> After Germanic tribes wiped out three legions in the [[Battle of the Teutoburg Forest]] in 9 AD, the number of legions was increased from 25 to around 30.{{sfnp|Goldsworthy|2003|p=183}} The army had about 300,000 soldiers in the 1st century, and under 400,000 in the 2nd, "significantly smaller" than the collective armed forces of the conquered territories. No more than 2% of adult males living in the Empire served in the Imperial army.{{r|n=MorrisScheidel2009_196|r={{harvp|Morris|Scheidel|2009|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=XnDtcvRwsrgC&pg=PA196 196]}}.}} Augustus also created the [[Praetorian Guard]]: nine cohorts, ostensibly to maintain the public peace, which were garrisoned in Italy. Better paid than the legionaries, the Praetorians served only sixteen years.<ref>{{Cite book |editor-last=Penrose |editor-first=Jane |date=2005 |title=Rome and Her Enemies: An Empire Created and Destroyed by War |publisher=[[Osprey Publishing|Osprey]] |at=Part 3 - Early Empire 27 BC–AD 235 (p. [https://archive.org/details/romeherenemiesem0000unse/page/183/mode/1up 183]) |isbn=9781841769325 }}</ref>

The ''[[auxilia]]'' were recruited from among the non-citizens. Organized in smaller units of roughly cohort strength, they were paid less than the legionaries, and after 25 years of service were rewarded with [[Roman citizenship]], also extended to their sons. According to [[Tacitus]]{{sfnp|Tacitus' Annals||loc=Book [[s:The Annals (Tacitus)/Book 4#5|4.5]]}} there were roughly as many auxiliaries as there were legionaries—thus, around 125,000 men, implying approximately 250 auxiliary regiments.{{sfnp|Goldsworthy|2003|p=51}} The [[Roman cavalry]] of the earliest Empire were primarily from Celtic, Hispanic or Germanic areas. Several aspects of training and equipment derived from the Celts.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Connolly |first=Peter |author-link=Peter Connolly (classical scholar) |date=1986 |title=A Reconstruction of a Roman Saddle |journal=Britannia |volume=17 |pages=353–355 |doi=10.2307/526559 |jstor=526559 |s2cid=164155025}}{{br}}^ {{Cite journal |last1=Connolly |first1=Peter |last2=Van Driel-Murray |first2=Carol |author-link2=Carol van Driel-Murray |date=1991 |title=The Roman Cavalry Saddle |journal=Britannia |volume=22 |pages=33–50 |doi=10.2307/526629 |jstor=526629 |s2cid=161535316}}</ref>

The [[Roman navy]] not only aided in the supply and transport of the legions but also in the protection of the [[Limes (Roman Empire)|frontiers]] along the rivers [[Rhine]] and [[Danube]]. Another duty was protecting maritime trade against pirates. It patrolled the Mediterranean, parts of the [[Atlantic|North Atlantic]] coasts, and the [[Black Sea]]. Nevertheless, the army was considered the senior and more prestigious branch.{{sfnp|Goldsworthy|2003|p=114}}

===Provincial government===

An [[Annexation|annexed territory]] became a [[Roman province]] in three steps: making a register of cities, taking a census, and surveying the land.{{sfnp|Potter|2009|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=g4ZmqsyC5kEC&pg=PA183 183]}} Further government recordkeeping included births and deaths, real estate transactions, taxes, and juridical proceedings.{{efn|"Most government records that are preserved come from Roman Egypt, where the climate preserved the papyri."{{sfnp|Potter|2009|pp=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=g4ZmqsyC5kEC&pg=PA177 177–9]}}}} In the 1st and 2nd centuries, the central government sent out around 160 officials annually to govern outside Italy.{{r|Potter2009_179}} Among these officials were the [[Roman governor]]s: [[executive magistrates of the Roman Empire|magistrates elected at Rome]] who in the name of the [[SPQR|Roman people]] governed [[senatorial province]]s; or governors, usually of equestrian rank, who held their ''imperium'' on behalf of the emperor in [[imperial province]]s, most notably [[Roman Egypt]].{{efn|"The exclusion of Egypt from the senatorial provinces dates to the rise of Octavian before he became Augustus: Egypt had been the stronghold of his last opposition, [[Mark Antony]] and his ally [[Cleopatra]]."{{r|Potter2009_179}}}} A governor had to make himself accessible to the people he governed, but he could delegate various duties.{{r|n=Potter2009_180|r={{harvp|Potter|2009|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=g4ZmqsyC5kEC&pg=PA180 180]}}.}} His staff, however, was minimal: his official attendants (''[[apparitor]]es''), including [[lictor]]s, heralds, messengers, [[Scriba (ancient Rome)|scribes]], and bodyguards; [[legates]], both civil and military, usually of equestrian rank; and friends who accompanied him unofficially.{{r|Potter2009_180}}

Other officials were appointed as supervisors of government finances.{{r|Potter2009_179}} Separating fiscal responsibility from justice and administration was a reform of the Imperial era, to avoid provincial governors and [[tax farmers]] exploiting local populations for personal gain.{{sfnp|Potter|2009|pp=179, [https://books.google.ca/books?id=g4ZmqsyC5kEC&pg=PA187 187]}} Equestrian [[Procurator (Roman)|procurators]], whose authority was originally "extra-judicial and extra-constitutional", managed both state-owned property and the personal property of the emperor (''[[res privata]]'').{{r|Potter2009_180}} Because Roman government officials were few, a provincial who needed help with a legal dispute or criminal case might seek out any Roman perceived to have some official capacity.{{r|Potter2009_180}}{{sfnp|Fuhrmann|2012|pp=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=yspXtgPVoJQC&pg=PA197 197], 214, [https://books.google.ca/books?id=yspXtgPVoJQC&pg=PA224 224]}}

In the High Empire, Italy was legally distinguished from the provinces, and along with some favored provincial communities, enjoyed immunity from the [[Tributum soli|property tax]] and [[Tributum capitis|poll tax]]. However, under the Emperor [[Diocletian]], Italy lost these privileges and was subdivided into [[Roman diocese|provinces]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Cooley |first=Alison E. |author-link=Alison E. Cooley |date=2016 |chapter=Italy during the High Empire, from the Flavians to Diocletian |editor-last=Cooley |editor-first=Alison E. |title=A Companion to Roman Italy |publisher=[[Wiley-Blackwell]] |pages=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=Lk0gDAAAQBAJ&pg=PA130 130–1] |isbn=9781444339260 }}</ref>

===Law===
{{Main|Roman law}}

{{Multiple image
| align     = right
| direction = horizontal
| image1    = Giovane con rotolo.JPG
| width1    = 220
| image2    = MANNapoli 120620 a Fresco young man with rolls from Pompeii Italy.jpg
| width2    = 220
| footer    = [[Roman portraiture]] [[fresco]]s from [[Pompeii]], 1st century AD, depicting two different men wearing [[laurel wreath]]s, one holding the ''[[rotulus]]'' ([[blond]]ish figure, left), the other a ''[[History of scrolls|volumen]]'' ([[Brown hair|brunet]] figure, right), both made of [[papyrus]]
}}

Roman courts held [[original jurisdiction]] over cases involving Roman citizens throughout the empire, but there were too few judicial functionaries to impose Roman law uniformly in the provinces. Most parts of the Eastern Empire already had well-established law codes and juridical procedures.{{r|GarnseySaller2015_107_11}} Generally, it was Roman policy to respect the ''mos regionis'' ("regional tradition" or "law of the land") and to regard local laws as a source of legal precedent and social stability.{{r|GarnseySaller2015_107_11}}{{r|n=Potter2009_184_5|r={{harvp|Potter|2009|pp=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=g4ZmqsyC5kEC&pg=PA184 184–5]}}.}} The compatibility of Roman and local law was thought to reflect an underlying ''[[ius gentium]]'', the "law of nations" or [[international law]] regarded as common and customary.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Bozeman |first=Adda B. |date=2002 |orig-date=1960 |title=Politics and Culture in International History from the Ancient Near East to the Opening of the Modern Age |edition=2nd |publisher=[[Transaction Publishers]] |pages=208–20 |isbn=1560007354 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Nx0uDwAAQBAJ }}</ref> If provincial law conflicted with Roman law or custom, Roman courts heard [[Appellate court|appeals]], and the emperor held final decision-making authority.{{r|GarnseySaller2015_107_11|Potter2009_184_5}}{{Efn|This practice was established in the Republic; see for instance the case of [[Gaius Valerius Flaccus#Contrebian water rights|Contrebian water rights]] heard by G. Valerius Flaccus as governor of [[Hispania]] in the 90s–80s BC.}}

In the West, law had been administered on a highly localized or tribal basis, and [[private property rights]] may have been a novelty of the Roman era, particularly among [[Celts]]. Roman law facilitated the acquisition of wealth by a pro-Roman elite.{{r|GarnseySaller2015_107_11}} The extension of universal citizenship to all free inhabitants of the Empire in 212 required the uniform application of Roman law, replacing local law codes that had applied to non-citizens. Diocletian's efforts to stabilize the Empire after the [[Crisis of the Third Century]] included two major compilations of law in four years, the ''[[Codex Gregorianus]]'' and the ''[[Codex Hermogenianus]]'', to guide provincial administrators in setting consistent legal standards.<ref>{{Cite book |last=DePalma Digeser |first=Elizabeth |author-link=Elizabeth Digeser |date=2000 |title=The Making of a Christian Empire: Lactantius and Rome |publisher=[[Cornell University Press|CUP]] |page=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=wbjbgRl4QTkC&pg=PA53 53] |isbn=0801435943 }}</ref>

The pervasiveness of Roman law throughout Western Europe enormously influenced the Western legal tradition, reflected by continued use of [[List of Latin legal terms|Latin legal terminology]] in modern law.

===Taxation===
{{Further|Taxation in ancient Rome}}
[[File:Foro_romano_tempio_Saturno_09feb08_01.jpg|thumb|left|The [[Temple of Saturn]], a religious monument that housed the treasury in ancient Rome]]

Taxation under the Empire amounted to about 5% of its [[Roman gross domestic product|gross product]].{{sfnp|Morris|Scheidel|2009|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=XnDtcvRwsrgC&pg=PA183 183]}} The typical tax rate for individuals ranged from 2 to 5%.{{r|n=Potter2009_187|r={{harvp|Potter|2009|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=g4ZmqsyC5kEC&pg=PA187 187]}}.}} The tax code was "bewildering" in its complicated system of [[direct taxation|direct]] and [[indirect taxes]], some paid in cash and some [[barter|in kind]]. Taxes might be specific to a province, or kinds of properties such as [[fisheries]]; they might be temporary.{{sfnp|Potter|2009|pp=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=g4ZmqsyC5kEC&pg=PA185 185–7]}} Tax collection was justified by the need to maintain the military,{{r|MorrisScheidel2009_184}}{{r|n=Potter2009_185|r={{harvp|Potter|2009|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=g4ZmqsyC5kEC&pg=PA185 185]}}.}} and taxpayers sometimes got a refund if the army captured a surplus of booty.{{r|Potter2009_185}} In-kind taxes were accepted from less-[[monetization|monetized]] areas, particularly those who could supply grain or goods to army camps.{{r|Potter2009_188|r={{harvp|Potter|2009|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=g4ZmqsyC5kEC&pg=PA188 188]}}.}}

The primary source of direct tax revenue was individuals, who paid a [[poll tax]] and a tax on their land, construed as a tax on its produce or productive capacity.{{r|Potter2009_187}} Tax obligations were determined by the census: each head of household provided a headcount of his household, as well as an accounting of his property.{{sfnp|Potter|2009|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=g4ZmqsyC5kEC&pg=PA186 186]}} A major source of indirect-tax revenue was the ''portoria'', customs and tolls on trade, including among provinces.{{r|Potter2009_187}} Towards the end of his reign, Augustus instituted a 4% tax on the sale of slaves,{{sfnp|Dio's Roman History||loc=Vol. 6, [https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Cassius_Dio/55*.html#31 Book 55, 31.4] (p. 475)}} which Nero shifted from the purchaser to the dealers, who responded by raising their prices.{{sfnp|Tacitus' Annals||loc=Book [[s:The Annals (Tacitus)/Book 13#31|13.31]]}} An owner who manumitted a slave paid a "freedom tax", calculated at 5% of value.{{Efn|This was the ''vicesima libertatis'', "the twentieth for freedom"{{r|Potter2009_187}}}} An [[inheritance tax]] of 5% was assessed when Roman citizens above a certain net worth left property to anyone outside their immediate family. Revenues from the estate tax and from an auction tax went towards the veterans' pension fund (''[[aerarium militare]]'').{{r|Potter2009_187}}

Low taxes helped the Roman aristocracy increase their wealth, which equalled or exceeded the revenues of the central government. An emperor sometimes replenished his treasury by confiscating the estates of the "super-rich", but in the later period, the [[tax resistance|resistance]] of the wealthy to paying taxes was one of the factors contributing to the collapse of the Empire.{{r|MorrisScheidel2009_184}}

==Economy==
{{Main|Roman economy}}

[[File:Green glass Roman cup unearthed at Eastern Han tomb, Guixian, China.jpg|thumb|right|A green [[Roman glass]] cup unearthed from an [[Eastern Han dynasty]] (25–220 AD) tomb in [[Guangxi]], China]]

The Empire is best thought of as a network of regional economies, based on a form of "political capitalism" in which the state regulated commerce to assure its own revenues.{{sfnp|Potter|2009|pp=286, [https://books.google.ca/books?id=g4ZmqsyC5kEC&pg=PA295 295]}} Economic growth, though not comparable to modern economies, was greater than that of most other societies prior to [[Industrial Revolution|industrialization]].{{sfnp|Potter|2009|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=g4ZmqsyC5kEC&pg=PA286 286]}} Territorial conquests permitted a large-scale reorganization of [[land use]] that resulted in agricultural surplus and specialization, particularly in north Africa.{{r|n=Potter2009_285|r={{harvp|Potter|2009|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=g4ZmqsyC5kEC&pg=PA285 285]}}.}} Some cities were known for particular industries. The scale of urban building indicates a significant construction industry.{{r|Potter2009_285}} Papyri preserve complex accounting methods that suggest elements of [[economic rationalism]],{{r|Potter2009_285}} and the Empire was highly monetized.{{sfnp|Potter|2009|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=g4ZmqsyC5kEC&pg=PA292 292]}} Although the means of communication and transport were limited in antiquity, transportation in the 1st and 2nd centuries expanded greatly, and trade routes connected regional economies.{{sfnp|Potter|2009|pp=285–6, [https://books.google.ca/books?id=g4ZmqsyC5kEC&pg=PA296 296 ff]}} The [[Economics of the Roman army|supply contracts for the army]] drew on local suppliers near the base (''[[castrum]]''), throughout the province, and across provincial borders.{{sfnp|Potter|2009|p=296}}
[[Economic historians]] vary in their calculations of the gross domestic product during the Principate.<ref>{{Cite book |editor-last1=Scheidel |editor-first1=Walter |editor-link1=Walter Scheidel |editor-last2=Morris |editor-first2=Ian |editor-link2=Ian Morris (historian) |editor-last3=Saller |editor-first3=Richard P. |editor-link3=Richard Saller |date=2007 |title=The Cambridge Economic History of the Greco-Roman World |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press|BUP]] |isbn=9780521780537 }}</ref>{{pn|date=September 2026}} In the sample years of 14, 100, and 150 AD, estimates of per capita GDP range from 166 to 380 ''[[Sestertius|HS]]''. The GDP per capita of [[Italia (Roman Empire)|Italy]] is estimated as 40<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lo Cascio |first1=Elio |author-link=Elio Lo Cascio |last2=Malanima |first2=Paolo |author-link2=Paolo Malanima |date=2009 |title=GDP in Pre-Modern Agrarian Economies (1–1820 AD). A Revision of the Estimates |journal=Rivista di Storia Economica |volume=25 |issue=3 |pages=391–420 (391–401) |doi=10.1410/30919:y:2009:i:3:p:391-420 |doi-broken-date=15 October 2026 |access-date=18 September 2026 |url=https://EconPapers.repec.org/RePEc:mul:jrkmxm:doi:10.1410/30919:y:2009:i:3:p:391-420}}</ref> to 66%<ref>{{Cite book |last=Maddison |first=Angus |author-link=Angus Maddison |date=2007 |title=Contours of the World Economy, 1–2030 AD. Essays in Macro-Economic History |publisher=[[OUP]] |pages=47–51 |isbn=9780199227211 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=a-JGGp2suQUC }}</ref> higher than in the rest of the Empire, due to tax transfers from the provinces and the concentration of elite income.

Economic dynamism resulted in social mobility. Although aristocratic values permeated traditional elite society, wealth requirements for [[#Census rank|rank]] indicate a strong tendency towards [[plutocracy]]. Prestige could be obtained through investing one's wealth in grand estates or townhouses, luxury items, [[#Spectacles|public entertainments]], funerary monuments, and [[votum|religious dedications]]. Guilds (''[[collegia]]'') and corporations (''corpora'') provided support for individuals to succeed through networking.{{r|Verboven_Peachin}} "There can be little doubt that the lower classes of ... provincial towns of the Roman Empire enjoyed a high [[standard of living]] not equaled again in Western Europe until the 19th century".<ref>{{Cite book |last=Dyson |first=Stephen L. |date=1992 |title=Community and Society in Roman Italy |publisher=[[JHUP]] |at=p. [https://archive.org/details/communitysociety0000dyso/page/177/mode/1up?q=equalled 177] |isbn=0801841755  |postscript=none }}, quoting {{Cite book |last=Packer |first=J.E. |date=1975 |chapter=Middle and Lower Class Housing in Pompeii and Herculaneum: A Preliminary Survey |editor1=Bernard Andreae |editor2=Helmut Kyrieleis |title=Neue Forschungen in Pompeji und den anderen vom Vesuvausbruch 79 n. Chr. verschütteten Städten |location=[[Recklinghausen]] |publisher=Bongers |pages=133–42 |isbn=3764702702 }}</ref> Households in the top 1.5% of [[income distribution]] captured about 20% of income. The "vast majority" produced more than half of the total income, but lived near [[subsistence]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Scheidel |first1=Walter |author-link=Walter Scheidel |last2=Friesen |first2=Steven J. |date=2009 |title=The Size of the Economy and the Distribution of Income in the Roman Empire |journal=Journal of Roman Studies |volume=99 |pages=61–91 |doi=10.3815/007543509789745223 |s2cid=202968244 |url=https://archive.org/details/scheidel-friesen-2009-roman-economy/mode/1up |access-date=18 September 2026 }}</ref>

===Currency and banking===
<!--Linked from infobox above-->
{{See also|Roman currency|Roman finance}}
[[File:HADRIANUS RIC II 938-789065.jpg|thumb|''[[Sestertius]]'' issued under [[Hadrian]] {{Circa|134–138 AD}}]]
[[File:Solidus Constantine II-heraclea RIC vII 101.jpg|thumb|''[[Solidus]]'' issued in the name of [[Constantine II (emperor)|Constantine II]] as ''caesar'' by Constantine the Great, depicting [[Victoria (mythology)|Victoria]] on the [[Obverse and reverse|reverse]], one of the last deities to commonly appear on Roman coins, which gradually transformed into an [[Angel#Christianity|angel]] under Christian rule<ref>{{Cite book |editor-last1=Temporini |editor-first1=Hildegard  |editor-last2=Haase |editor-first2=Wolfgang |date=1981 |title=Aufstieg und Niedergang der römischen Welt / Rise and Decline of the Roman World |volume=17/2. Teilband Religion |publisher=[[De Gruyter]] |postscript=none }}:{{br}}* {{Cite book |last=Fears |first=J. Rufus |author-link=J. Rufus Fears |title=The Theology of Victory at Rome: Approaches and Problem |pages=752, 824 }}{{br}}* {{Cite book |last=Fears |first=J. Rufus |author-link=J. Rufus Fears |title=The Cult of Virtues and Roman Imperial Ideology |page=908 }}</ref>]]

The early Empire was monetized to a near-universal extent, using money as a way to express [[price]]s and [[debt]]s.{{r|n=KesslerTemin2010_137ff|r=Kessler, David; Temin, Peter. ''Money and Prices in the Early Roman Empire''. In {{harvp|Harris|2010|pp= [https://archive.org/details/monetarysystemso0000unse/page/137/mode/1up 137 ff.]}}.}} The ''[[sestertius]]'' (English "sesterces", symbolized as ''HS'') was the basic unit of reckoning value into the 4th century,{{r|n=Harl1996_12535|r={{Cite book |last=Harl |first=Kenneth W. |author-link=Kenneth W. Harl |date=19 June 1996 |title=Coinage in the Roman Economy, 300 B.C. to A.D. 700 |publisher=[[Johns Hopkins University Press|JHUO]] |pages=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=5yPDL0EykeAC&pg=PA125 125–35] |isbn=0801852919 }}}} though the silver ''[[denarius]]'', worth four sesterces, was also used beginning in the [[Severan dynasty]].{{sfnp|Bowman|Garnsey|Cameron|2005|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=MNSyT_PuYVMC&pg=PA333 333]}} The smallest coin commonly circulated was the bronze ''[[As (Roman coin)|as]]'', one-tenth ''denarius''.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Wells |first=Colin M. |author-link=Colin Wells (historian) |date=2004 |orig-date=1984 |title=The Roman Empire |edition=2nd reprinted |publisher=[[Harvard University Press|HUP]] |page=[https://archive.org/details/romanempire00well/page/8/mode/1up 8] |isbn=0674777700 }}</ref> [[Bullion]] and [[ingot]]s seem not to have counted as ''pecunia'' ("money") and were used only on the frontiers. Romans in the first and second centuries counted coins, rather than weighing them—an indication that the coin was valued on its face. This tendency towards [[fiat money]] led to the [[debasement]] of Roman coinage in the later Empire.{{r|n=Harris2010_174ff|r=Harris, William V. ''The Nature of Roman Money''. In {{harvp|Harris|2010|pp= [https://archive.org/details/monetarysystemso0000unse/page/174/mode/1up 174 ff.]}}.}} The standardization of money throughout the Empire promoted trade and market integration.{{r|KesslerTemin2010_137ff}} The high amount of metal coinage in circulation increased the [[money supply]] for trading or saving.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Scheidel|first=Walter |author-link=Walter Scheidel |date=2010 |chapter=The Monetary Systems of the Han and Roman Empires |editor-last=Scheidel |editor-first=Walter |title=Rome and China. Comparative Perspectives on Ancient World Empires |publisher=[[OUP]] |pages=137–207 ([https://books.google.ca/books?id=Fz8I3INERwsC&pg=PA205 205]) |isbn=9780199758357 }}</ref>

Rome had no [[central bank]], and regulation of the banking system was minimal. Banks of classical antiquity typically kept [[fractional reserve banking|less in reserves]] than the full total of customers' [[deposits]]. A typical bank had fairly limited [[Financial capital|capital]], and often only one principal. [[Seneca the Younger|Seneca]] assumes that anyone involved in [[Roman commerce]] needs access to [[credit]].{{r|Harris2010_174ff}} A professional deposit banker received and held deposits for a fixed or indefinite term, and lent money to third parties. The senatorial elite were involved heavily in private lending, both as creditors and borrowers.{{r|Harris2010_174ff}}<ref>{{Cite book |last=Andreau |first=Jean |author-link=Jean Andreau |date=1999 |title=Banking and Business in the Roman World |translator=Janet Lloyd |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press|CUP]] |page=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=ZnhaVqk6siEC&pg=PA2 2] |isbn=0521389321 }}</ref> The holder of a debt could use it as a means of payment by transferring it to another party, without cash changing hands. Although it has sometimes been thought that ancient Rome lacked [[negotiable instrument|documentary transactions]], the system of banks throughout the Empire permitted the exchange of large sums without physically transferring coins, in part because of the risks of moving large amounts of cash. Only one serious credit shortage is known to have occurred in the early Empire, in 33 AD;{{sfnp|Tacitus' Annals||loc=Book [[s:The Annals (Tacitus)/Book 6#17|6.17]]}} generally, available capital exceeded the amount needed by borrowers.{{r|Harris2010_174ff}} The central government itself did not borrow money, and without [[public debt]] had to fund [[deficits]] from cash reserves.{{sfnp|Duncan-Jones|1994|pp=3–4}}

Emperors of the [[Antonine dynasty|Antonine]] and [[Severan]] dynasties debased the currency, particularly the ''[[denarius]]'', under the pressures of meeting military payrolls.{{r|Harl1996_12535}} Sudden inflation under [[Commodus]] damaged the credit market.{{r|Harris2010_174ff}} In the mid-200s, the supply of [[specie]] contracted sharply.{{r|Harl1996_12535}} Conditions during the [[Crisis of the Third Century]]—such as reductions in long-distance trade, disruption of mining operations, and the physical transfer of gold coinage outside the empire by invading enemies—greatly diminished the money supply and the banking sector.{{r|Harl1996_12535|Harris2010_174ff}} Although Roman coinage had long been fiat money or [[fiduciary currency]], general economic anxieties came to a head under [[Aurelian]], and bankers lost confidence in coins. Despite [[Diocletian]]'s introduction of the gold ''[[solidus]]'' and monetary reforms, the credit market of the Empire never recovered its former robustness.{{r|Harris2010_174ff}}

===Mining and metallurgy===
{{Main|Mining in ancient Rome|Roman metallurgy}}

[[File:Panorámica de Las Médulas.jpg|thumb|Landscape resulting from the {{Lang|la|[[ruina montium]]}} mining technique at [[Las Médulas]], Spain, one of the most important gold mines in the Roman Empire]]
The main mining regions of the Empire were the Iberian Peninsula (silver, copper, lead, iron and gold);{{r|DK_VisualHistory_276}} Gaul (gold, silver, iron);<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Silva-Sánchez |first1=Noemí |last2=Armada |first2=Xose-Lois |date=2023 |title=Environmental Impact of Roman Mining and Metallurgy and Its Correlation with the Archaeological Evidence: A European Perspective |journal=Environmental Archaeology |page=1-15 |doi=10.1080/14614103.2023.2181295 |issn=1461-4103 |url=https://doi.org/10.1080/14614103.2023.2181295 }}</ref> Britain (mainly iron, lead, tin),<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Edmondson |first=J. C. |date=1989 |title=Mining in the Later Roman Empire and beyond: Continuity or Disruption? |journal=The Journal of Roman Studies |volume=79 |pages=84–102 |doi=10.2307/301182 |jstor=301182 |issn=0075-4358 |s2cid=161980467|url-access=limited |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/301182 }}</ref> the [[Danubian provinces]] (gold, iron);{{r|n=Hirt2020_123|r={{cite book |last=Hirt |first=Alfred M. |date=2020 |chapter=Gold and Silver Mining in the Roman Empire |editor-last=Butcher |editor-first=Kevin |title=Debasement. Manipulation of Coin Standards in Pre-Modern Monetary Systems |publisher=[[Casemate Publishers#History|Oxbow books]] |pages=12–3 |isbn=9781789253986 |chapter-url=https://livrepository.liverpool.ac.uk/3066254/3/Hirt%20Warwick%20Publ.%20III%20%28revised%29.pdf }}}} [[Macedonia (Roman province)|Macedonia]] and [[Thracia|Thrace]] (gold, silver); and Asia Minor (gold, silver, iron, tin). Intensive large-scale mining—of alluvial deposits, and by means of [[open-cast mining]] and [[underground mining]]—took place from the reign of Augustus up to the early 3rd century, when the instability of the Empire disrupted production.{{r|Hirt2020_123}}

[[Hydraulic mining]] allowed [[base metal|base]] and [[precious metal]]s to be extracted on a proto-industrial scale.<ref name="wilson">{{Cite journal |last=Wilson |first=Andrew |author-link=Andrew Wilson (classical archaeologist) |date=2002 |title=Machines, Power and the Ancient Economy |journal=The Journal of Roman Studies |volume=92 |pages=1–32 |doi=10.2307/3184857 |jstor=3184857 |s2cid=154629776 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/3184857 }}</ref> The total annual iron output is estimated at 82,500&nbsp;[[tonnes]].{{efn|Healy (1978) assumes a productive capacity of {{Circa|1.5&nbsp;kg}} per capita.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Healy |first=John F. |author-link=John F. Healy |date=1978 |title=Mining and Metallurgy in the Greek and Roman World |publisher=[[Thames & Hudson]] |page=196 |isbn=0500400350 }}</ref>}}<ref>{{Cite book |last=Craddock |first=Paul T. |chapter=Mining and Metallurgy |date=2008 |editor-last=Oleson |editor-first=John Peter |editor-link=John Peter Oleson |title=The Oxford Handbook of Engineering and Technology in the Classical World |publisher=[[OUP]] |page=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=jrsVDAAAQBAJ&pg=PA108 108] |isbn=9780195187311 }}{{br}}^ {{Cite book |last1=Sim |first1=David |last2=Ridge |first2=Isabel |date=2002 |title=Iron for the Eagles. The Iron Industry of Roman Britain |publisher=[[The History Press|Tempus]] |page=23 |isbn=0752498274 }}</ref> Copper and lead production levels were unmatched until the [[Industrial Revolution]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hong |first1=S. |last2=Candelone |first2=J.-P. |last3=Patterson |first3=C. C. |last4=Boutron |first4=C. F. |date=1996 |title=History of Ancient Copper Smelting Pollution During Roman and Medieval Times Recorded in Greenland Ice |journal=Science |volume=272 |issue=5259 |page=246 |doi=10.1126/science.272.5259.246 |bibcode=1996Sci...272..246H |s2cid=176767223 |url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.272.5259.246 }}{{br}}^ {{Cite journal |last1=Hong |first1=S |last2=Candelone |first2=J. P. |last3=Patterson |first3=C. C. |last4=Boutron |first4=C. F. |date=1994 |title=Greenland Ice Evidence of Hemispheric Lead Pollution Two Millennia Ago by Greek and Roman Civilizations  |journal=Science |volume=265 |issue=5180 |pmid=17797222 |pages=1841–1843 |doi=10.1126/science.265.5180.1841 |bibcode=1994Sci...265.1841H |s2cid=45080402 |url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.265.5180.1841 }}</ref>{{r|n=DeCallataÿ2015_361372|r={{Cite journal |last=de Callataÿ |first=François |date=2005 |title=The Graeco-Roman economy in the super long-run: Lead, copper, and shipwrecks |url-access=registration |journal=Journal of Roman Archaeology |volume=18 |pages=361–372 |doi=10.1017/S104775940000742X |s2cid=232346123 |url=https://www.academia.edu/2236050 }}}} At its peak around the mid-2nd century, the Roman silver stock is estimated at 10,000&nbsp;t, five to ten times larger than the combined silver mass of [[Early Middle Ages|medieval Europe]] and the [[Abbasid Caliphate|Caliphate]] around 800&nbsp;AD.{{r|DeCallataÿ2015_361372}}<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Patterson |first=C. C. |date=1972 |title=Silver Stocks and Losses in Ancient and Medieval Times |journal=The Economic History Review |volume=25 |issue=2 |pages=205–235 (tables 2, 6) |doi=10.2307/2593904 |jstor=2593904 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2593904 }}</ref> As an indication of the scale of Roman metal production, lead pollution in the [[Greenland ice sheet]] quadrupled over prehistoric levels during the Imperial era and dropped thereafter.{{sfnp|Morris|Scheidel|2009|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=XnDtcvRwsrgC&pg=PA197 197]}}

===Transportation and communication===
{{Further|Cursus publicus}}
[[File:TabulaPeutingeriana Roma.jpg|thumb|The [[Tabula Peutingeriana]] ([[Latin]] for "The Peutinger Map") an ''[[Itinerarium]]'', often assumed to be based on the Roman ''cursus publicus'']]
The Empire completely encircled the Mediterranean, which they called "our sea" (''[[Mare Nostrum]]'').{{sfnp|Greene|1990|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=k7SUh_3lcP4C&pg=PA17 17]}} Roman sailing vessels navigated the Mediterranean as well as major rivers.{{r|BowmanEtal2000_721}} Transport by water was preferred where possible, as moving commodities by land was more difficult.{{sfnp|Bowman|Garnsey|Rathbone|2000|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=mhNUGgG2eacC&pg=PA714 714]}} Vehicles, wheels, and ships indicate the existence of a great number of skilled woodworkers.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Ulrich |first=Roger Bradley |date=2007 |title=Roman Woodworking |publisher=[[Yale University Press|YUP]] |pages=[https://archive.org/details/RomanWoodworking/page/n17/mode/1up 1–2] |isbn=9780300103410 }}</ref>

Land transport utilized the advanced system of [[Roman roads]], called "''viae''". These roads were primarily built for military purposes,<ref>{{Cite book |last=Van Tilburg |first=Cornelis |date=2007 |title=Traffic and Congestion in the Roman Empire |publisher=[[Routledge]] |page=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=0i5LHy4b6kgC&pg=PA33 33] |isbn=9780415409995 }}</ref> but also served commercial ends. The in-kind taxes paid by communities included the provision of personnel, animals, or vehicles for the ''[[cursus publicus]]'', the state mail and transport service established by Augustus.{{r|Potter2009_188}} Relay stations were located along the roads every seven to twelve [[Roman mile]]s, and tended to grow into villages or trading posts.{{r|n=Stambaugh1988_253|r={{harvp|Stambaugh|1988|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=k0mZufizhH0C&pg=PA253 253]}}.}} A ''[[mansio]]'' (plural ''mansiones'') was a privately run service station franchised by the imperial bureaucracy for the ''cursus publicus''. The distance between ''mansiones'' was determined by how far a wagon could travel in a day.{{r|Stambaugh1988_253}} Carts were usually pulled by mules, travelling about 4&nbsp;mph.<ref>{{cite book |last=Laurence |first=Ray |author-link=Ray Laurence |date=2012 |orig-date=1998 |chapter=Land Transport in Roman Italy: Costs, Practice and the Economy |editor1=Helen Parkins |editor2=Christopher Smith |editor-link2=Christopher Smith (classicist)  |title=Trade, Traders and the Ancient City |publisher=[[Routledge]] |page=129 |isbn=9780415518925 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=v6OXL9yi2fMC }}</ref>

===Trade and commodities===
{{See also|Roman commerce|Indo-Roman trade relations|Sino-Roman relations}}

Roman provinces traded among themselves, but trade extended outside the frontiers to regions as far away as [[Ancient China|China]] and [[Gupta Empire|India]].{{sfnp|Bowman|Garnsey|Rathbone|2000|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=mhNUGgG2eacC&pg=PA713 713]}} Chinese trade was mostly conducted overland through middlemen along the [[Silk Road]]; Indian trade also occurred by sea from [[Roman Egypt|Egyptian]] ports. The main [[commodity]] was grain.{{sfnp|Bowman|Garnsey|Rathbone|2000|p=710}} Also traded were olive oil, foodstuffs, ''[[garum]]'' ([[fish sauce]]), slaves, ore and manufactured metal objects, fibres and textiles, timber, [[ancient Roman pottery|pottery]], [[Roman glass|glassware]], marble, [[papyrus]], spices and ''[[materia medica]]'', ivory, pearls, and gemstones.{{sfnp|Bowman|Garnsey|Rathbone|2000|pp=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=mhNUGgG2eacC&pg=PA717 717–29]}} Though most provinces could produce wine, [[Ancient Rome and wine|regional varietals]] were desirable and wine was a central trade good.<ref>{{harvp|Bowman|Garnsey|Cameron|2005|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=MNSyT_PuYVMC&pg=PA404 404]}}.{{br}}^ {{harvp|Bowman|Garnsey|Rathbone|2000|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=mhNUGgG2eacC&pg=PA719 719]}}.</ref>

===Labour and occupations===
[[File:Pompeii - Fullonica of Veranius Hypsaeus 1 - MAN.jpg|thumb|right|Workers at a cloth-processing shop, in a painting from the ''[[fullonica]]'' of Veranius Hypsaeus in Pompeii]]
Inscriptions record 268 different occupations in Rome and 85 in Pompeii.{{r|MorrisScheidel2009_196}} Professional associations or trade guilds (''collegia'') are attested for a wide range of occupations, some quite specialized.{{r|Verboven_Peachin}}

Work performed by slaves falls into five general categories: domestic, with epitaphs recording at least 55 different household jobs; [[Slavery in ancient Rome#Public and imperial slaves|imperial or public service]]; urban crafts and services; agriculture; and mining. Convicts provided much of the labour in the mines or quarries, where conditions were notoriously brutal.{{sfnp|Gagarin|2010|p=323}} In practice, there was little division of labour between slave and free,{{r|GarnseySaller2015_107_11}} and most workers were illiterate and without special skills.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Temin |first=Peter |author-link=Peter Temin |date=2004 |title=The Labor Market of the Early Roman Empire |journal=Journal of Interdisciplinary History |volume=34 |issue=4 |pages=513–538 |doi=10.1162/002219504773512525 |s2cid=33380115 |url=https://doi.org/10.1162/002219504773512525 }}</ref> The greatest number of common labourers were employed in agriculture: in Italian industrial farming (''[[latifundia]]''), these may have been mostly slaves, but elsewhere slave farm labour was probably less important.{{r|GarnseySaller2015_107_11}}

Textile and clothing production was a major source of employment. Both textiles and finished garments were traded and products were often named for peoples or towns, like a [[fashion brand|fashion "label"]].{{sfnp|Jones|1960|pp=184–5}} Better ready-to-wear was exported by local businessmen (''negotiatores'' or ''mercatores'').{{sfnp|Jones|1960|p=192}} Finished garments might be retailed by their sales agents, by ''vestiarii'' (clothing dealers), or peddled by itinerant merchants.{{sfnp|Jones|1960|p=192}} The [[fulling|fullers]] (''[[fullonica|fullones]]'') and dye workers (''coloratores'') had their own guilds.{{sfnp|Jones|1960|pp=190–1}} ''Centonarii'' were guild workers who specialized in textile production and the recycling of old clothes into [[patchwork|pieced goods]].{{Efn|The college of ''centonarii'' is an elusive topic in scholarship, since they are also widely attested as urban firefighters.{{sfnp|Vout|1996|p=212}}{{sfnp|Liu|2009|p=150-1}} Historian [[Jinyu Liu]] sees them as "primarily tradesmen and/or manufacturers engaged in the production and distribution of low- or medium-quality woolen textiles and clothing, including felt and its products".{{sfnp|Liu|2009|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=5CsAHkjAkYoC&pg=PA69 69]}}}}

[[File:Cacera Centcelles panoràmica.jpg|thumb|upright=3|center|Recreation of a deer hunt inspired by hunting scenes represented in Roman art]]

==Architecture and engineering==
{{Main|Ancient Roman architecture|Roman engineering|Roman technology}}

[[File:Colosseum in Rome, Italy - April 2007.jpg|thumb|The Flavian Amphitheatre, more commonly known as the [[Colosseum]]]]
The chief [[Ancient Roman architecture|Roman contributions to architecture]] were the [[arch]], [[Vault (architecture)|vault]], and [[dome]]. Some Roman structures still stand today, due in part to sophisticated methods of making cements and [[Roman concrete|concrete]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=MacDonald |first=William L. |author-link=William L. MacDonald |date=1982 |orig-date=1965 |title=The Architecture of the Roman Empire |volume=1 - An introductory study |edition=Revised |publisher=[[Yale University Press|YUP]] |at=Plate 131B |isbn=0300028199 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=jEjyGQretfgC }}{{br}}^ {{Cite journal |last1=Lechtman |first1=Heather N. |author-link1=Heather Lechtman |last2=Hobbs |first2=Linn W. |date=January 1986 |title=Roman Concrete and the Roman Architectural Revolution |journal=[[Journal of the American Ceramic Society]] |volume=3 |pages=81–128 |url=https://scispace.com/papers/roman-concrete-and-the-roman-architectural-revolution-1eoaponn3c }}</ref> [[Roman temple]]s developed [[Etruscan architecture|Etruscan]] and Greek forms, with some distinctive elements. [[Roman roads]] are considered the most advanced built until the early 19th century.{{cn|date=August 2024}}

[[Roman bridges]] were among the first large and lasting bridges, built from stone (and in most cases concrete) with the arch as the basic structure. The largest Roman bridge was [[Trajan's bridge]] over the lower Danube, constructed by [[Apollodorus of Damascus]], which remained for over a millennium the longest bridge to have been built.<ref>{{cite EBO |short=yes |last1=Rodriguez |first1=Emily |last2=Jain |first2=Parul |date=2008–2019 |title=Apollodorus of Damascus |url=https://www.britannica.com/biography/Apollodorus-of-Damascus |display-authors=1 }}{{br}}^ {{Cite journal |last=Sarton |first=George |author-link=George Sarton |date=January 1936 |title=The Unity and Diversity of the Mediterranean World |journal=Osiris |volume=2 |pages=406–463 (430) |doi=10.1086/368462 |s2cid=143379839 |url=https://doi.org/10.1086/368462 }}{{br}}^ {{Cite book |last1=Abdulkarim |first1=Maamoun |date=2003 |chapter=Syria in the times of Apollodorus of Damascus |editor-last=Calcini |editor-first=Giuliana |title=Apollodorus of Damascus and Trajan's Column: From Tradition to Project |location=Rome |publisher=L'Erma di Bretschneider |page=11 |isbn=9788882652333 |url=https://en.lerma.it/libro/9788882652333 }}{{br}}^ {{Cite book |editor-last1=Yan |editor-first1=Hong-Sen |editor-link1=Yan Hong-sen |editor-last2=Ceccarelli |editor-first2=Marco |date=2009 |title=International Symposium on History of Machines and Mechanisms: Proceedings of HMM 2008 |publisher=[[Springer Science+Business Media|Springer]] |isbn=9781402094842 |page=86 }}</ref> The Romans built many [[List of Roman dams and reservoirs|dams and reservoirs]] for water collection, such as the [[Subiaco Dams]], two of which fed the [[Anio Novus]], one of the largest aqueducts of Rome.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Smith |first=Norman |date=1970 |title=The Roman Dams of Subiaco |journal=Technology and Culture |volume=11 |issue=1 |pages=58–68 |doi=10.2307/3102810 |jstor=3102810 |s2cid=111915102 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/3102810 }}{{br}}^ {{Cite book |last=Smith |first=Norman |date=1972 |title=A History of Dams |publisher=[[Kensington Publishing|Citadel Press]] |page=[https://archive.org/details/historyofdams0000smit/page/26/mode/1up?q=Anio 26] |isbn=0806502916 }}{{br}}^ {{Cite journal |last=Schnitter |first=Niklaus |date=1978 |title=Römische Talsperren |lang=de |journal=Antike Welt |volume=9 |issue=2 |pages=25–32 (28) |jstor=44431542 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/44431542 }}</ref>

[[File:Pont du Gard BLS.jpg|thumb|upright=1.3|The [[Pont du Gard]] aqueduct, which crosses the river [[Gardon]] in southern France, is on [[UNESCO]]'s list of [[World Heritage Site]]s.]]
The Romans constructed numerous [[Roman aqueduct|aqueducts]]. ''[[De aquaeductu]]'', a treatise by [[Frontinus]], who served as [[Curator Aquarum|water commissioner]], reflects the administrative importance placed on the water supply. Masonry channels carried water along a precise [[grade (slope)|gradient]], using [[gravity]] alone. It was then collected in tanks and fed through pipes to public fountains, baths, [[Sanitation in ancient Rome|toilets]], or industrial sites.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Chandler |first1=Fiona |last2=Taplin |first2=Sam |last3=Bingham |first3=Jane |date=2002 |title=The Usborne Internet Linked Encyclopedia of the Roman World |publisher=[[Usborne Publishing]] / EDC Publishing |page=[https://archive.org/details/usborneinternetl0000chan_v4w0/page/80/mode/1up?q=gravity 80] |isbn=9781580863865 }}</ref> The main aqueducts in Rome were the [[Aqua Claudia]] and the [[Aqua Marcia]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Forman |first=Joan |date=1975 |title=The Romans |location=[[London]] |publisher=Macdonald Educational |page=[https://archive.org/details/romans00form/page/34/mode/1up?q=limestone 34] |isbn=0382061209 }}</ref> The complex system built to supply Constantinople had its most distant supply drawn from over 120&nbsp;km away along a route of more than 336&nbsp;km.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Crow |first=James |date=2007 |chapter=The Infrastructure of a Great City: Earth, walls and water in Late Antique Constantinople |editor-last1=Lavan |editor-first1=Luke |editor-last2=Zanini |editor-first2=Enrico |editor-last3=Sarantis |editor-first3=Alexander |title=Technology in Transition AD 300–650 |publisher=[[Brill Publishers|Brill]] |isbn=9789004165496 |pages=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=LAgxAJNXhFwC&pg=PA271 271-2] }}</ref> Roman aqueducts were built to remarkably fine [[Engineering tolerance|tolerance]], and to a technological standard not equalled until modern times.{{sfnp|Greene|1990|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=k7SUh_3lcP4C&pg=PA39 39]}} The Romans also used aqueducts in their extensive mining operations across the empire.{{sfnp|Jones|Bird|1972|pp=59–74}}

[[Insulated glazing]] (or "double glazing") was used in the construction of [[thermae|public baths]]. Elite housing in cooler climates might have [[hypocaust]]s, a form of central heating. The Romans were the first culture to assemble all essential components of the much later [[steam engine]]: the crank and connecting rod system, [[Hero of Alexandria|Hero]]'s [[aeolipile]] (generating steam power), the [[Pneumatic cylinder|cylinder]] and [[piston]] (in metal force pumps), non-return [[valves]] (in water pumps), and [[Gear train|gearing]] (in water mills and clocks).<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ritti |first1=Tullia |last2=Grewe |first2=Klaus |last3=Kessener |first3=Paul |date=2007 |title=A Relief of a Water-powered Stone Saw Mill on a Sarcophagus at Hierapolis and its Implications |journal=Journal of Roman Archaeology |volume=20 |pages=138–163 (156, fn. 74) |doi=10.1017/S1047759400005341 |s2cid=161937987 |url=https://doi.org/10.1017/S1047759400005341 }}</ref>

==Daily life==
{{Main|Culture of ancient Rome}}

[[File:Altrömische Wandmalerei in der Villa of P. Fannius Synistor, Wandmalerei-Detail nach Bühnenmanie, Boscoreale, Campaia.jpg|thumb|upright|[[Cityscape]] from the [[Villa Boscoreale]] (60s AD)]]

===City and country===
The city was viewed as fostering civilization by being "properly designed, ordered, and adorned".{{r|n=Potter2009_192|r={{harvp|Potter|2009|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=g4ZmqsyC5kEC&pg=PA192 192]}}.}} Augustus undertook a vast building programme in Rome, supported public displays of art that expressed imperial ideology, and [[14 regions of Augustan Rome|reorganized the city]] into neighbourhoods ''([[vicus|vici]])'' administered at the local level with police and firefighting services.{{r|n=Rehak2006_4_8|r={{Cite book |last=Rehak |first=Paul |author-link=Paul Rehak |date=2006 |editor=John G. Younger |title=Imperium and Cosmos: Augustus and the Northern Campus Martius |publisher=[[University of Wisconsin Press|UWP]] |pages=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=uZKRVA331_gC&pg=PA4 4–8] |isbn=0299220109 }}}} A focus of Augustan monumental architecture was the [[Campus Martius]], an open area outside the city centre: the Altar of Augustan Peace ({{Lang|la|[[Ara Pacis Augustae]]}}) was located there, as was [[Obelisk of Montecitorio|an obelisk]] imported from Egypt that formed the pointer (''[[gnomon]]'') of a [[Solarium Augusti|horologium]]. With its public gardens, the Campus was among the most attractive places in Rome to visit.{{r|Rehak2006_4_8}}

City planning and urban lifestyles was influenced by the Greeks early on,{{sfnp|Stambaugh|1988|pp=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=k0mZufizhH0C&pg=PA23 23 ff.], [https://books.google.ca/books?id=k0mZufizhH0C&pg=PA244 244]}} and in the Eastern Empire, Roman rule shaped the development of cities that already had a strong Hellenistic character. Cities such as [[Ancient Athens|Athens]], [[Aphrodisias]], [[Ephesus]] and [[Gerasa]] tailored city planning and architecture to imperial ideals, while expressing their individual identity and regional preeminence.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Raja |first=Rubina |author-link=Rubina Raja |date=2012 |title=Urban Development and Regional Identity in the Eastern Roman Provinces 50 BC–AD 250: Aphrodisias, Ephesos, Athens, Gerasa |publisher=[[Museum Tusculanum Press]] |pages=215–8 |isbn=9788763526067 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=0VK6uPyhFLAC }}{{br}}^ {{Cite book |last=Sperber |first=Daniel |author-link=Daniel Sperber |date=1998 |title=The City in Roman Palestine |publisher=[[OUP]] |isbn=019509882X |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FsLnCwAAQBAJ }}</ref>{{pn|date=September 2026}} In areas inhabited by Celtic-speaking peoples, Rome encouraged the development of urban centres with stone temples, forums, monumental fountains, and amphitheatres, often on or near the sites of preexisting walled settlements known as ''[[oppida]]''.{{sfnp|Stambaugh|1988|pp=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=k0mZufizhH0C&pg=PA252 252-3]}}{{r|n=Longfellow2011_1_2|r={{Cite book |last=Longfellow |first=Brenda |date=2011 |title=Roman Imperialism and Civic Patronage: Form, Meaning and Ideology in Monumental Fountain Complexes |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press|CUP]] |pages=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=jRNfu372CyQC&pg=PA1 1–2] |isbn=9780521194938 }}}}{{Efn|Julius Caesar first applied the Latin word ''oppidum'' to this type of settlement, and even called [[Avaricum]] ([[Bourges]], France), a center of the [[Bituriges Cubi|Bituriges]], an ''urbs'', "city". Archaeology indicates that ''oppida'' were centers of religion, trade (including import/export), and industrial production, walled for the purposes of defence, but they may not have been inhabited by concentrated populations year-round.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Harding |first=Dennis W. |author-link=Dennis Harding |date=2007 |title=The Archaeology of Celtic Art |publisher=[[Routledge]] |pages=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=dDV-AgAAQBAJ&pg=PA211 211–2] |isbn=9780415428668 }}{{br}}^ {{Cite book |last=Collis |first=John |author-link=John Collis |date=2000 |chapter='Celtic' Oppida |editor-last=Hansen |editor-first=Mogens Herman |editor-link=Mogens Herman Hansen |title=A Comparative Study of Thirty City-state Cultures. An Investigation |location=[[Copenhagen]] |publisher=C.A. Reitzels |pages=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=8qvY8pxVxcwC&pg=PA229 229–38] |isbn=8778761778 }}{{br}}^ {{Cite book |editor-last1=Arnold |editor-first1=Bettina |editor-last2=Gibson |editor-first2=D. Blair |date=1995 |title=Celtic Chiefdom, Celtic State: The Evolution of Complex Social Systems in Prehistoric Europe |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press|CUP]] |page=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=eVz2NDNoD3oC&pg=PA61 61] |isbn=0521585791 }}</ref>}} Urbanization in Roman Africa expanded on Greek and Punic coastal cities.{{r|Stambaugh1988_253}}

[[File:Baños Romanos, Bath, Inglaterra, 2014-08-12, DD 39-41 HDR.JPG|thumb|left|[[Roman Baths (Bath)|Aquae Sulis]] in [[Bath, Somerset|Bath]], England: architectural features above the level of the pillar bases are a later reconstruction.]]
The network of cities ({{Lang|la|[[coloniae]]}}, ''[[municipia]]'', ''[[civitates]]'' or in Greek terms ''[[poleis]]'') was a primary cohesive force during the Pax Romana.{{sfnp|Millar|1983|p=76}} Romans of the 1st and 2nd centuries were encouraged to "inculcate the habits of peacetime".{{r|Potter2009_192}}.{{sfnp|Virgil's_Aeneid||loc=Book [https://classics.mit.edu/Virgil/aeneid.6.vi.html VI], 852}} As the classicist [[Clifford Ando]] noted:
