{{Blockquote|Most of the cultural [[wikt:appurtenance|appurtenances]] popularly associated with imperial culture—[[Religion in ancient Rome|public cult]] and its [[ludi|games]] and [[epulones|civic banquets]], competitions for artists, speakers, and athletes, as well as the funding of the great majority of public buildings and public display of art—were financed by private individuals, whose expenditures in this regard helped to justify their economic power and legal and provincial privileges.{{sfnp|Potter|2009|pp=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=g4ZmqsyC5kEC&pg=PA185 185–6]}}}}

[[File:Ostia-Toilets.JPG|thumb|Public toilets (''latrinae'') from [[Ostia Antica]]]]
In the city of Rome, most people lived in multistory apartment buildings (''[[Insula (building)|insulae]]'') that were often squalid firetraps. Public facilities—such as baths (''[[thermae]]''), toilets with running water (''latrinae''), basins or elaborate fountains (''[[nymphaeum|nymphea]]'') delivering fresh water,{{r|Longfellow2011_1_2}} and large-scale entertainments such as [[chariot races]] and [[gladiator|gladiator combat]]—were aimed primarily at the common people.{{sfnp|Wilson-Jones|2003}}{{pn|date=September 2026}}

The public baths served hygienic, social and cultural functions.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Evans |first=Harry B. |date=1997 |orig-date=1994 |title=Water Distribution in Ancient Rome: The Evidence of Frontinus |publisher=[[University of Michigan Press|UMP]] |pages=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=hYIVlENKMD4C&pg=PA9 9–10] |isbn=0472084461 }}</ref> Bathing was the focus of daily socializing.{{sfnp|Peachin|2011|loc=([[Garrett G. Fagan]], Socializing at the Baths), p. [https://books.google.ca/books?id=RDSI1V12ueIC&pg=PA366 366]}} Roman baths were distinguished by a series of rooms that offered communal bathing in three temperatures, with amenities that might include an [[palaestra|exercise room]], [[sudatorium|sauna]], [[Exfoliation (cosmetology)|exfoliation]] spa, [[sphaeristerium|ball court]], or outdoor swimming pool. Baths had [[hypocaust]] heating: the floors were suspended over hot-air channels.{{r|n=Fagan2001_article|r={{Cite journal |last=Fagan |first=Garrett G. |author-link=Garrett G. Fagan |date=2001 |title=The Genesis of the Roman Public Bath: Recent Approaches and Future Directions |journal=American Journal of Archaeology |volume=105 |issue=3 |pages=403–426 |doi=10.2307/507363 |jstor=507363 |s2cid=31943417 |url=http://www.arch.mcgill.ca/prof/sijpkes/aaresearch-2012/in-extremis-file/Roman-Baths-origin.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210224182626/http://www.arch.mcgill.ca/prof/sijpkes/aaresearch-2012/in-extremis-file/Roman-Baths-origin.pdf |archive-date=24 February 2021 |access-date=12 January 2017 }}}} Public baths were part of urban culture [[List of Roman public baths|throughout the provinces]], but in the late 4th century, individual tubs began to replace communal bathing. Christians were advised to go to the baths only for hygiene.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Ward |first=Roy Bowen |date=April 1992 |title=Women in Roman Baths |journal=Harvard Theological Review |volume=85 |issue=2 |pages=125–47 |doi=10.1017/S0017816000028820 |jstor=1509900 |s2cid=161983440 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1509900 }}</ref>

[[File:Ricostruzione del giardino della casa dei vetii di pompei (mostra al giardino di boboli, 2007) 01.JPG|thumb|left|Reconstructed peristyle garden based on the [[House of the Vettii]]]]
Rich families from Rome usually had two or more houses: a townhouse (''[[domus]]'') and at least one luxury home (''[[Roman villa|villa]]'') outside the city. The ''domus'' was a privately owned single-family house, and might be furnished with a private bath (''balneum''),{{r|Fagan2001_article}} but it was not a place to retreat from public life.{{sfnp|Clarke|1991|pp=1–2}} Although some neighbourhoods show a higher concentration of such houses, they were not segregated enclaves. The ''domus'' was meant to be visible and accessible. The atrium served as a reception hall in which the ''[[paterfamilias]]'' (head of household) met with [[Patronage in ancient Rome|clients]] every morning.{{r|Rehak2006_4_8}} It was a centre of family religious rites, containing a [[lararium|shrine]] and [[Roman funerals and burial#Funerary art|images of family ancestors]].{{sfnp|Clarke|1991|pp=11–2}} The houses were located on busy public roads, and ground-level spaces were often rented out as shops (''[[taberna]]e'').{{sfnp|Clarke|1991|p=2}} In addition to a kitchen garden—windowboxes might substitute in the ''insulae''—townhouses typically enclosed a [[peristyle]] garden.<ref>{{harvp|Stambaugh|1988|pp=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=k0mZufizhH0C&pg=PA144 144, 147]}}. ^ {{harvp|Clarke|1991|pp=12, 17, 22 ff}}.</ref>

The villa by contrast was an escape from the city, and in literature represents a lifestyle that balances intellectual and artistic interests (''[[otium]]'') with an appreciation of nature and agriculture.{{sfnp|Gazda|1991|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=5zTTX_mvVowC&pg=PA9 9]}} Ideally a villa commanded a view or vista, carefully framed by the architectural design.{{sfnp|Clarke|1991|p=19}}

Augustus' programme of urban renewal, and the growth of Rome's population to as many as one million, was accompanied by nostalgia for rural life. Poetry idealized the lives of farmers and shepherds. Interior decorating often featured painted gardens, fountains, landscapes, vegetative ornament,{{sfnp|Clarke|1991|p=19}} and animals, rendered accurately enough to be identified by species.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Feemster Jashemski |first1=Wilhelmina |last2=Meyer |first2=Frederick G. |date=2002 |title=The Natural History of Pompeii |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press|CUP]] |page=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=3xfjyTqqR7IC&pg=PA404 404] |isbn=0521800544}}</ref> On a more practical level, the central government took an active interest in supporting [[Agriculture in ancient Rome|agriculture]].{{sfnp|Morris|Scheidel|2009|p=191}} Producing food was the priority of land use.{{sfnp|Bowman|Garnsey|Rathbone|2000|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=mhNUGgG2eacC&pg=PA679 679]}} Larger farms (''[[latifundia]]'') achieved an [[economy of scale]] that sustained urban life.{{sfnp|Morris|Scheidel|2009|p=191}} Small farmers benefited from the development of local markets in towns and trade centres. Agricultural techniques such as [[crop rotation]] and [[selective breeding]] were disseminated throughout the Empire, and new crops were introduced from one province to another.{{sfnp|Morris|Scheidel|2009|pp=195–6}}

[[File:Sale bread MAN Napoli Inv9071 n01.jpg|thumb|upright|Bread stall, from a Pompeiian wall painting]]
Maintaining an affordable food supply to the city of Rome had become a major political issue in the late Republic, when the state began to provide a grain dole ([[Cura Annonae]]) to citizens who registered for it{{sfnp|Morris|Scheidel|2009|p=191}} (about 200,000–250,000 adult males in Rome).{{efn|Morris & Scheidel (2009) estimate that the surplus of wheat from the province of Egypt alone could meet and exceed the needs of the city of Rome and the provincial armies.{{sfnp|Morris|Scheidel|2009|p=191}}}} The dole cost at least 15% of state revenues,{{sfnp|Morris|Scheidel|2009|p=191}} but improved living conditions among the lower classes,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Wiseman |first=T. P. |author-link=T. P. Wiseman |date=2012 |title=The Census in the First Century B.C |journal=Journal of Roman Studies |volume=59 |issue=1/2 |pages=59–75 |doi=10.2307/299848 |jstor=299848 |s2cid=163672978 |url=https://doi.org/10.2307/299848 }}</ref> and subsidized the rich by allowing workers to spend more of their earnings on the wine and olive oil produced on estates.{{sfnp|Morris|Scheidel|2009|p=191}} The grain dole also had symbolic value: it affirmed the emperor's position as universal benefactor, and the right of citizens to share in "the fruits of conquest".{{sfnp|Morris|Scheidel|2009|p=191}} The ''annona'', public facilities, and spectacular entertainments mitigated the otherwise dreary living conditions of lower-class Romans, and kept social unrest in check. The satirist [[Juvenal]], however, saw "[[bread and circuses]]" (''panem et circenses'') as emblematic of the loss of republican political liberty:<ref>{{Cite book |last=Keane |first=Catherine |date=2006 |title=Figuring Genre in Roman Satire |publisher=[[OUP]] |pages=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=cBfiBwAAQBAJ&pg=PA36 36] |isbn=9780195183306 }}{{br}}^ {{Cite book |last=Köhne |first=Eckhart |date=2000 |chapter=Bread and Circuses: The Politics of Entertainment |editor-last1=Köhne |editor-first1=Eckhart |editor-last2=Ewigleben |editor-first2=Cornelia |editor-link2=Cornelia Ewigleben |title=Gladiators and Caesars: The Power of Spectacle in Ancient Rome |publisher=[[University of California Press|UCP]] |page=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=5pzs975hnpoC&pg=PA8 8] |isbn=9780520227989 }}</ref>

{{Blockquote|The public has long since cast off its cares; the people that once bestowed commands, consulships, legions and all else, now meddles no more and longs eagerly for just two things — Bread and Games!{{sfnp|Juvenal's Satires||loc=Book IV -  [https://archive.org/details/juvenalpersiuswi00juveuoft/juvenalpersiuswi00juveuoft/page/198/mode/2up X.77-81 (p. 199)]}}}}

===Health and disease===
{{Further|Disease in Imperial Rome|Antonine plague|Plague of Cyprian}}
[[Epidemics]] were common in the ancient world, and occasional [[pandemic]]s in the Empire killed millions. The Roman population was unhealthy. About 20 percent—a large percentage by ancient standards—lived in cities, Rome being the largest. The cities were a "demographic sink": the death rate exceeded the birth rate and constant immigration was necessary to maintain the population. Average lifespan is estimated at the mid-twenties, and perhaps more than half of children died before reaching adulthood. Dense urban populations and [[Sanitation in ancient Rome|poor sanitation]] contributed to disease. Land and sea connections facilitated and sped the transfer of infectious diseases across the empire's territories. The rich were not immune; only two of emperor Marcus Aurelius's fourteen children are known to have reached adulthood.{{sfnp|Harper|2019|pp=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=cOslDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA10 10], [https://books.google.ca/books?id=cOslDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA30 30–1], [https://books.google.ca/books?id=cOslDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA67 67–91]}}

The importance of a good diet to health was recognized by medical writers such as [[Galen]] (2nd century). Views on nutrition were influenced by beliefs like [[humoral theory]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Grant |first=Mark |date=2000 |title=Galen on Food and Diet |publisher=[[Routledge]] |pages=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=tyip3Kf68TYC&pg=PA7 7, 11] |isbn=0415232333 }}</ref> A good indicator of nutrition and disease burden is average height: the average Roman was shorter in stature than the population of pre-Roman Italian societies and medieval Europe.<ref>{{harvp|Harper|2019|pp=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=cOslDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA75 75–9]}}.{{br}}^ {{Cite journal |last1=Koepke |first1=Nikola |last2=Baten |first2=Jörg |author-link2=Jörg Baten |date=April 2005 |orig-date=2003 |title=The biological standard of living in Europe during the last two millennia |journal=European Review of Economic History |volume=9 |issue=1 |pages=61–95 |doi=10.1017/S1361491604001388 |jstor=41378413 |hdl-access=free |hdl=10419/47594 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/41378413 }}</ref>

===Food and dining===

{{Main|Food and dining in the Roman Empire}}

{{See also|Ancient Roman cuisine|Ancient Rome and wine}}
[[File:Still life Tor Marancia Vatican.jpg|thumb|[[Still life]] on a 2nd-century [[Roman mosaic]]]]

Most apartments in Rome lacked kitchens, though a charcoal [[brazier]] could be used for rudimentary cookery.<ref>{{harvp|Stambaugh|1988|pp=144, [https://books.google.ca/books?id=k0mZufizhH0C&pg=PA178 178]}}.{{br}}^ {{Cite book |last=Hinds |first=Kathryn |date=2010 |title=Everyday Life in the Roman Empire |publisher=[[Marshall Cavendish]] |page=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=pNIbYdAkFt4C&pg=PA90 90] |isbn=9780761444848 }}</ref> Prepared food was sold at pubs and bars, inns, and food stalls (''[[taberna]]e'', ''cauponae'', ''[[popina]]e'', ''[[thermopolia]]'').{{sfnp|Holleran|2012|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=oO7NwmbyxwAC&pg=PA136 136 ff]}} [[Carryout]] and restaurants were for the lower classes; [[fine dining]] appeared only at dinner parties in wealthy homes with a [[chef]] (''archimagirus'') and kitchen staff,{{sfnp|Gagarin|2010|p=299}} or banquets hosted by social clubs (''[[collegia]]'').<ref>{{Cite book |last=Faas |first=Patrick |date=2005 |orig-date=1994 |title=Around the Roman Table: Food and Feasting in Ancient Rome |publisher=[[University of Chicago Press|UCP]] |page=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=YXGlAr17oekC&pg=PA29 29] |isbn=0226233472 }}</ref>

Most Romans consumed at least 70% of their daily [[calorie]]s in the form of cereals and [[legumes]].{{r|n=BowmanEtall2000_681|r={{harvp|Bowman|Garnsey|Rathbone|2000|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=mhNUGgG2eacC&pg=PA681 681]}}.}} ''[[Puls (food)|Puls]]'' (pottage) was considered the food of the Romans,<ref>{{harvp|Pliny's Natural History||loc=Vol. 4 - Book XVIII.19, p. [https://archive.org/details/57011150RX4.nlm.nih.gov/page/30/mode/1up 30-1]}}.{{br}}^ {{harvp|Gowers|2003|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=yPwSuAA4BvEC&pg=PA17 17]}}.{{br}}^ {{harvp|Gagarin|2010|p=198}}.</ref> and could be elaborated to produce dishes similar to [[polenta]] or [[risotto]].{{sfnp|Stambaugh|1988|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=k0mZufizhH0C&pg=PA144 144]}} Urban populations and the military preferred bread.{{r|BowmanEtall2000_681}} By the reign of [[Aurelian]], the state had begun to distribute the ''annona'' as a daily ration of bread baked in state factories, and added [[olive oil]], wine, and pork to the dole.<ref>{{harvp|Morris|Scheidel|2009|p=191}}. ^ {{harvp|Stambaugh|1988|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=k0mZufizhH0C&pg=PA146 146]}}. ^ {{harvp|Holleran|2012|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=oO7NwmbyxwAC&pg=PA134 134]}}.</ref>

Roman literature focuses on the dining habits of the upper classes,{{r|n=Potter2009_354|r={{harvp|Potter|2009|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=g4ZmqsyC5kEC&pg=PA354 354]}}.}} for whom the evening meal (''[[cena]]'') had important social functions.{{sfnp|Potter|2009|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=g4ZmqsyC5kEC&pg=PA356 356]}} Guests were entertained in a finely decorated dining room (''[[triclinium]]'') furnished with couches. By the late Republic, women dined, reclined, and drank wine along with men.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Roller |first=Matthew B. |date=2006 |title=Dining posture in ancient Rome: bodies, values, and status |publisher=[[Princeton University Press|PUP]] |pages=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=m0NYvESG3zAC&pg=PA96 96 ff.] |isbn=9780691124575 }}</ref> The poet Martial describes a dinner, beginning with the ''gustatio'' ("tasting" or "appetizer") salad. The main course was [[goat meat|kid]], beans, greens, a chicken, and leftover ham, followed by a dessert of fruit and wine.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Alcock |first=Joan P. |author-link=Joan P. Alcock |date=2006 |title=Food in the Ancient World |publisher=[[Greenwood Publishing Group]] |page=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=tOXEEAAAQBAJ&pg=PA184 184] |isbn=0313330034 }}</ref> Roman "[[foodie]]s" indulged in [[wild game]], [[fowl]] such as [[peacock]] and [[flamingo]], large fish ([[mullet (fish)|mullet]] was especially prized), and [[shellfish]]. Luxury ingredients were imported from the far reaches of empire.<ref>{{harvp|Suetonius' The Lives of the Caesars|loc=''Vitellius'', Book VII [https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Suetonius/12Caesars/Vitellius*.html#13.2 13.2], (vol. II p. [https://archive.org/details/suetonius-lives-of-the-caesars-with-an-english-translation-by-j.-c.-rolfe-pp-1004/page/266/mode/2up 267])}}.{{br}}^ {{harvp|Gowers|2003|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=yPwSuAA4BvEC&pg=PA20 20]}}.</ref> A book-length collection of Roman recipes is attributed to [[Apicius]], a name for several figures in antiquity that became synonymous with "[[gourmet]]".<ref>{{Cite book |last=Kaufman |first=Cathy K. |date=2001 |chapter=Remembrance of Meals Past: Cooking by Apicius' Book |editor-last=Walker |editor-first=Harlan |title=Food and the Memory. Proceedings of the Oxford Symposium on Food and Cookery 2000 |publisher=[[Prospect Books]] |pages=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=uRap8THh29gC&pg=PA125 125 ff.] |isbn=1903018161 }}</ref>

Refined cuisine could be moralized as a sign of either civilized progress or decadent decline.{{sfnp|Gagarin|2010|p=201}} Most often, because of the importance of landowning in Roman culture, produce—cereals, legumes, vegetables, and fruit—were considered more civilized foods than meat. The [[Mediterranean diet|Mediterranean staples]] of [[Sacramental bread|bread]], [[Sacramental wine|wine]], and [[chrism|oil]] were [[sanctification|sacralized]] by Roman Christianity, while Germanic meat consumption became a mark of [[Germanic paganism|paganism]].{{r|n=FlandrinMontanari1999_1657|r={{Cite book |editor-last1=Flandrin |editor-first1=Jean-Louis |editor-link1=Jean-Louis Flandrin |editor-last2=Montanari |editor-first2=Massimo |editor-link2=Massimo Montanari |date=1999 |orig-date=1996 |title=Food: A Culinary History from Antiquity to the Present |others= English edition by Albert Sonnenfeld |publisher=[[Columbia University Press|CUP]] |pages=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=FnwnXzTRA44C&pg=PA165 165–7] |isbn=0231111541 }}}} Some philosophers and Christians resisted the demands of the body and the pleasures of food, and adopted [[fasting]] as an ideal.{{sfnp|Potter|2009|pp=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=g4ZmqsyC5kEC&pg=PA365 365–6]}} Food became simpler in general as urban life in the West diminished and trade routes were disrupted;{{r|FlandrinMontanari1999_1657}} the Church formally discouraged [[gluttony]],{{sfnp|Bowersock|Brown|Grabar|1999|p=[https://archive.org/details/lateantiquitygui00bowe/page/455/mode/1up 455]}} and hunting and [[pastoralism]] were seen as simple and virtuous.{{r|FlandrinMontanari1999_1657}}

{{Anchor|spectacle}}<!-- [[Public spectacle]] redirects here -->

===Spectacles===
{{See also|Ludi|Chariot racing|Recitationes}}
[[File:Winner of a Roman chariot race.jpg|thumb|left|A victor in his [[quadriga|four-horse chariot]]]]
When [[Juvenal]] complained that the Roman people had exchanged their political liberty for "bread and circuses", he was referring to the state-provided grain dole and the ''circenses'', events held in the entertainment venue called a ''[[circus (building)|circus]]''. The largest such venue in Rome was the [[Circus Maximus]], the setting of [[horse races]], [[chariot races]], the equestrian [[Lusus Troiae|Troy Game]], staged beast hunts (''[[venatio]]nes''), athletic contests, [[gladiator|gladiator combat]], and [[historical re-enactment]]s. From earliest times, several [[Roman festivals|religious festivals]] had featured games (''[[ludi]]''), primarily horse and chariot races (''ludi circenses'').<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Beard |first1=Mary |author-link1=Mary Beard (classicist) |last2=North |first2=John |last3=Price |first3=Simon |author-link3=Simon Price (classicist) |date=2002 |orig-date=1998 |title=Religions of Rome |volume=1 - A History |edition=Reprinted |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press|CUP]] |page=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=2rtaTFYuM3QC&pg=PA66 66] |isbn=0521316820 }}</ref> The races retained religious significance in connection with agriculture, [[initiation]], and the cycle of birth and death.{{Efn|Such as the [[Consualia]] and the [[October Horse]] sacrifice.<ref>{{harvp|Humphrey|1986|pp=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=couetXBQO9AC&pg=PA544 544], 558}}.{{br}}^ {{Cite book |last=Bouché-Leclercq |first=Auguste |author-link=Auguste Bouché-Leclercq |date=1886 |title=Manuel des Institutions Romaines |lang=fr |publisher=[[Hachette Livre|Hachette]] |page=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=rRxbRHi7-40C&pg=PA549 549] }}{{br}}^ {{Cite book |last=Saladino |first=Vincenzo |chapter=Purificazione - Mondo Romano |date=2004 |editor=Pierre Müller |title=Thesaurus Cultus et Rituum Antiquorum (ThesCRA) |volume=2 -Purification - Initiation - Heroization - Apotheosis - Banquet - Dance - Music - Cult Images |lang=en, it, de, fr |publisher=[[Getty Publications]] |page=[https://archive.org/details/thes-cra/Thesaurus%20Cultus%20et%20Rituum%20Antiquorum%20%28ThesCRA%29/ThesCRA_II_Textus/page/n52/mode/1up 83] |display-editors=etal }}</ref>}}

Under Augustus, public entertainments were presented on 77 days of the year; by the reign of Marcus Aurelius, this had expanded to 135.{{sfnp|Dyson|2010|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=wfN5dd5wbWgC&pg=PA240 240]}} Circus games were preceded by an elaborate parade (''[[pompa circensis]]'') that ended at the venue.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Versnel |first=H. S. |author-link=H. S. Versnel |date=1970 |title=Triumphus: An Inquiry into the Origin, Development and Meaning of the Roman Triumph |publisher=[[Brill Publishers|Brill]] |pages=96–7 |isbn= 90-04-02325-9|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=pPjBSq2jCrcC }}</ref> Competitive events were held also in smaller venues such as the [[Roman amphitheater|amphitheatre]], which became the characteristic Roman spectacle venue, and stadium. Greek-style athletics included [[Stadion (running race)|footraces]], [[Ancient Greek boxing|boxing]], [[Greek wrestling|wrestling]], and the [[pancratium]].{{sfnp|Potter|Mattingly|1999|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=HPjqJWakX7IC&pg=PA242 242]}} Aquatic displays, such as the mock sea battle (''[[naumachia]]'') and a form of "water ballet", were presented in engineered pools.{{sfnp|Potter|Mattingly|1999|pp=235–6}} State-supported [[#Performing arts|theatrical events]] (''[[ludi scaenici]]'') took place on temple steps or in grand stone theatres, or in the smaller enclosed theatre called an ''[[Odeon (building)|odeon]]''.{{sfnp|Potter|Mattingly|1999|pp=223–4}}

Circuses were the largest structure regularly built in the Roman world.{{r|n=PotterMattingly1999_303|r={{harvp|Potter|Mattingly|1999|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=HPjqJWakX7IC&pg=PA303 303]}}.}} The Flavian Amphitheatre, better known as the [[Colosseum]], became the regular arena for blood sports in Rome.{{r|n=Humphrey1986_1_3|r={{harvp|Humphrey|1986|pp=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=couetXBQO9AC&pg=PA1–3 1-3]}}.}} Many [[Roman amphitheatres]], [[Circus (building)#List of Roman circuses|circuses]] and [[Roman theatre (structure)|theatres]] built in cities outside Italy are visible as ruins today.{{r|Humphrey1986_1_3}} The local ruling elite were responsible for sponsoring spectacles and arena events, which both enhanced their status and drained their resources.{{r|Coleman1990}} The physical arrangement of the amphitheatre represented the order of Roman society: the emperor in his opulent box; senators and equestrians in reserved advantageous seats; women seated at a remove from the action; slaves given the worst places, and everybody else in-between.<ref>{{harvp|Edmondson|1996|pp=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=PpKop1jpJnwC&pg=PA73 73–4], [https://books.google.ca/books?id=PpKop1jpJnwC&pg=PA106 106]}}.{{br}}^ {{harvp|Auguet|2012|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=A-3BfuPqIeUC&pg=PA54 54]}}.{{br}}^ {{harvp|McClelland|2007|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=OUuQAgAAQBAJ&pg=PA67 67]}}.</ref> The crowd could call for an outcome by booing or cheering, but the emperor had the final say. Spectacles could quickly become sites of social and political protest, and emperors sometimes had to deploy force to put down crowd unrest, most notoriously at the [[Nika riots]] in 532.{{r|n=Dyson2010_238_9|r={{harvp|Dyson|2010|pp=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=wfN5dd5wbWgC&pg=PA238 238–9]}}.}}<ref>{{harvp|Gagarin|2010|p=85}}.{{br}}^ {{harvp|Humphrey|1986|p=461}}. ^ {{harvp|McClelland|2007|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=OUuQAgAAQBAJ&pg=PA61 61]}}.</ref>

[[File:Bestiarii.jpg|thumb|The [[Zliten mosaic]], from a dining room in present-day Libya, depicts a series of arena scenes: from top, musicians; gladiators; [[bestiarii|beast fighters]]; and convicts [[damnatio ad bestias|condemned to the beasts]]<ref>{{Cite book |last=Wiedemann |first=Thomas |author-link=Thomas Ernst Josef Wiedemann |date=2014 |orig-date=1992 |title=Emperors and Gladiators |publisher=[[Routledge]] |page=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=pr2JAgAAQBAJ&pg=PA15 15] |isbn=9780415121644 }}</ref>]]
The chariot teams were known by the colours they wore, with the two main teams being [[Blues and Greens in the Byzantine Empire|the Blues and the Greens]]. Fan loyalty was fierce and at times erupted into [[sports riots]].<ref>{{harvp|Gagarin|2010|p=85}}.{{br}}^ {{harvp|Humphrey|1986|pp=459, 461, 512, [https://books.google.ca/books?id=couetXBQO9AC&pg=PA630 630–1]}}.{{br}}^ {{harvp|Dyson|2010|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=wfN5dd5wbWgC&pg=PA237 237]}}.</ref> Racing was perilous, but charioteers were among the most celebrated and well-compensated athletes.{{sfnp|Dyson|2010|p=238}} Circuses were designed to ensure that no team had an unfair advantage and to minimize collisions (''naufragia''),<ref>{{harvp|Humphrey|1986|pp=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=couetXBQO9AC&pg=PA18 18–21]}}. ^ {{harvp|Gagarin|2010|p=84}}.</ref> which were nonetheless frequent and satisfying to the crowd.<ref>{{harvp|Auguet|2012|pp=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=A-3BfuPqIeUC&pg=PA131 131–2]}}. ^ {{harvp|Potter|Mattingly|1999|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=HPjqJWakX7IC&pg=PA237 237]}}</ref> The races retained a magical aura through their early association with [[chthonic]] rituals: circus images were considered protective or lucky, [[curse tablet]]s have been found buried at the site of racetracks, and charioteers were often suspected of sorcery.{{r|Dyson2010_238_9}}<ref>{{harvp|Auguet|2012|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=A-3BfuPqIeUC&pg=PA144 144]}}.{{br}}^ {{harvp|Dickie|2003|pp=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=TgfLYOZPHSMC&pg=PA282 282–7]}}.{{br}}^ {{Cite book |last=D'Ambra |first=Eva |date=2007 |chapter=Racing with Death: Circus Sarcophagi and the Commemoration of Children in Roman Italy |editor-last1=Cohen |editor-first1=Ada |editor-link=Ada Cohen |editor-last2=Rutter |editor-first2=Jeremy B. |title=Constructions of Childhood in Ancient Greece and Italy |series=[[Hesperia (journal)|Hesperia Supplement 41]] |publisher=[[ASCSA]] |pages=348–[https://books.google.ca/books?id=bJG0g_M854AC&pg=PA349 9] |isbn=9780876615416 }}{{br}}^ {{harvp|Rüpke|2011|p=289}}.</ref> Chariot racing continued into the Byzantine period under imperial sponsorship, but the decline of cities in the 6th and 7th centuries led to its eventual demise.{{r|PotterMattingly1999_303}}

The Romans thought gladiator contests had originated with [[funeral games]] and [[Sacrifice in ancient Roman religion|sacrifices]]. Some of the earliest [[List of Roman gladiator types|styles of gladiator fighting]] had ethnic designations such as "[[Thraex|Thracian]]" or "Gallic".{{r|Potter2009_354}}{{r|n=Edwards2007_59|r={{harvp|Edwards|2007|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=Ioq6GmIyLQIC&pg=PA59 59]}}.}}{{sfnp|Potter|Mattingly|1999|p=305}} The staged combats were considered {{Lang|la|munera}}, "services, offerings, benefactions", initially distinct from the festival games (''ludi'').{{r|Edwards2007_59}}{{sfnp|Potter|Mattingly|1999|p=305}} To mark the opening of the Colosseum, [[Titus]] presented [[Inaugural games of the Flavian Amphitheatre|100 days of arena events]], with 3,000 gladiators competing on a single day.{{r|Humphrey1986_1_3}}{{Sfnp|Dio's Roman History||loc=Vol. 8, [https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Cassius_Dio/66*.html#25 Epitome of Book 66, 25] (pp. 311-3)}}{{r|n=Edwards2007_55|r={{harvp|Edwards|2007|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=Ioq6GmIyLQIC&pg=PA55 55]}}.}} Roman fascination with gladiators is indicated by how widely they are depicted on mosaics, wall paintings, lamps, and in graffiti.{{sfnp|Edwards|2007|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=Ioq6GmIyLQIC&pg=PA49 49]}} Gladiators were trained combatants who might be slaves, convicts, or free volunteers.{{sfnp|Edwards|2007|p=50}} Death was not a necessary or even desirable outcome in matches between these highly skilled fighters, whose training was costly and time-consuming.{{r|Edwards2007_55}}<ref>{{harvp|Potter|Mattingly|1999|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=HPjqJWakX7IC&pg=PA307 307]}}.{{br}}^ {{harvp|McClelland|2007|loc=p. [https://books.google.ca/books?id=OUuQAgAAQBAJ&pg=PA66 66], citing, among others, {{harvp|Junkelmann|2000|p=194}}}}.</ref> By contrast, ''noxii'' were convicts sentenced to the arena with little or no training, often unarmed, and with no expectation of survival; physical suffering and humiliation were considered appropriate [[retributive justice]].{{r|Coleman1990}} These executions were sometimes staged or ritualized as re-enactments of [[Greek mythology|myths]], and amphitheatres were equipped with elaborate [[stagecraft|stage machinery]] to create special effects.{{r|Coleman1990}}<ref>{{harvp|Suetonius' The Lives of the Caesars|loc=''Nero'', Book VI [https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Suetonius/12Caesars/Nero*.html#12.2 12.2], (vol. II p. [https://archive.org/details/suetonius-lives-of-the-caesars-with-an-english-translation-by-j.-c.-rolfe-pp-1004/page/104/mode/2up 105])}}.{{br}}^ {{harvp|Edmondson|1996|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=PpKop1jpJnwC&pg=PA73 73]}}.</ref>

Modern scholars have found the pleasure Romans took in the "theatre of life and death"<ref>{{Cite book |editor-last1=McDonald |editor-first1=Marianne |editor-link1=Marianne McDonald |editor-last2=Walton |editor-first2=J. Michael |date=2007 |title=The Cambridge Companion to Greek and Roman Theatre |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press|CUP]] |page=8 |isbn=9780521542340 }}</ref> difficult to understand.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Kyle |first=Donald G. |date=2001 |orig-date=1998 |title=Spectacles of Death in Ancient Rome |edition=Reprinted |publisher=[[Routledge]] |page=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=1GYH63-fARUC&pg=PA8 8] |isbn=0415248426 }}{{br}}^ {{harvp|Edwards|2007|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=Ioq6GmIyLQIC&pg=PA63 63]}}.</ref> [[Pliny the Younger]] rationalized gladiator spectacles as good for the people, "to inspire them to face honourable wounds and despise death, by exhibiting love of glory and desire for victory".<ref>{{harvp|Pliny the Younger, Letters||loc=Panegyric, Vol. 2 Ch. 33.1 - p. [https://archive.org/details/letterspanegyric0002plin/page/393/mode/1up 393 (1969 ed.)]}}.{{br}}^ {{harvp|Edwards|2007|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=Ioq6GmIyLQIC&pg=PA52 52]}}.</ref> Some Romans such as [[Seneca the Younger|Seneca]] were critical of the brutal spectacles, but found virtue in the courage and dignity of the defeated fighter{{sfnp|Edwards|2007|pp=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=Ioq6GmIyLQIC&pg=PA66 66–7], 72}}—an attitude that finds its fullest expression with the [[Christian martyr|Christians martyred]] in the arena. Tertullian considered deaths in the arena to be nothing more than a dressed-up form of [[human sacrifice]].<ref>{{harvp|Tertullian's De spectaculis||at=[https://www.tertullian.org/anf/anf03/anf03-09.htm#P937_380057 Ch 12] (p. 263)}}.{{br}}^ {{harvp|Edwards|2007|pp=59–60}}{{br}}^ {{harvp|Potter|Mattingly|1999|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=HPjqJWakX7IC&pg=PA224 224]}}.</ref> Even [[acts of the martyrs|martyr literature]], however, offers "detailed, indeed luxuriant, descriptions of bodily suffering",{{sfnp|Edwards|2007|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=Ioq6GmIyLQIC&pg=PA212 212]}} and became a popular genre at times indistinguishable from fiction.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Bowersock |first=G.W. |author-link=Glen Bowersock |date=2002 |orig-date=1995 |title=Martyrdom and Rome |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press|CUP]] |pages=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=H7iTiK_kEkoC&pg=PA25 25–6] |isbn=0521530490 }}{{br}}^ {{harvp|Cavallo|Chartier|2003|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=gxOnGrlWIssC&pg=PA79 79]}}.{{br}}^ {{Cite book |last=Huber-Rebenich |first=Gerlinde |author-link=Gerlinde Huber-Rebenich |chapter=Hagiographic Fiction as Entertainment |date=2004 |orig-date=1999 |editor-last=Hofmann |editor-first=Heinz |title=Latin Fiction: The Latin Novel in Context |publisher=[[Routledge]] |pages=158–178 }}{{br}}^ {{Cite book |last1=Llewelyn |first1=S.R. |chapter=The Earliest Dated Reference to Sunday in the Papyri |last2=Nobbs |first2=A.M. |date=2002 |title=New Documents Illustrating Early Christianity |publisher=[[Wm. B. Eerdmans]] |page=109}}{{br}}^ {{Cite book |last=Hildebrandt |first=Henrik |date=2006 |chapter=Early Christianity in Roman Pannonia – Fact among Fiction? |editor1=F. Young |editor2=M. Edwards |editor3=P. Parvis |title=Studia Patristica |series=Volumes 39-43 - Papers Presented at the Fourteenth International Conference on Patristic Studies Held in Oxford 2003 |publisher=[[Peeters Publishers|Peeters]] |pages=59–64 }}{{br}}^ {{harvp|Ando|2000|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=BXqIG1NIU2IC&pg=PA382 382]}}.</ref>

===Recreation===
[[File:Villa Romana del Casale BW 2025-04-28 11-11-12.jpg|thumb|So-called "Bikini Girls" mosaic from the [[Villa del Casale]], [[Roman Sicily]], 4th century]]

The singular ''[[Ludus (ancient Rome)|ludus]]'', "play, game, sport, training", had a wide range of meanings such as "word play", "theatrical performance", "board game", "primary school", and even "gladiator training school" (as in ''[[Ludus Magnus]]'').<ref>{{Cite book |editor-last=Bryan-Brown |editor-first=A.N. |date=1968 |title=Oxford Latin Dictionary |publisher=[[Clarendon Press]] |pages=[https://archive.org/details/oxford-latin-dictionary/page/1048/mode/1up 1048–9]}}{{br}}^ {{harvp|Habinek|2005|pp=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=Em_XpAvaT9oC&pg=PA5 5], 143}}.</ref> Activities for children and young people in the Empire included [[Hoop rolling#Ancient Rome and Byzantium|hoop rolling]] and [[knucklebones]] (''astragali'' or "jacks"). Girls had [[doll]]s made of wood, [[terracotta]], and especially [[Ivory carving|bone and ivory]].{{sfnp|Rawson|2003|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=Ah9XwjhyM8gC&pg=PA128 128]}} Ball games include [[Trigon (game)|trigon]] and [[harpastum]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=McDaniel |first=Walton Brooks |date=1906 |title=Some Passages concerning Ball-Games |journal=Transactions and Proceedings of the American Philological Association |volume=37 |pages=121–134 |doi=10.2307/282704 |jstor=282704 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/282704 }}</ref> People of all ages played [[board game]]s, including ''[[latrunculi]]'' ("Raiders") and ''[[XII scripta]]'' ("Twelve Marks").<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Austin |first=R.G. |date=October 1934 |title=Roman Board Games. I |journal=Greece and Rome |volume=4 |issue=10 |pages=24–34 |doi=10.1017/S0017383500002941 |s2cid=162861940 |url=https://doi.org/10.1017/S0017383500002941}}</ref> A game referred to as ''alea'' (dice) or ''tabula'' (the board) may have been similar to [[backgammon]].<ref name="games">{{Cite journal |last=Austin |first=R. G. |date=February 1935 |title=Roman Board Games. II |journal=Greece and Rome |volume=4 |issue=11 |pages=76–82 |doi=10.1017/S0017383500003119 |s2cid=248520932 |url=https://doi.org/10.1017/S0017383500003119 }}</ref> [[Dice|Dicing]] as a form of gambling was disapproved of, but was a popular pastime during the festival of the [[Saturnalia]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Moritz |first=Ludwig A. |title="dicing" |date=1999 |url=https://archive.org/details/the-oxford-classical-dictionary-simon-hornblower-antony-spawforth-1999_202405/page/464/mode/1up}} In {{harvp|''The Oxford Classical Dictionary'' (1999)||}}.</ref>

After adolescence, most physical training for males was of a military nature. The [[Campus Martius]] originally was an exercise field where young men learned horsemanship and warfare. Hunting was also considered an appropriate pastime. According to [[Plutarch]], conservative Romans disapproved of Greek-style athletics that promoted a fine body for its own sake, and condemned [[Quinquennial Neronia|Nero's efforts to encourage Greek-style athletic games]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Eyben |first=Emiel |date=1993 |orig-date=1977 |title=Restless Youth in Ancient Rome |publisher=[[Routledge]] |pages=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=Pv2JAgAAQBAJ&pg=PA79 79–82], [https://books.google.ca/books?id=Pv2JAgAAQBAJ&pg=PA110 110] |isbn=0415043662 }}</ref> Some women trained as gymnasts and dancers, and a rare few as [[female gladiators]]. The "Bikini Girls" mosaic shows young women engaging in routines comparable to [[rhythmic gymnastics]].{{Efn|Scholars are divided in their relative emphasis on the athletic and dance elements of these exercises: {{Cite journal |last=Lee |first=H. |date=1984 |title=Athletics and the Bikini Girls from Piazza Armerina |journal=Stadion |volume=10 |pages=45–75}} sees them as gymnasts, while Torelli thinks they are dancers at the games.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Torelli |first=Mario |author-link=Mario Torelli |date=1988 |chapter=Piazza Armerina: Note di iconologia |editor-last=Rizza |editor-first=G. |title=La Villa romana del Casale di Piazza Armerina |publisher=Catania |page=152}}</ref>}}{{sfnp|Dunbabin|2006|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=U7Uu_Dq8oY4C&pg=PA133 133]}} Women were encouraged to maintain health through activities such as playing ball, swimming, walking, or reading aloud (as a breathing exercise).<ref>{{Cite book |last=Hanson |first=Ann Ellis |author-link=Ann Ellis Hanson |date=1991 |chapter=The Restructuring of Female Physiology at Rome |title=Les écoles médicales à Rome |publisher=Université de Nantes |pages=260, 264 |postscript=,}} particularly citing the ''Gynecology'' of [[Soranus of Ephesus|Soranus]].</ref>

===Clothing===
{{Main|Clothing in ancient Rome}}

{{Further|Roman hairstyles|Roman jewelry|Cosmetics in ancient Rome}}
[[File:Statua togata, dalla palestra di foruli (civitatomassa), età claudia.jpg|thumb|left|upright|Togate statue in the [[Museo Archeologico Nazionale d'Abruzzo]]]]
In a status-conscious society like that of the Romans, clothing and personal adornment indicated the etiquette of interacting with the wearer.{{sfnp|Gagarin|2010|p=230}} Wearing the correct clothing reflected a society in good order.{{r|n=Coon1997_57_8|r={{Cite book |last=Coon |first=Lynda L. |date=1997 |title=Sacred Fictions: Holy Women and Hagiography in Late Antiquity |publisher=[[University of Pennsylvania Press|UPP]] |pages=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=w_1-t_K2ZuMC&pg=PA57 57–8] |isbn=0812233719 }}}} There is little direct evidence of how Romans dressed in daily life, since portraiture may show the subject in clothing with symbolic value, and surviving textiles are rare.{{r|n=Bieber1959_374ff|r={{Cite journal |last=Bieber |first=Margarete |author-link=Margarete Bieber |date=1959 |title=Roman Men in Greek Himation ''(Romani Palliati)'' a Contribution to the History of Copying |journal=Proceedings of the American Philosophical Society |volume=103 |issue=3 |pages=374–417 |jstor=985474 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/985474 }}}}<ref>{{harvp|Vout|1996|pp=206, 211}}. ^ {{Harvp|Métraux|2008|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=bYCCpqdgSAgC&pg=PA286 286]}}.</ref>

The [[toga]] was the distinctive national garment of the male citizen, but it was heavy and impractical, worn mainly for conducting political or court business and religious rites.{{r|Bieber1959_374ff}}{{sfnp|Vout|1996|p=216}} It was a "vast expanse" of semi-circular white wool that could not be put on and draped correctly without assistance.{{sfnp|Vout|1996|p=216}} The drapery became more intricate and structured over time.{{Sfnp|Métraux|2008|pp=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=bYCCpqdgSAgC&pg=PA282 282-3]}} The ''toga praetexta'', with a [[Tyrian purple|purple or purplish-red]] stripe representing inviolability, was worn by children who had not come of age, [[Executive magistrates of the Roman Empire|curule magistrates]], and state priests. Only the emperor could wear an all-purple toga (''toga picta'').<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Cleland |first1=Liza |last2=Davies |first2=Glenys |last3=Llewellyn-Jones |first3=Lloyd |author-link3=Lloyd Llewellyn-Jones |date=2007 |title=Greek and Roman Dress from A to Z |publisher=[[Routledge]] |page=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=nTaCAgAAQBAJ&pg=PA194 194] |isbn=9780415226615 }}</ref>

Ordinary clothing was dark or colourful. The basic garment for all Romans, regardless of gender or wealth, was the simple sleeved [[tunic]], with length differing by wearer.{{sfnp|Gagarin|2010|p=231}} The tunics of poor people and labouring slaves were made from coarse wool in natural, dull shades; finer tunics were made of lightweight wool or linen. A man of the senatorial or equestrian order wore a tunic with two purple stripes (''clavi'') woven vertically: the wider the stripe, the higher the wearer's status.{{sfnp|Gagarin|2010|p=231}} Other garments could be layered over the tunic. Common male attire also included cloaks, and in some regions, [[braccae|trousers]].{{sfnp|Vout|1996|p=218}} In the 2nd century, emperors and elite men are often portrayed wearing the [[Pallium (Roman cloak)|pallium]], an originally Greek mantle; women are also portrayed in the pallium. [[Tertullian]] considered the pallium an appropriate garment both for Christians, in contrast to the toga, and for educated people.{{r|Coon1997_57_8}}{{r|Bieber1959_374ff}}<ref>[[Tertullian]], ''De Pallio'' 5.2.</ref>

Roman clothing styles changed over time.{{sfnp|Gagarin|2010|p=232}} In the [[Dominate]], clothing worn by both soldiers and bureaucrats became highly decorated with geometrical patterns, stylized plant motifs, and in more elaborate examples, human or animal figures.<ref>{{Cite book |last=D'Amato |first=Raffaele |date=2005 |title=Roman Military Clothing (3): AD 400–640 |publisher=[[Osprey Publishing|Osprey]] |pages=7–9 |isbn=184176843X }}</ref> Courtiers of the later Empire wore elaborate silk robes. The militarization of Roman society, and the waning of urban life, affected fashion: heavy military-style belts were worn by bureaucrats as well as soldiers, and the toga was abandoned,<ref>{{Cite book |last=Wickham |first=Chris |author-link=Chris Wickham |date=2009 |title=The Inheritance of Rome - A History of Europe from 400 to 1000 |publisher=[[Viking Press|Viking]] |page=[https://archive.org/details/isbn_9780670020980/page/106/mode/1up 106] |isbn=9780670020980 }}</ref> replaced by the pallium as a garment embodying social unity.{{sfnp|Vout|1996|p=217}}

==Arts==
{{Main|Roman art|Art collection in ancient Rome}}

[[ancient Greek art|Greek art]] had a profound influence on Roman art.{{sfnp|Kousser|2008|pp=4–5, 8}} [[Public art]]—including [[Roman sculpture|sculpture]], monuments such as [[List of Roman victory columns|victory columns]] or [[triumphal arch]]es, and the iconography on [[Roman currency|coins]]—is often analysed for historical or ideological significance.<ref>{{harvp|Kousser|2008|p=1}}. ^ {{harvp|Potter|2009|pp=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=g4ZmqsyC5kEC&pg=PA75 75–6]}}.</ref> In the private sphere, artistic objects were made for [[votum|religious dedications]], [[Roman funerals and burial|funerary commemoration]], domestic use, and commerce.{{sfnp|Gazda|1991|pp=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=5zTTX_mvVowC&pg=PA1 1–3]}} The wealthy advertised their appreciation of culture through artwork and [[decorative arts]] in their homes.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Zanker |first=Paul |author-link=Paul Zanker |date=1998 |orig-date=1995 |title=Pompeii: Public and Private Life |translator-last=Schneider |translator-first=Deborah Lucas |publisher=[[Harvard University Press|HUP]] |page=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=Z0y1aPzKgOEC&pg=PA189 189] |isbn=0674689674 }}</ref> Despite the value placed on art, even famous artists were of low social status, partly as they worked with their hands.{{sfnp|Gagarin|2010|pp=312–313}}

===Portraiture===
{{Main|Roman portraiture}}

{{Multiple image
| width  = 125
| footer = Two portraits {{Circa|130 AD}}: the empress [[Vibia Sabina]] (left); and the ''[[Antinous Mondragone]]''
| image1 = Busto de Vibia Sabina (M. Prado) 01.jpg
| image2 = Antinous Mandragone profil.jpg
}}

Portraiture, which survives mainly in sculpture, was the most copious form of imperial art. Portraits during the Augustan period utilize [[classicism|classical proportions]], evolving later into a mixture of realism and idealism.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Toynbee |first=Jocelyn M.C. |author-link=Jocelyn Toynbee |date=December 1971 |title=Roman Art (Helga von Heintze: Römische Kunst. 1969) |journal=The Classical Review |volume=21 |issue=3 |pages=439–442 |doi=10.1017/S0009840X00221331 |s2cid=163488573 |url=https://doi.org/10.1017/S0009840X00221331}}</ref> Republican portraits were characterized by [[verism]], but as early as the 2nd century BC, Greek [[heroic nudity]] was adopted for conquering generals.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Zanker |first=Paul |author-link=Paul Zanker |date=1990 |orig-date=1988 |title=The Power of Images in the Age of Augustus |translator-last=Shapiro |translator-first=Alan |publisher=[[University of Michigan Press|UMP]] |pages=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=pDc2fp73B2oC&pg=PA5 5 ff.] |isbn=0472081241 }}</ref> Imperial portrait sculptures may model a mature head atop a youthful nude or semi-nude body with perfect musculature.{{sfnp|Gagarin|2010|p=451}} Clothed in the toga or military regalia, the body communicates rank or role, not individual characteristics.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Fejfer |first=Jane |date=2008 |title=Roman Portraits in Context |publisher=[[Walter de Gruyter]] |page=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=VdVMMTGDzK4C&pg=PA10 10] |isbn=9783110186642 }}</ref>

Portraiture in painting is represented primarily by the [[Fayum mummy portrait]]s, which evoke Egyptian and Roman traditions of commemorating the dead with realistic painting. Marble portrait sculpture were painted, but traces have rarely survived.{{sfnp|Gagarin|2010|p=453}}

===Sculpture and sarcophagi===
{{Main|Roman sculpture|Ancient Roman sarcophagi}}

[[File:10 2023 - Palazzo Altemps, Roma, Lazio, 00186, Italia - Sarcofago Grande Ludovisi (Grande Ludovisi sarcophagus) - Arte Romana - Photo Paolo Villa FO232047 ombre gimp bis.jpg|thumb|left|upright=1.2|On the [[Ludovisi sarcophagus]]]]

Examples of Roman sculpture survive abundantly, though often in damaged or fragmentary condition, including freestanding statuary in marble, bronze and [[Ancient Roman pottery#Terracotta figurines|terracotta]], and [[relief]]s from public buildings and monuments. Niches in amphitheatres were originally filled with statues,<ref>{{Harvp|Kousser|2008|p=13}}{{br}}^ {{Cite book |last=Strong |first=Donald E. |author-link=Donald Emrys Strong |date=1988 |orig-date=1976 |title=Roman Art |edition=2nd |publisher=[[Yale University Press|YUP]] |page=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=mFTYtEWy_H4C&pg=PA11 11] |isbn=0300052936 }}</ref> as were [[Roman gardens|formal garden]]s.{{sfnp|Gagarin|2010|pp=274–275}} Temples housed cult images of deities, often by famed sculptors.{{sfnp|Gagarin|2010|p=242}}

Elaborately carved marble and limestone [[sarcophagi]] are characteristic of the 2nd to 4th centuries.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Newby |first=Zahra |author-link=Zahra Newby |date=2011 |chapter=Myth and Death: Roman Mythological Sarcophagi|editor-last1=Dowden |editor-first1=Ken |editor-link1=Ken Dowden |editor-last2=Livingstone |editor-first2=Niall |editor-link2= Niall Livingstone |title=A Companion to Greek Mythology |publisher=Wiley Blackwell |page=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=_XsN0O_BQ0cC&pg=PA303 301] |isbn=9781405111782 }}</ref> Sarcophagus relief has been called the "richest single source of Roman iconography",{{sfnp|Elsner|Huskinson|2011|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=pQjrqo62-IwC&pg=PA14 14]}} depicting [[classical mythology|mythological scenes]]{{sfnp|Elsner|Huskinson|2011|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=pQjrqo62-IwC&pg=PA12 12]}} or Jewish/Christian imagery{{sfnp|Elsner|Huskinson|2011|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=pQjrqo62-IwC&pg=PA1 1], 9}} as well as the deceased's life.
{{Clear}}

===Painting===
{{Main|Painting in ancient Rome}}

[[File:Zeffiro-e-clori---pompeii.jpg|thumb|''The Wedding of [[Zephyrus]] and [[Chloris]]'' (54–68 AD, [[Pompeian Styles|Pompeian Fourth Style]]) within painted architectural panels from the Casa del Naviglio]]

Initial Roman painting drew from [[Etruscan art#Wall-painting|Etruscan]] and [[Ancient Greek art#Painting|Greek]] models and techniques. Examples of Roman paintings can be found in [[List of ancient monuments in Rome#Palaces|palaces]], [[List of ancient monuments in Rome#Cemeteries|catacombs]] and [[Roman villa|villas]]. Much of what is known of Roman painting is from the interior decoration of private homes, particularly as preserved by the [[eruption of Vesuvius]]. In addition to decorative borders and panels with geometric or vegetative motifs, wall painting depicts scenes from mythology and theatre, landscapes and gardens, [[#Spectacles|spectacles]], everyday life, and [[Erotic art in Pompeii and Herculaneum|erotic art]].

===Mosaic===
{{Main|Roman mosaic}}

[[File:Neptune Roman mosaic Bardo Museum Tunis.jpg|thumb|''[[Neptune (mythology)|The Triumph of Neptune]]'' floor mosaic from [[Africa Proconsularis]] (present-day Tunisia){{sfnp|Gagarin|2010|p=463}}]]
[[Mosaic]]s are among the most enduring of Roman [[decorative arts]], and are found on floors and other architectural features. The most common is the [[opus tessellatum|tessellated mosaic]], formed from uniform pieces ''([[tessera]]e)'' of materials such as stone and glass.{{sfnp|Gagarin|2010|p=459}} ''[[Opus sectile]]'' is a related technique in which flat stone, usually coloured marble, is cut precisely into shapes from which geometric or figurative patterns are formed. This more difficult technique became especially popular for luxury surfaces in the 4th century (e.g. the [[Basilica of Junius Bassus]]).{{sfnp|Dunbabin|2006|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=U7Uu_Dq8oY4C&pg=PA254 254 ff]}}

[[Figurative art|Figurative]] mosaics share many themes with painting, and in some cases use almost identical [[Composition (visual arts)|compositions]]. Geometric patterns and mythological scenes occur throughout the Empire. In North Africa, a particularly rich source of mosaics, homeowners often chose scenes of life on their estates, hunting, agriculture, and local wildlife.{{sfnp|Gagarin|2010|p=463}} Plentiful and major examples of Roman mosaics come also from present-day Syria (particularly the [[Antioch mosaics]]<ref>{{Cite book |last=Belis |first=Alexis |date=2016 |chapter=Syria - Antioch and the Bath of Apolausis – History of the excavations |title=Roman Mosaics In The J. Paul Getty Museum |publisher=[[J. Paul Getty Museum]] |at=p. 43. See also [https://www.getty.edu/publications/romanmosaics/ www.getty.edu] |isbn=9781606064979 |chapter-url=https://archive.org/details/roman-mosaics-in-the-j.-paul-getty-museum-2016./page/43/mode/1up }}</ref>), Italy, southern France, Spain, and Portugal.

===Decorative arts===
{{Further|Ancient Roman pottery|Roman glass}}
[[Decorative arts]] for luxury consumers included fine pottery, silver and bronze vessels and implements, and glassware. Pottery manufacturing was economically important, as were the glass and metalworking industries. Imports stimulated new regional centres of production. Southern Gaul became a leading producer of the finer red-gloss pottery (''[[terra sigillata]]'') that was a major trade good in 1st-century Europe.{{sfnp|Gagarin|2010|p=202}} [[Glassblowing]] was regarded by the Romans as originating in Syria in the 1st century BC, and by the 3rd century, Egypt and the [[Rhineland]] had become noted for fine glass.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Butcher |first=Kevin |date=2003 |title=Roman Syria and the Near East |publisher=[[J. Paul Getty Museum]] |pages=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=YJPn3-rRjC0C&pg=PA201 201 ff.] |isbn=0892367156}}.{{br}}^  {{harvp|Bowman|Garnsey|Cameron|2005|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=MNSyT_PuYVMC&pg=PA421 421]}}.</ref>
<gallery mode="packed" heights="120">
File:Skyphos Boscoreale Louvre Bj2367.jpg|Silver [[skyphos|cup]], from the [[Boscoreale Treasure]] (early 1st century AD)
